items.title: Syllogism Rules, Venn Diagram Method and Possibility Cases
items.description: Learn syllogism for IBPS, SBI and SSC: all, some, no and only a few statements, Venn diagram method, either-or cases and possibility conclusions.
items.intro: Syllogism is a near-certain guest in the Reasoning section of IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO, SBI Clerk and RBI Grade B Phase I, usually as a set of three to five questions. SSC CGL and CHSL ask it less often, normally one question at a time. The questions look easy, which is the trap: most marks are lost by reading 'some' as 'all' or by missing an either-or pair. Once you draw the minimum Venn diagram for every statement, each question takes under 40 seconds.

concepts.heading: The four basic statements
concepts.text: 'All A are B' puts circle A fully inside B. 'Some A are B' means at least one A is a B, and it may even be that all A are B. 'No A is B' keeps the circles apart. 'Some A are not B' means at least one A lies outside B. Always draw the minimum overlap the statement forces, never more.

concepts.heading: Definite conclusions versus possibilities
concepts.text: A definite conclusion must be true in every diagram that satisfies the statements. A possibility conclusion ('All X being Y is a possibility') only needs one valid diagram where it is true without breaking any statement. So 'Some A are B is a possibility' is true when A and B are not forced apart, and false when a 'No' statement directly or indirectly separates them.

concepts.heading: Either-or pairs
concepts.text: When neither conclusion is definite on its own, check whether the two together cover every case. 'Some A are B' and 'No A is B' form a complementary pair, as do 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not B'. Both must have the same two terms, and neither may already follow. Then the answer is 'Either I or II follows'.

concepts.heading: Only a few
concepts.text: 'Only a few A are B' means some A are B and some A are not B. It therefore kills the possibility 'All A are B'. Many students miss this second half and wrongly mark 'All A being B is a possibility' as true.

shortcuts: Some + All gives Some: Some A are B, All B are C → Some A are C. But All + Some gives nothing: All A are B, Some B are C → no link between A and C.
All + No gives No: All A are B, No B is C → No A is C. That also means 'Some C are A is a possibility' is false.
Some + No gives 'Some ... not': Some A are B, No B is C → Some A are not C (not 'Some C are not A').
'Some' and 'No' conclusions can be reversed (Some A are B = Some B are A), but 'All' cannot: All mangoes are fruits does not mean all fruits are mangoes.
Before choosing either-or, confirm the pair uses the same subject and predicate and that neither part is already definite.

examples.question: Statements: All pens are books. Some books are bags. Conclusions: I. Some pens are bags. II. Some bags are books.
examples.solution: Draw pens inside books. The 'some' overlap between books and bags can sit in the part of books that has no pens, so I is not definite. II is just the reverse of 'Some books are bags', so it follows. Answer: only II follows.

examples.question: Statements: Some cups are plates. No plate is a spoon. Conclusions: I. Some cups are spoons. II. No cup is a spoon.
examples.solution: Cups that are plates cannot be spoons, but cups outside plates may or may not touch spoons. So neither I nor II is definite. They have the same terms and are complementary (some versus none). Answer: either I or II follows.

examples.question: Statements: All rivers are lakes. No lake is a pond. Conclusions: I. No river is a pond. II. Some ponds being rivers is a possibility.
examples.solution: Rivers sit inside lakes and lakes are fully separate from ponds, so rivers are separate from ponds too. I follows. Because the separation is forced, II cannot be a possibility. Answer: only I follows.

examples.question: Statements: Only a few teachers are writers. All writers are poets. Conclusions: I. Some teachers are poets. II. All teachers being poets is a possibility.
examples.solution: Teachers who are writers are also poets, so I follows. For II, the teachers who are not writers can still be placed inside the poets circle without breaking any statement, so II is a valid possibility. Answer: both follow. Note that 'All teachers being writers' would not have been possible here.

practice: Statements: All coins are notes. No note is a cheque. Conclusions: I. No coin is a cheque. II. Some cheques are coins.
Coins lie inside notes and notes are fully separate from cheques, so no coin can be a cheque. II contradicts I, so only I follows.
Statements: Some apples are mangoes. All mangoes are grapes. Conclusions: I. Some apples are grapes. II. Some grapes are apples.
The apples that are mangoes are also grapes, so I follows. II is simply I reversed, and a 'some' statement can be reversed, so both follow.
Statements: All doors are windows. Some windows are walls. Conclusions: I. Some doors are walls. II. No door is a wall.
Neither conclusion is forced because the window-wall overlap may or may not include doors. The two conclusions use the same terms and are complementary, so either I or II follows.
Statements: No bat is a ball. All balls are stumps. Conclusions: I. Some stumps are not bats. II. All bats being stumps is a possibility.
Balls are stumps and are not bats, so those stumps are not bats; I follows. Bats outside balls can still sit inside stumps, so II is a valid possibility. Both follow.
Statements: Only a few cars are buses. No bus is a truck. Conclusions: I. Some cars are not trucks. II. All cars are trucks.
The cars that are buses can never be trucks, so some cars are definitely not trucks. That same fact makes 'All cars are trucks' false, so only I follows.
faqs: Is the Venn diagram method better than rules for syllogism?

For new-pattern questions with 'only a few' and possibility conclusions, the Venn diagram method is safer because you can test each case visually. Rules are faster for simple two-statement questions. Most toppers learn a few rules for speed but always fall back on the minimum diagram when a conclusion looks doubtful.
How many syllogism questions come in IBPS and SBI prelims?

In recent prelims papers syllogism has usually appeared as a set of about three to five questions inside the 35-question Reasoning section, though the number varies by year and shift. Treat it as a scoring area: with practice the full set can be finished in about two minutes.

items.title: Inequality Reasoning: Direct, Coded and Either-Or Cases
items.description: Solve direct and coded inequality questions for bank exams: how to combine signs, when no relation exists and how to spot either-or conclusions quickly.
items.intro: Inequality questions appear in almost every IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO, SBI Clerk and RBI Grade B prelims paper, typically as a set of three to five questions. They come in two forms: direct statements like P > Q ≥ R, and coded statements where symbols such as @ or % stand for the signs. Both reward one skill — reading a chain correctly and knowing when two letters have no fixed relation. Accuracy matters more than speed here because the options are designed around typical mistakes.

concepts.heading: Combining signs along a chain
concepts.text: Two letters can be compared only if every sign between them points the same way. > with ≥ gives >, ≥ with ≥ gives ≥, and = keeps whatever the other sign is. So A > B ≥ C = D gives A > D. If any sign on the path points the other way, as in A > B < C, there is no definite relation between A and C.

concepts.heading: Either-or in inequalities
concepts.text: If the chain proves only X ≥ Y, then neither 'X > Y' nor 'X = Y' follows alone, but together they cover every case. That makes the answer 'Either I or II follows'. The same applies for X ≤ Y split into X < Y and X = Y. Either-or is never possible when the two letters have no relation at all.

concepts.heading: Coded inequalities
concepts.text: Here each symbol is defined, for example '@' means '>', '%' means '≥', '$' means '='. Convert the whole statement to real signs first, write it on your rough sheet, and only then read the conclusions. Trying to work directly with the symbols is the most common source of errors.

concepts.heading: Combined statements
concepts.text: Some questions give two or three separate statements, such as F ≤ G < H and H ≥ I > J. Join them through the common letter (H here) to form one chain before comparing. If there is no common letter, no relation can be built across the statements.

shortcuts: Look for the opposite-direction sign first. In P > Q < R, the moment you see > and < meeting at Q, mark 'no relation' between P and R.
'=' is neutral: A ≥ B = C behaves exactly like A ≥ C.
A strict sign anywhere in a same-direction chain makes the result strict: A ≥ B > C ≥ D gives A > D.
For either-or, the two conclusions must use the same pair of letters and one must be '>' while the other is '='.
In coded questions, rewrite all five symbols in a small table at the top of your rough sheet once; reuse it for the whole set.

examples.question: Statement: P > Q ≥ R = S < T. Conclusions: I. P > S. II. T > Q.
examples.solution: For I, the path P > Q ≥ R = S has signs in one direction with a strict sign, so P > S is true. For II, the path from Q to T reads Q ≥ R = S < T; the direction flips at S, so T and Q have no relation. Answer: only I follows.

examples.question: Statement: J ≥ K = L ≥ M. Conclusions: I. J > M. II. J = M.
examples.solution: The chain gives J ≥ M only. Neither J > M nor J = M is certain, but one of them must be true. Same letters, complementary signs, so either I or II follows.

examples.question: In a code, '@' means '>', '#' means '<', '$' means '=', '%' means '≥' and '&' means '≤'. Statement: M @ N $ O % P. Conclusions: I. M @ P. II. O @ P.
examples.solution: Decode: M > N = O ≥ P. For I, M > P is true, so M @ P follows. For II, we only know O ≥ P, so O > P is not definite. Answer: only I follows.

examples.question: Statements: F ≤ G < H; H ≥ I > J. Conclusions: I. G < I. II. H > J.
examples.solution: Join at H: F ≤ G < H ≥ I > J. G to I runs G < H ≥ I, which changes direction, so I does not follow. H to J runs H ≥ I > J, all one way with a strict sign, so H > J follows. Answer: only II follows.

practice: Statement: B ≥ C > D = E ≤ F. Conclusions: I. B > E. II. F > C.
B ≥ C > D = E gives B > E, so I follows. Between C and F the chain flips at E, so II has no definite relation.
Statements: K < L ≤ M; M = N > O. Conclusions: I. O < L. II. N > K.
Combined chain K < L ≤ M = N > O. N and K are linked one way with a strict sign, so N > K holds. L and O meet across a flip at N, so I is not definite.
Statement: R ≥ S = T ≥ U. Conclusions: I. R > U. II. R = U.
The chain gives only R ≥ U. Neither part is certain alone, but they are complementary with the same letters, so either I or II follows.
In a code, '@' means '≥', '#' means '<', '%' means '=', '&' means '>' and '$' means '≤'. Statement: G # H % J & K. Conclusions: I. G # J. II. K # H.
Decoded, the statement is G < H = J > K. So G < J is true, and since H = J > K, K < H is also true. Both conclusions follow.
Statements: P > Q < R; R ≥ S > T. Conclusions: I. Q > T. II. P > S.
Q to T runs Q < R ≥ S > T, which flips direction, so no relation. P to S runs P > Q < R, also a flip. Neither conclusion follows.
faqs: What does 'no relation' mean in an inequality question?

It means the given statements allow the two letters to be in any order. For example, in A > B < C, A could be bigger, smaller or equal to C depending on actual values. When two letters have no relation, no conclusion comparing them follows, and they cannot form an either-or pair either.
Should I memorise sign-combination tables for coded inequalities?

You only need two ideas: signs pointing the same way combine, and a strict sign makes the result strict. Instead of a big table, decode each coded statement into real signs on your rough sheet. This takes a few seconds and removes almost all symbol-confusion errors.

items.title: Coding-Decoding Tricks: Letter Shift, Opposites, Word Codes
items.description: Coding-decoding for bank and SSC exams: letter shifting, opposite letters, number coding, sentence-based word codes and mixed patterns, with worked examples.
items.intro: Coding-decoding is tested in IBPS and SBI prelims, RBI Grade B, and every SSC tier that has a reasoning paper. Bank exams prefer sentence-based 'new pattern' coding sets of three to five questions, while SSC asks single letter-shift or number-coding questions. The topic is very learnable because the patterns repeat: once you know alphabet positions by heart and can spot a reversed word, most questions fall in under a minute.

concepts.heading: Alphabet positions and opposites
concepts.text: Know A=1 to Z=26 forward and backward. Opposite letters always add to 27: A–Z, B–Y, M–N. A quick memory aid is EJOTY for 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. With these two facts you can decode most letter-based codes without writing the full alphabet.

concepts.heading: Letter shifting
concepts.text: Each letter moves forward or backward by a fixed number (+1, −2) or by a changing number (+1, +2, +3...). Compare the first two letters of the word and its code, then confirm the rule on the third letter before applying it to the new word.

concepts.heading: Reversal and mixed operations
concepts.text: Examiners combine steps: reverse the word, then shift each letter; or swap the first and second halves, then shift. If a simple shift does not fit, check whether the code read backwards matches the word shifted.

concepts.heading: Sentence (word) coding
concepts.text: Several sentences are coded word for word, but the code order is jumbled. Find the word common to two sentences and the code common to the same two sentences; they belong together. Continue by elimination. Bank exams often add a twist where each code is built from the first letter of the word plus a number.

concepts.heading: Number coding
concepts.text: A word may be coded as the sum, product or concatenation of letter positions. CAT as 24 means 3 + 1 + 20. Test the simplest operation (sum) first.

shortcuts: Opposite-letter check: if each pair of letter and code adds to 27, it is an opposite code. B(2) and Y(25) → 27.
If the code length equals the word length but the letters look unrelated, try reversing the code first.
In sentence coding, a word that appears in only one sentence cannot be fixed unless all other words of that sentence are decoded.
Write positions above letters for long words; it avoids counting errors under time pressure.
When the shift changes (+1, +2, +3), the code is usually built position by position, so write the increments under each letter.

examples.question: If MANGO is written as NBOHP, how is APPLE written in that code?
examples.solution: M→N, A→B, N→O, G→H, O→P: each letter moves +1. Apply to APPLE: A→B, P→Q, P→Q, L→M, E→F. Code: BQQMF.

examples.question: In a code, BANK is written as YZMP. How is LOAN written?
examples.solution: B(2)+Y(25) = 27, A(1)+Z(26) = 27, N(14)+M(13) = 27. It is an opposite-letter code. L→O, O→L, A→Z, N→M. LOAN = OLZM.

examples.question: 'sun rises early' is 'ka pi mo', 'early bird sings' is 'mo tu ra', and 'bird sun flies' is 'tu ka zo'. What is the code for 'rises'?
examples.solution: 'early' is common to sentences 1 and 2, as is 'mo', so early = mo. 'sun' is common to 1 and 3, as is 'ka', so sun = ka. The only code left in sentence 1 is 'pi', so rises = pi.

examples.question: If CAT is coded as 24, what is the code for DOG?
examples.solution: C(3) + A(1) + T(20) = 24, so the code is the sum of positions. D(4) + O(15) + G(7) = 26.

examples.question: If STOCK is written as LDPUT, how is BOND written?
examples.solution: Reverse STOCK to get KCOTS, then shift each letter +1: K→L, C→D, O→P, T→U, S→T = LDPUT. For BOND: reverse to DNOB, shift +1 to get EOPC.

practice: If FIRM is written as GJSN, how is BANK written in that code?
Each letter of FIRM moves one step forward in the alphabet. Applying +1 to B, A, N, K gives C, B, O, L, so the code is CBOL.
In a code where each letter is replaced by its opposite letter (A↔Z, B↔Y and so on), how is GOLD written?
Opposite letters add up to 27. G(7)→T(20), O(15)→L(12), L(12)→O(15), D(4)→W(23). The code is TLOW.
'loan rate high' is 'pa ki lo', 'rate cut soon' is 'ki mu ze', and 'soon loan approved' is 'ze pa ro'. What is the code for 'high'?
Rate = ki (common to sentences 1 and 2) and loan = pa (common to 1 and 3). The remaining code in the first sentence, lo, must stand for high.
If BAT is coded as 23, what is the code for CAR?
BAT gives 2 + 1 + 20 = 23, so letters are replaced by their positions and added. CAR gives 3 + 1 + 18 = 22.
If TRADE is written as FEBSU, how is PRICE written in that code?
TRADE reversed is EDART and each letter then moves +1 to give FEBSU. PRICE reversed is ECIRP; shifting each letter +1 gives FDJSQ.
faqs: How do I memorise alphabet positions quickly?

Learn the anchor letters E(5), J(10), O(15), T(20), Y(25) using the word EJOTY, then count one or two steps from the nearest anchor. Pair this with the rule that opposite letters add to 27. A week of five-minute daily drills is usually enough to make positions automatic.
Why do bank exams have sentence-based coding instead of letter shifts?

Sentence coding tests elimination and attention rather than simple counting, and it lets the examiner ask three or more questions from one set of statements. SSC still prefers single letter-shift questions. Practise both, but give extra time to sentence coding if you are targeting IBPS or SBI.

items.title: Blood Relations Reasoning: Family Tree Method and Codes
items.description: Blood relation questions for bank and SSC exams: family tree notation, pointing-to-photo puzzles, coded relations and maternal versus paternal traps.
items.intro: Blood relations appear in SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS almost every shift, and in IBPS, SBI and RBI prelims either as standalone questions or as a coded set of three. The concepts never change: generations, gender and marriage links. Mistakes come from rushing — assuming a person's gender from a name, or confusing 'my mother's only son' with a brother when the speaker could be that son. A neat family tree drawn in 15 seconds prevents both errors.

concepts.heading: Standard family tree notation
concepts.text: Use a square or '+' for male and a circle or '−' for female, a vertical line for parent–child, a horizontal line for siblings, and a double line for husband–wife. Put each generation on its own level. Drawing on levels shows at a glance whether the answer is grandfather (two levels up) or uncle (one level up, sideways).

concepts.heading: Never assume gender
concepts.text: A name like 'Kiran' or 'Ashu' could be male or female. If the question does not state gender, the answer may be 'cannot be determined' or a gender-neutral word like 'child' or 'sibling'. Options are often built around this trap.

concepts.heading: Maternal versus paternal
concepts.text: Relatives on the mother's side are maternal: mother's father is maternal grandfather, mother's brother is maternal uncle (mama). Father's side is paternal. Indian exams like asking this because Hindi words (chacha, mama, bua, mausi) make the difference natural for many candidates.

concepts.heading: Coded relations
concepts.text: Symbols are defined as relations, for example 'P × Q' means P is the mother of Q. Decode the expression link by link, from left to right, drawing as you go. Each new symbol adds one person to the tree, so the final relation is usually two or three links long.

shortcuts: 'My grandfather's only son' is the speaker's father; 'my mother's only daughter' is the speaker herself or her sister, depending on who is speaking.
In-laws: your spouse's brother is your brother-in-law, and so is your sister's husband.
When a statement says 'only son' or 'only daughter', it fixes one person uniquely; use that to collapse the tree.
Reading a chain like 'A is the brother of B, B is the daughter of C': A is C's child too, and A is male, so A is C's son.
Check the direction of the question: 'How is A related to B?' asks for A's relation, not B's.

examples.question: Pointing to a man, Riya says, 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' How is the man related to Riya?
examples.solution: Riya's grandfather's only son is Riya's father. The son of Riya's father is Riya's brother (Riya is female, so she cannot be that son). Answer: brother.

examples.question: A is the brother of B. B is the daughter of C. C is the husband of D. How is A related to D?
examples.solution: B is the daughter of C and D (C and D are married). A is B's brother, so A is also their child, and A is male. A is D's son.

examples.question: 'P × Q' means P is the mother of Q; 'P + Q' means P is the brother of Q; 'P − Q' means P is the father of Q. What does M × N + O − R show about M and R?
examples.solution: M is the mother of N. N is the brother of O, so M is O's mother too. O is the father of R. So M is R's father's mother: M is the paternal grandmother of R.

examples.question: Pointing to a woman, Arjun says, 'Her mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is the woman related to Arjun?
examples.solution: The only daughter of Arjun's mother is Arjun's sister (Arjun is male). The woman is his sister's daughter, so she is Arjun's niece.

practice: Pointing to a boy, Neha says, 'He is the son of my mother's only son.' How is the boy related to Neha?
Neha's mother's only son is Neha's brother, because Neha is female. The boy is her brother's son, which makes him Neha's nephew.
X is the sister of Y. Y is the father of Z. Z is the son of W, who is a woman. How is X related to W?
W is Z's mother and Y is Z's father, so W is Y's wife. X is Y's sister, which makes X the sister-in-law of W.
'A # B' means A is the wife of B; 'A @ B' means A is the son of B. If P @ Q # R, how is R related to P?
P is the son of Q, and Q is the wife of R. So R is Q's husband and P's father.
How is Rahul's father's only brother's wife related to Rahul?
Rahul's father's only brother is Rahul's paternal uncle. That uncle's wife is Rahul's aunt (chachi).
K is the father of L. L is the brother of M. M is the mother of N. How is K related to N?
M is a daughter of K, and N is M's child. K is the father of N's mother, so K is N's maternal grandfather.
faqs: What if the gender of a person is not given?

Do not assume it from the name. If the relation depends on gender, look for a gender-neutral option such as 'child' or 'sibling', or choose 'cannot be determined'. Examiners deliberately use names like Kiran and Ashu to test this.
Is it worth drawing a family tree for simple questions?

Yes. A three-person tree takes ten seconds and removes guesswork. For coded questions with three or four symbols, solving mentally is the main cause of wrong answers. Over a few weeks of practice your drawings become fast and compact.

items.title: Direction Sense Test: Turns, Distances and Shadow Questions
items.description: Direction sense questions made simple: left and right turns, shortest distance with Pythagoras, shadow problems and point-based direction puzzles.
items.intro: Direction sense questions appear regularly in SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS and in IBPS and SBI prelims, where the newer form is a point-based set ('A is 5 m east of B...') with three questions. Most problems need only two tools: tracking which way a person faces after each turn, and Pythagoras for the straight-line distance. Shadow questions add a small twist based on the position of the sun.

concepts.heading: The eight directions
concepts.text: North at the top, east on the right, south at the bottom, west on the left. The four corners are north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west. A person facing north has east on the right; a person facing south has east on the left. Always turn relative to the direction the person is facing.

concepts.heading: Turns in degrees
concepts.text: A right turn is 90° clockwise and a left turn is 90° anticlockwise. A 45° clockwise turn from north gives north-east. For multiple turns, add clockwise angles and subtract anticlockwise ones, then reduce modulo 360.

concepts.heading: Shortest distance
concepts.text: Net out all east–west movement and all north–south movement separately, then combine them with Pythagoras.

concepts.heading: Shadow rule
concepts.text: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the west. In the evening the sun is in the west and shadows fall to the east. At noon in India the shadow is very short and is generally ignored in these questions.

shortcuts: Treat the start as (0, 0); east is +x and north is +y. Add each leg as a coordinate change.
Common Pythagorean triples save time: 3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.
If the final x and y are both positive, the person is north-east of the start; both negative means south-west.
Three left turns equal one right turn, and two turns either way reverse the direction.
For shadow questions, first fix where the shadow points (west in the morning), then work out which side of the person that is.

examples.question: Sameer walks 6 km north, turns right and walks 8 km. How far and in which direction is he from the start?
examples.solution: After facing north, a right turn makes him face east. Position: 8 km east, 6 km north. Distance = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 km, towards the north-east.

examples.question: Pooja walks 5 km east, turns left and walks 3 km, turns left and walks 9 km, then turns left and walks 3 km. Where is she now?
examples.solution: East 5 → (5, 0). Left from east is north: (5, 3). Left from north is west, 9 km: (−4, 3). Left from west is south, 3 km: (−4, 0). She is 4 km west of the start.

examples.question: Early one morning Ravi stands facing a pole. The pole's shadow falls exactly to his right. Which direction is Ravi facing?
examples.solution: In the morning the sun is in the east, so the shadow points west. The shadow is on his right, so his right side is west. A person whose right is west is facing south.

examples.question: Point P is 4 m west of point Q. Point R is 3 m north of Q. What is the distance and direction of R from P?
examples.solution: Take Q at (0, 0). P is (−4, 0), R is (0, 3). From P, R is 4 m east and 3 m north. Distance = √(16 + 9) = 5 m, and R lies north-east of P.

practice: Anil walks 12 m south, turns left and walks 5 m. How far is he from his starting point?
Turning left while facing south makes him face east. He is 12 m south and 5 m east, so the distance is √(144 + 25) = 13 m.
A man faces north. He turns 90° clockwise, then 180° anticlockwise, then 45° clockwise. Which direction does he face now?
North plus 90° clockwise is east. Turning 180° anticlockwise from east gives west. A further 45° clockwise from west points north-west.
Kiran walks 10 km west, turns right and walks 4 km, then turns right again and walks 10 km. Where is Kiran from the start?
West 10, then right (north) 4, then right (east) 10. The east and west legs cancel, leaving Kiran 4 km north of the start.
In the evening, Meena stands so that her shadow falls directly behind her. Which direction is she facing?
In the evening the sun is in the west, so shadows fall towards the east. If the shadow is behind her, her back is to the east and she faces west.
Point M is 6 km east of point N. Point O is 8 km south of M. How far and in which direction is O from N?
O is 6 km east and 8 km south of N. The distance is √(36 + 64) = 10 km, and the direction is south-east.
faqs: How do I avoid left-right confusion while turning?

Write the current facing direction after every turn. Facing north, right is east; facing south, right is west; facing east, right is south; facing west, right is north. Writing one arrow per leg on your rough sheet is quicker than rotating mentally and avoids the most common mistake.
Do shadow questions consider noon?

Most exam questions use early morning or evening, when the sun is clearly in the east or west. At noon the shadow is directly below or very short in India, so questions usually avoid it. If a question mentions noon, read the options carefully for 'no shadow' or 'cannot be determined'.

items.title: Linear Seating Arrangement: Facing North, South and Mixed
items.description: Solve linear seating arrangement puzzles: facing north or south, mixed directions, case-based solving, and a fully worked seven-person row puzzle.
items.intro: Linear seating arrangement is one of the heaviest areas in bank exam reasoning. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims often carry one row-based puzzle of five questions, and the mains papers use double-row versions. IBPS and SBI Clerk prefer simpler single-row puzzles. The skill is not cleverness but order: fix definite information first, branch into cases only when forced, and know how left and right change with the direction people face.

concepts.heading: Left and right depend on facing direction
concepts.text: For people facing north (away from you, as you look at the page), their left is your left. For people facing south (towards you), their left is your right. In mixed-facing puzzles, mark each person's direction with an arrow before placing neighbours.

concepts.heading: Immediate versus 'second to the left'
concepts.text: 'Immediately to the left' means adjacent. 'Second to the left' means one person in between. 'To the left' alone means anywhere on that side. Misreading these is the biggest source of wrong rows.

concepts.heading: Definite clues first
concepts.text: Clues like 'sits at an extreme end', 'sits exactly in the middle' or 'third from the left end' fix a position. Place them first, then attach relative clues to them. Negative clues ('does not sit at an end') are used last, to kill cases.

concepts.heading: Case-making
concepts.text: When a clue allows two positions, draw both rows side by side and carry them forward together. Usually one case dies within two more clues. Writing cases neatly beats trying to hold them in memory.

shortcuts: Number seats 1 to n from the left end of the page. For north-facing people, 'k places to the right' means seat + k.
For south-facing people, 'k places to the right' means seat − k on your page numbering.
'Only two people sit between A and B' means their seat numbers differ by 3.
In a row of n people, the middle seat (odd n) is (n + 1) / 2; it is often a definite anchor.
If a question asks 'how many people sit between', subtract seat numbers and then subtract one.

examples.question: Seven friends A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a row facing north. G sits exactly in the middle. A sits immediately to the left of G. D sits at the right end. Only two people sit between C and E. C does not sit at an end. F is not an immediate neighbour of E. B sits somewhere to the right of E. Find the arrangement.
examples.solution: Seats 1–7 from the left. G = 4, A = 3, D = 7. C and E need seat numbers differing by 3, with C not at seat 1 or 7. Free seats are 1, 2, 5 and 6, so (C, E) is (2, 5) or (5, 2). If E = 2, B to the right of E and F not beside E leaves F at seat 1 next to E — not allowed. So C = 2, E = 5. B must be right of E, so B = 6 and F = 1. Row: F C A G E B D.

examples.question: In the row above, who sits second to the right of A, and how many people sit between F and B?
examples.solution: A is in seat 3; second to the right is seat 5, which is E. F is in seat 1 and B in seat 6, so 6 − 1 − 1 = 4 people sit between them.

examples.question: Five people sit in a row facing south. P sits at the extreme right end of the row (from P's own point of view). On the page, where should you draw P if you number seats from your left?
examples.solution: People facing south face you. Their right is your left. So P, at their extreme right, goes in seat 1 at your left end. Drawing this correctly first avoids reversing the entire arrangement later.

practice: Five persons J, K, L, M and N sit in a row facing north. L sits in the middle. K sits at the left end. M sits immediately to the right of L. N is not an immediate neighbour of K. Who sits at the right end?
L takes seat 3, K seat 1 and M seat 4. Seats 2 and 5 remain for J and N; N cannot sit next to K, so N is in seat 5 at the right end.
Six people sit in a row facing north. U is third from the left end and V sits second to the right of U. How many people sit to the right of V?
U is in seat 3, so V is in seat 5. In a row of six only seat 6 lies to the right of V, so exactly one person sits there.
Five people A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north. A sits at the right end. E sits immediately to the left of A. B sits second to the left of D. D does not sit at an end. Who sits in the middle?
A is in seat 5 and E in seat 4. D must be in seat 2 or 3 and B two seats to its left; only D = 3 with B = 1 works. C takes seat 2, so D sits in the middle.

Six people P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row facing north. P sits fourth to the left of Q. Q does not sit at the right end. R sits immediately to the right of Q. S does not sit at an end, and T sits second to the right of S. Who sits between S and T?
Q must be in seat 5 (seat 6 is ruled out), so P = 1 and R = 6. Seats 2, 3 and 4 remain; T = S + 2 gives S = 2 and T = 4, leaving U between them in seat 3.
Seven people sit in a row, all facing south. G sits at the extreme left end from G's own point of view, and H sits third to the right of G. Which seat does H occupy?
Counting in the row's own frame, G is at position 1 from the left and H is three places to the right, at position 4. In a row of seven, position 4 is the exact middle.
faqs: Why does my arrangement come out mirror-reversed?

Usually because some people face south and you placed them as if they faced north. Mark every person's facing direction before reading relative clues. For south-facing people, their left is your right, so 'to the left of A' moves towards your right side of the page.
How long should a linear seating puzzle take?

A five-question puzzle with seven or eight people typically takes six to eight minutes for a well-practised candidate in prelims, including answering the questions. If you are past ten minutes and still in three cases, it is often smarter to move on and return later.

items.title: Circular Seating Arrangement: Facing Centre and Outside
items.description: Circular seating arrangement explained: left is clockwise when facing the centre, opposite seats, mixed facing and a fully solved eight-person table puzzle.
items.intro: Circular seating puzzles are a staple of IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims, and simpler versions with five or six people appear in clerk exams and SSC. One puzzle generally carries five questions. The single fact that unlocks the topic is which way 'left' runs around the table. Once that is fixed, the method is the same as linear seating: anchor definite clues, branch when needed, and use negative clues to eliminate cases.

concepts.heading: Facing the centre
concepts.text: When people face the centre, a person's left is the clockwise direction around the table and their right is anticlockwise. Draw the circle, fix the first person at the bottom, and move clockwise for 'to the left'.

concepts.heading: Facing outside
concepts.text: When people face away from the centre, the directions reverse: left is anticlockwise and right is clockwise. In mixed puzzles, draw a small inward or outward arrow at each seat before applying relative clues.

concepts.heading: Opposite seats
concepts.text: At a table with an even number n of people, the person opposite sits n/2 places away in either direction. With eight people, opposite means four places away. With an odd number of people there is no exact opposite, so such clues appear only in even-sized puzzles.

concepts.heading: No fixed start
concepts.text: A circle has no ends, so you may place the first definite person anywhere. Choose the person mentioned most often in the clues as your anchor; it reduces redrawing.

shortcuts: With n people facing the centre, 'k to the right' is the same seat as 'n − k to the left'. In a group of eight, third to the right = fifth to the left.
'Second to the left of A' and 'second to the right of A' point to the same seat only when n = 4.
Neighbours are always the seats immediately on both sides; 'neighbour' does not depend on facing direction.
For square or rectangular tables, people at the corners and the middles of sides usually face the centre unless stated; treat the table like a circle of seats.
Use negative clues ('is not a neighbour of') at the very end to choose between surviving cases.

examples.question: Eight people A–H sit around a circular table facing the centre. B sits fourth to the right of A. C sits second to the right of A. D sits immediately to the right of B. E sits immediately to the left of C. F sits second to the left of D. G is an immediate neighbour of A. Find the arrangement and say who sits fourth to the right of F.
examples.solution: Fix A at seat 0 and number seats 0–7 going to the right (anticlockwise). B = 4 and C = 2. D = 5 (right of B). E = 1 (left of C). F = 5 − 2 = 3. Seats 6 and 7 remain for G and H. A's neighbours are seats 1 and 7; seat 1 is E, so G = 7 and H = 6. Going right from A: A, E, C, F, B, D, H, G. Fourth to the right of F (seat 3) is seat 7: G. Note that B and A are opposite each other, as 'fourth to the right' always gives the opposite seat in a group of eight.

examples.question: Six people R, P, Q, S, T and U sit around a circular table facing the centre. P sits second to the right of R. Q sits third to the right of P. S sits immediately to the left of Q. T is not an immediate neighbour of R. Who sits opposite R?
examples.solution: Place R at seat 0, numbering to the right. P = 2. Q = 5 (opposite P). S is immediately to the left of Q, so S = 4. Seats 1 and 3 remain. T cannot neighbour R, so T is not at seat 1; T = 3 and U = 1. Opposite R (three seats away) is seat 3: T. U sits between R and P.

examples.question: Five friends sit around a table facing the centre. Kunal sits second to the left of Isha. How many seats to the right of Isha is Kunal?
examples.solution: With five seats, two to the left equals 5 − 2 = 3 to the right. Kunal is third to the right of Isha.

practice: Five people A, B, C, D and E sit around a circular table facing the centre. B sits immediately to the right of A. C sits immediately to the left of A. D is an immediate neighbour of B. Who sits immediately to the left of C?
Going right from A: A, B, then D next to B, and C is just left of A. The order to the right is A, B, D, E, C, so E sits immediately to the left of C.

Eight people sit around a circular table facing the centre. Q sits fourth to the right of P. R sits immediately to the right of P. S sits immediately to the right of Q. T sits second to the right of R. U sits immediately to the left of P. Who sits fourth to the right of S?
Numbering seats to the right from P = 0 gives R = 1, T = 3, Q = 4, S = 5 and U = 7. Fourth to the right of S is seat (5 + 4) − 8 = 1, which is R.
Six people sit around a circular table facing the centre. How many places to the left of a person is the seat that is second to the right?
In a circle of six, moving two seats to the right reaches the same seat as moving 6 − 2 = 4 seats to the left.
Six people sit around a circular table facing away from the centre. Which direction around the table is a person's left?
For people facing the centre, left is clockwise. Facing outward reverses that, so a person's left becomes the anticlockwise direction around the table.
At a circular table with eight people facing the centre, how many seats away is the person sitting directly opposite you?
Opposite means halfway round the table. With eight seats that is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 places away in either direction.
faqs: Why is left clockwise when people face the centre?

Imagine standing at the bottom of the circle facing up towards the centre. Your left hand points towards the 9 o'clock side, and moving from 6 to 9 o'clock is clockwise. That is why, for centre-facing people, 'to the left' means moving clockwise around the table.
How do I handle puzzles where some people face outside?

Mark each person with an arrow pointing in or out. For an inward-facing person use left = clockwise; for outward-facing, left = anticlockwise. Apply each clue using the direction of the person named in that clue, not the person being placed.

items.title: Floor Puzzles in Reasoning: Step-by-Step Solving Method
items.description: Crack floor-based puzzles for IBPS and SBI exams: numbering floors, 'above' versus 'immediately above', building cases and a fully worked seven-floor puzzle.
items.intro: Floor puzzles ask you to place people on the floors of a building using clues such as 'lives immediately above' or 'only two people live between'. IBPS PO, SBI PO, IBPS Clerk and RBI Grade B prelims commonly include one floor or floor-and-flat puzzle carrying five questions, and mains papers add a second variable such as city or profession. The method is mechanical: a vertical table, definite clues first, then cases, then negative clues.

concepts.heading: Number from the bottom
concepts.text: The lowest floor is floor 1 unless the question says the ground floor is numbered 0. Write floors top to bottom in a column on your rough sheet, with the highest number at the top, exactly as a building looks. Read the first line of the puzzle carefully for 'ground floor' wording.

concepts.heading: Above, immediately above and between
concepts.text: 'Above' means any higher floor. 'Immediately above' means the very next floor. 'Only two people live between X and Y' means their floor numbers differ by three. 'X lives on an odd-numbered floor' cuts the options in half and is often the clue that kills a case.

concepts.heading: Floor-and-flat variants
concepts.text: Some puzzles have two flats per floor (flat A to the west, flat B to the east). Draw a grid with floors as rows and flats as columns. 'Same flat type' means same column; 'directly above' means same column, next row.

concepts.heading: Extra attributes
concepts.text: When each person also has a colour, city or job, add columns to the table. Never start a new table for the second attribute; keeping one table makes cross-clues ('the person who likes red lives above the doctor') easy to apply.

shortcuts: The top and bottom floors behave like the two ends of a row; clues tying someone to them are your anchors.
'Only two people between' in a seven-floor building, with one person on floor 7, puts the other on floor 4.
When a clue gives a range ('B lives above A'), hold it until a definite clue narrows it.
Use odd/even floor clues to eliminate cases rather than to place people first.
Before answering, re-read every clue once against the final table; it takes 20 seconds and catches slips.

examples.question: Seven people A–G live on a seven-floor building, one per floor (floor 1 is the lowest). D lives on the top floor. Only two people live between D and E. A lives immediately below E. B lives on an even-numbered floor above E. C lives on a floor below F. G does not live on floor 1 or 2. Find the arrangement.
examples.solution: D = 7. Two people between D and E puts E on floor 4. A = 3. B is above E on an even floor: 6. Floors 1, 2 and 5 remain for C, F and G. G is not on 1 or 2, so G = 5. C is below F, so C = 1 and F = 2. Building from the bottom: C, F, A, E, G, B, D.

examples.question: Using the building above, who lives between A and B, and how many floors above C does B live?
examples.solution: A is on floor 3 and B on floor 6, so E (4) and G (5) live between them. B is on floor 6 and C on floor 1, so B lives five floors above C.

examples.question: Six people live on floors 1–6. A lives on floor 2. B lives three floors above A. C lives immediately above B. D lives below A. E lives below F. Who lives on floor 4?
examples.solution: A = 2, B = 5, C = 6, and D must be on floor 1. Floors 3 and 4 remain for E and F. E is below F, so E = 3 and F = 4. F lives on floor 4.

practice: Five people P, Q, R, S and T live on floors 1 to 5 (1 is the lowest). R lives on floor 3. P lives immediately above R. T lives below R. Q does not live on floor 5 and lives below T. S lives above T. Who lives on the top floor?
R is on floor 3 and P on floor 4. T and Q must share floors 1 and 2 with Q below T, so Q = 1 and T = 2. Only floor 5 is left, which goes to S.
In a seven-floor building, D lives on floor 7 and exactly two people live between D and E. On which floor does E live?
Two people between them means their floor numbers differ by three. Since D is on the top floor, E must be on floor 7 − 3 = 4.
Six people live on floors 1–6. A lives on floor 2. B lives three floors above A. C lives immediately above B. D lives below A. E lives below F. Who lives immediately above E?
A = 2, B = 5, C = 6 and D = 1. E and F take floors 3 and 4 with E below F, so F lives immediately above E.
In a floor puzzle, 'X lives above Y' is given. What can you conclude without other clues?
X lives on the floor just above Y
X lives on the top floor
X's floor number is greater than Y's
Only one person lives between X and Y
'Above' without 'immediately' means any higher floor. It only tells you X's floor number is higher than Y's, not how many floors separate them.
Seven people live on floors 1–7. C lives on floor 1, F on floor 2, A on floor 3, E on floor 4, G on floor 5, B on floor 6 and D on floor 7. How many people live between F and G?
F is on floor 2 and G on floor 5. The floors between them are 3 and 4, occupied by A and E, so two people live between them.
faqs: What if the puzzle says the ground floor is numbered 0?

Then the lowest floor is 0 and the top floor of a seven-storey building is 6. Odd and even clues change accordingly, so re-label your table before placing anyone. This single detail flips many answers, which is why examiners include it.
Should I solve floor puzzles in the order the clues are given?

No. Scan all clues first and start with the definite ones (top floor, bottom floor, a fixed floor number). Then use clues linked to already-placed people. Use negative and range clues last to choose between cases.

items.title: Box and Stacking Puzzles: Method, Cases and Practice
items.description: Learn box-based (stacking) puzzles for bank exams: reading 'kept above', counting boxes between, handling cases and solving a six-box puzzle in full.
items.intro: Box puzzles are a variant of floor puzzles in which boxes are stacked one above another, often with an extra attribute like colour or number of items. They are common in IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims and mains, usually as a five-question set. The trickiest part is that clues are often tied to boxes that are themselves not yet placed, so neat case-making matters even more than in floor puzzles.

concepts.heading: Stack orientation
concepts.text: Unless stated otherwise, the bottom box is position 1. Draw the stack vertically with position 1 at the bottom. Some questions number from the top; read the first line before you draw.

concepts.heading: Boxes between
concepts.text: 'Two boxes are kept between P and T' means their positions differ by three, without telling you which is higher. That creates two cases (P lower or T lower). Write both and keep them until a clue removes one.

concepts.heading: Unknown-count stacks
concepts.text: Harder puzzles do not state how many boxes there are: 'Three boxes are kept between A and B, and A is the fourth box from the bottom.' Here you must work out the total from the clues. Keep the stack open at the top until all clues are used.

concepts.heading: Attribute clues
concepts.text: If boxes have colours or contain a number of items, make a second column. Clues like 'the green box is kept immediately below the box with 12 items' connect columns; apply them only once one side is fixed.

shortcuts: Place the box tied to the top or bottom first; it is the only true anchor in a stack.
'Immediately above' links two boxes as a single block; move the block together while testing cases.
When two cases survive, the question set usually contains a clue (often negative) that only one case passes — look for 'not' statements.
For unknown-count stacks, the answer to 'how many boxes are there' is fixed by the highest-placed box in the final case.
Count 'boxes between' as difference of positions minus one.

examples.question: Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U are kept one above another (position 1 is the bottom). Two boxes are kept between P and T. S is kept immediately above T. R is kept at the bottom. Q is kept above U but below T. Find the order.
examples.solution: R = 1. Q is below T and U is below Q, so at least R, U and Q sit under T, which makes T at least 4. S is directly above T, so T is 4 or 5. If T = 4, P would need position 1 or 7 to have two boxes between — both impossible. So T = 5, S = 6 and P = 2. U and Q take positions 3 and 4 with U below Q. Bottom to top: R, P, U, Q, T, S.

examples.question: In the stack above, how many boxes are kept between R and Q, and which box is immediately below T?
examples.solution: R is at 1 and Q at 4, so 4 − 1 − 1 = 2 boxes (P and U) are between them. Immediately below T (position 5) is Q (position 4).

examples.question: Six boxes G, H, J, K, L and M are stacked with position 1 at the bottom. K is third from the bottom. Only one box is kept between K and M. G is kept immediately above M. H is kept below K but not at the bottom. J is kept above L. Find the stack.
examples.solution: K = 3. One box between K and M puts M at 1 or 5. If M = 1, G = 2, and H (below K, not at the bottom) would need position 2 as well — a clash. So M = 5 and G = 6. H is below K and not at the bottom, so H = 2. Positions 1 and 4 remain; J must be above L, so L = 1 and J = 4. Bottom to top: L, H, K, J, M, G.

practice: Five boxes A, B, C, D and E are stacked, position 1 at the bottom. C is at the top. A is kept two positions below C. E is kept below A. B is not at the bottom. D is kept above A. Which box is at the bottom?
C = 5 and A = 3. D is above A, so D = 4. E is below A and B is not at the bottom, so E = 1 and B = 2.
In a stack of six boxes, Q is at position 4 and T is at position 5 from the bottom. How many boxes are kept between Q and T?
Positions 4 and 5 are adjacent, so Q is immediately below T and no box lies between them.
'Two boxes are kept between X and Y' in a stack where position 1 is the bottom. If X is at position 2, where is Y?
Positions must differ by three. Counting down from 2 gives −1, which does not exist, so Y must be at position 2 + 3 = 5.
Six boxes are stacked with R at the bottom, then P, U, Q, T and S in order upward. Which box is kept immediately above U?
Going upward the order is R, P, U, Q, T, S. The box directly above U, which is in position 3, is Q in position 4.
In a stack, the box with 12 items is kept immediately below the green box, and the green box is at position 4. Where is the box with 12 items?
'Immediately below' means the very next position downward. With the green box at position 4, the box with 12 items must be at position 3.
faqs: How are box puzzles different from floor puzzles?

The logic is the same vertical ordering, but box puzzles more often hide the total number of boxes and attach attributes like colour or item count to positions. That means more case-making and more cross-column clues. If you are strong at floor puzzles, box puzzles need only a few extra practice sets.
What should I do if both cases survive till the end?

Re-read the clues; usually one clue was applied loosely, often a 'not' clue or 'immediately'. If both cases genuinely satisfy every clue, check whether the question you are answering has the same answer in both. Exam setters ensure the asked questions are answerable.

items.title: Day, Week and Month Scheduling Puzzles Explained
items.description: Scheduling puzzles on days of the week and months for bank exams: 31-day months, 'before' versus 'immediately before', and two fully solved puzzles.
items.intro: Scheduling puzzles place people or events on days of a week, months of a year, or dates of a month. IBPS PO, SBI PO, IBPS Clerk and RBI Grade B prelims often include one such puzzle with five questions, and they appear in mains with a second attribute. They behave like linear arrangements, but the 'row' has a fixed natural order, and clues may use calendar facts such as the number of days in a month.

concepts.heading: Treat time as a numbered row
concepts.text: Monday to Sunday become 1 to 7; January to December become 1 to 12. 'Before' means a smaller number, 'after' a larger one, and 'immediately before' means the previous number. Write the row vertically with the earliest at the top so it reads like a timetable.

concepts.heading: Calendar facts examiners use
concepts.text: Months with 31 days: January, March, May, July, August, October and December. February has 28 or 29 days; April, June, September and November have 30. A clue such as 'R's exam is in a month with 31 days' among January–June leaves only January, March or May.

concepts.heading: Weeks that do not start on Monday
concepts.text: Some puzzles say the week starts on Sunday or that events happen only on weekdays. Fix the numbering accordingly before reading other clues. A wrong starting day shifts every 'first' and 'last' clue.

concepts.heading: Two events per slot
concepts.text: When two people share each day (morning and evening sessions), draw a grid of days by sessions. 'Same day' means the same row; 'immediately after' may mean the next session, so read how the puzzle defines order.

shortcuts: 'Only one person between J and L' on a five-day schedule means their day numbers differ by two.
Neither the first nor the last day can be 'immediately after' or 'immediately before' in both directions; use this to cut cases.
List the 31-day months on your rough sheet once if a puzzle mentions month lengths.
Pair clues like 'M is immediately after K' into a block of two; there are only a few positions such a block can occupy.
When a puzzle mentions the year, remember a leap year changes February only.

examples.question: J, K, L, M and O attend a training session, one on each day from Monday to Friday. J attends on Wednesday. Only one person attends between J and L. M attends on the day immediately after K. O attends before L. Find the schedule.
examples.solution: Number Monday–Friday as 1–5. J = 3. L is 1 or 5. If L = 1, O must be before Monday — impossible, so L = 5. The K–M block needs two consecutive free days: only Monday–Tuesday remain together, so K = 1, M = 2, and O = 4. Schedule: K, M, J, O, L.

examples.question: Six people P, Q, R, S, T and U have exams in different months from January to June. R's exam is in a month with 31 days. R's exam is two months after P's. T's exam is in June. S's exam is before Q's, and U's exam is in the month immediately after Q's. Find the order.
examples.solution: R must be in January, March or May, and P is two months earlier, so R = March with P = January, or R = May with P = March. T = June. Case R = May: January, February and April are free; the Q–U pair needs two consecutive months, so Q = January and U = February, leaving no month for S before Q. This case fails. Case R = March: February, April and May are free; Q = April and U = May form the pair, and S = February is before Q. Final order: P (Jan), S (Feb), R (Mar), Q (Apr), U (May), T (Jun).

examples.question: From the second schedule, how many people have exams between S and T?
examples.solution: S is in February and T in June. March, April and May lie between, held by R, Q and U. So three people have exams between them.

practice: Using the Monday–Friday schedule K, M, J, O, L, who attends the training immediately before L?
L attends on Friday. The day immediately before is Thursday, and the schedule places O on Thursday.
Which of these months has 31 days?
The 31-day months are January, March, May, July, August, October and December. September, June and November each have 30 days, so August is the answer.
Five people attend sessions Monday to Friday, one per day. A attends on Tuesday, and only one person attends between A and B. Which day is B's session?
With Monday–Friday as 1–5, A is day 2 and B must be day 2 + 2 = 4, because day 0 does not exist. Day 4 is Thursday.
Events are held on seven consecutive days of a week that starts on Sunday. An event held on the fourth day is held on which day?
With Sunday as day 1, Monday is day 2, Tuesday is day 3 and Wednesday is day 4.
In the January–June exam schedule P, S, R, Q, U, T, whose exam is in a 30-day month other than June?
Among January to May, only April has 30 days (February has 28 or 29). Q's exam is in April, so Q is the answer.
faqs: Do I need to memorise the number of days in every month?

Yes, it takes a few minutes and is used in both scheduling puzzles and calendar questions. The knuckle method works well: count months on your knuckles and the gaps between them; months on knuckles have 31 days, while months in the gaps have 30, except February.
How are scheduling puzzles different from linear seating?

The structure is the same, but the order is fixed by time, so there is no 'facing direction' trap. In return, examiners add calendar facts (month lengths, leap years, weekdays only) that you must apply correctly. Treat each day or month as a numbered seat and the method carries over directly.

items.title: Order and Ranking Questions: Formulas and Tricky Cases
items.description: Order and ranking for SSC and bank exams: position from both ends, persons between two people, interchange questions and minimum-number queue cases.
items.intro: Order and ranking is a short, formula-friendly topic that SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS ask in almost every paper, and that IBPS and SBI clerk prelims use for one or two quick questions or as part of a comparison puzzle (who is the tallest, the third heaviest and so on). It rewards a clear head about counting: whether a person is counted from both ends, and whether 'between' includes the two people named. Most questions take under 30 seconds once these rules are second nature.

concepts.heading: Position from both ends
concepts.text: If a person is p-th from the left and q-th from the right, the person is counted twice, so the total is p + q − 1. The same works for rank from top and bottom in a class. Rearranging gives the position from the other end: right = total − left + 1.

concepts.heading: People between two persons
concepts.text: Convert both positions to the same end, subtract and then subtract one more. If A is 8th from the left and B is 19th from the left, 19 − 8 − 1 = 10 people sit between them. If the positions overlap (A's position from the left is larger than B's), the persons are counted in the reverse order and the same subtraction applies.

concepts.heading: Interchange questions
concepts.text: When A and B swap places, A takes B's old position. So A's new position from the left is B's old position from the left. Combine that with B's known position from the right to find the total.

concepts.heading: Comparison ranking
concepts.text: Statements like 'P is taller than Q but shorter than S' build a chain. Write tallest to shortest in a vertical line and add each person as their position is fixed. Questions ask for the second tallest, the shortest and so on.

shortcuts: Left + right − 1 = total. 9th from the left and 14th from the right in a row means 22 people.
Position from the other end = total − position + 1. In a queue of 40, the 11th from the front is 30th from the back.
If a question says 'at least' or 'minimum number of people', test the overlapping case where the two people's positions cross over.
For interchange questions, write two lines: before and after. The person who moved inherits the other person's old number.
In comparison chains, a person 'taller than only one person' is second from the bottom.

examples.question: In a row, Rohit is 9th from the left end and 14th from the right end. How many people are in the row?
examples.solution: Rohit is counted in both positions, so total = 9 + 14 − 1 = 22.

examples.question: In a row, A is 10th from the left and B is 15th from the right. When they interchange positions, A becomes 18th from the left. How many people are in the row?
examples.solution: After the swap A occupies B's old seat, so B was 18th from the left. B was also 15th from the right. Total = 18 + 15 − 1 = 32.

examples.question: In a row of 30 students, P is 8th from the left and Q is 12th from the right. How many students sit between them?
examples.solution: Q from the left = 30 − 12 + 1 = 19. Students between = 19 − 8 − 1 = 10.

examples.question: In a queue, A is 7th from the front and B is 5th from the back. Exactly three people stand between A and B. What is the minimum number of people in the queue?
examples.solution: If A is ahead of B, the total is 7 + 3 + 5 = 15. But if B is ahead of A, B is at position 7 − 4 = 3 from the front. Being 5th from the back, the queue has 3 + 5 − 1 = 7 people, with A last. So the minimum is 7.

practice: Meera ranks 15th from the top and 21st from the bottom in her class. How many students are in the class?
Meera is counted in both ranks, so the class strength is 15 + 21 − 1 = 35 students.
In a row of 50 people, X is 20th from the left and Y is 18th from the right. How many people stand between X and Y?
Y's position from the left is 50 − 18 + 1 = 33. The number between them is 33 − 20 − 1 = 12.
Among P, Q, R, S and T, R is the tallest and T is the shortest. Q is taller than only T. P is shorter than S. Who is the third tallest?
Tallest to shortest: R first, T last, Q fourth because it is taller only than T. S is taller than P, so S is second and P is third.
In a row, M is 12th from the left and N is 9th from the right. They interchange places, and M becomes 20th from the left. How many people are in the row?
After the swap M is in N's old seat, so N was 20th from the left and 9th from the right. Total is 20 + 9 − 1 = 28.
Neeraj is 11th from the front in a queue of 40 people. What is his position from the back?
Position from the back equals total minus position from the front plus one, so 40 − 11 + 1 = 30th.
faqs: Why do we subtract one when adding positions from both ends?

Because the person is counted in both numbers. If Rohit is 9th from the left, he is included in those nine; if he is 14th from the right, he is included again. Adding 9 and 14 counts him twice, so we subtract one to get the true total of 22.
How do I handle 'at least how many people' questions?

Look for the arrangement where the two named people overlap, meaning the second person's position from the front comes before the first person's. That usually gives a much smaller total. Check both arrangements, and pick the smaller total only if every condition still holds.

items.title: Alphanumeric Series: Counting, Position and Symbol Rules
items.description: Alphanumeric series questions for IBPS and SBI clerk: position from the left and right, elements preceded or followed by symbols, and removal-based questions.
items.intro: Alphanumeric series questions give a line of letters, digits and symbols and ask you to count or locate elements under a condition. They are a favourite of IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and IBPS RRB style papers, and sometimes appear in PO prelims as a three-to-five-question set. Nothing here needs reasoning skill so much as disciplined counting. A clean method — numbering the series once and reusing it — turns this into one of the fastest scoring sets in the paper.

concepts.heading: Number the series once
concepts.text: Write small position numbers under every element before reading any question. Every later question ('7th from the left', '12th from the right') then becomes a lookup instead of a fresh count. With 22 elements, 12th from the right is position 22 − 12 + 1 = 11 from the left.

concepts.heading: Relative position questions
concepts.text: 'Which element is 5th to the left of the 12th from the right?' has two steps: find the reference element, then move. Moving left reduces the left-position; moving right increases it. Do the arithmetic on positions, not by counting with your finger.

concepts.heading: Immediately preceded and followed
concepts.text: 'A number immediately preceded by a letter' means the element just before the number is a letter. 'Followed by' looks at the element just after. Questions combining both ('symbols preceded by a number and followed by a letter') require checking three consecutive elements.

concepts.heading: Removal and rearrangement
concepts.text: Some questions say 'if all symbols are removed' or 'if the series is reversed'. Write the new series quickly in a separate line instead of adjusting positions mentally.

shortcuts: k-th from the right in a series of n = (n − k + 1)-th from the left.
For 'preceded by' questions, scan pairs left to right with two fingers; it halves the error rate.
Vowels are A, E, I, O, U — mark them once with a dot if questions refer to vowels.
When symbols are removed, only positions after the first symbol change; count from there.
Middle element of an odd-length series of n is at position (n + 1) / 2; for even n there are two middle elements.

examples.question: Series: R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6. Which element is 7th from the left, and how many elements are there in all?
examples.solution: Numbering gives R(1), 4(2), #(3), T(4), 7(5), K(6), @(7). So the 7th element is @. Counting to the end gives 22 elements.

examples.question: In the same series, which element is 5th to the left of the 12th element from the right?
examples.solution: 12th from the right is position 22 − 12 + 1 = 11 from the left, which is $. Five to the left is position 6: K.

examples.question: In the same series, how many numbers are immediately preceded by a letter?
examples.solution: Check each number: 4 (after R) yes, 7 (after T) yes, 2 (after @) no, 9 (after M) yes, 5 (after B) yes, 3 (after %) no, 8 (after D) yes, 6 (after J) yes. Total: 6.

examples.question: In the same series, how many symbols are immediately preceded by a number and immediately followed by a letter?
examples.solution: Symbols: # (4 before, T after) yes; @ (K before) no; $ (9 before, B after) yes; % (E before) no; & (8 before, J after) yes. Answer: 3.

practice: Series: R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6. If all the symbols are removed, which element is 8th from the right?
Without symbols the series reads R 4 T 7 K 2 M 9 B 5 E 3 W D 8 J 6, which has 17 elements. Counting eight from the right lands on 5.
In the series R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6, how many symbols are there?
The symbols are #, @, $, % and &, which makes five symbols in a series of 22 elements.
In the series R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6, which element is 7th from the right end?
With 22 elements, 7th from the right is position 22 − 7 + 1 = 16 from the left. Counting E as 14 and % as 15, position 16 is the digit 3.
In the series R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6, which element is 4th to the right of the 11th element from the left?
The 11th element from the left is $. Moving four places to the right reaches position 15, which is the symbol %.
In the series R 4 # T 7 K @ 2 M 9 $ B 5 E % 3 W D 8 & J 6, how many vowels are there?
The only vowel among the letters R, T, K, M, B, E, W, D and J is E, so there is exactly one vowel.
faqs: How can I avoid counting errors in long series?

Write position numbers under the series once, in small digits, before attempting any question. Convert every 'from the right' position into a left position with n − k + 1. This takes about 30 seconds but saves repeated counting across five questions and removes most errors.
Are alphanumeric series still asked in bank exams?

They appear less often in PO prelims than a decade ago but remain common in clerk-level and RRB-style papers. Because they need no concept learning, a few practice sets are enough to make them a reliable source of quick marks whenever they do appear.

items.title: Input-Output Machine Questions: Finding the Rule Fast
items.description: Machine input-output reasoning for IBPS PO and SBI PO: spot the arrangement rule from steps, predict later steps, and answer step-based questions quickly.
items.intro: Input-output (machine input) questions show a line of words and numbers and the steps a 'machine' uses to rearrange it. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B mains papers use them most, though they sometimes appear in prelims as a five-question set. You must decode the rule from the sample steps and apply it to a new input. The rules repeat across papers: dictionary order, ascending or descending numbers, alternating ends, or arithmetic changes to numbers.

concepts.heading: Arrangement machines
concepts.text: Each step places one or two elements in their final position, for example the word that comes first in the dictionary moves to the left end and the smallest number goes next to it. Elements not yet arranged keep their relative order. Compare input and step I to see which elements moved and where.

concepts.heading: Shifting machines
concepts.text: Some machines do not sort but rotate: each step shifts the whole line by a fixed number of places, or swaps two halves. Check whether every element changed position by the same amount.

concepts.heading: Calculation machines
concepts.text: Numbers may change at each step (add 3, multiply digits, take a square root) and words may gain or lose letters. The arrangement may stay fixed. Test the change on the first two numbers before assuming a rule.

concepts.heading: Last step and number of steps
concepts.text: The machine stops when the line is fully arranged. If the last few elements happen to be in order already, fewer steps are needed than elements. Questions like 'How many steps are needed?' test this.

shortcuts: Look at the final step first if it is given; it shows the complete target order and the rule becomes obvious.
Track only the elements that moved between two steps; the rest are just shifted.
In alternating machines, odd-numbered steps often move words and even-numbered steps move numbers — confirm with step II.
When an input is partially sorted, check after each step whether the line already matches the target.
Write steps one under another and align columns; questions like '3rd from the right in step II' become lookups.

examples.question: Input: fish 52 rope 17 cart 88 lamp 35. Step I: cart 17 fish 52 rope 88 lamp 35. Step II: cart 17 fish 35 52 rope 88 lamp. Step III: cart 17 fish 35 lamp 52 rope 88. What is the rule?
examples.solution: In each step the word that comes next in dictionary order moves to the left side, followed by the next smallest number, after the already-arranged pairs. The other elements keep their order. Step III is the last step because the line is fully arranged: cart, fish, lamp, rope with 17, 35, 52, 88 between them.

examples.question: Using the same machine, input: tree 64 bowl 29 sand 71 kite 13 drum 45. Write the steps.
examples.solution: Words in dictionary order: bowl, drum, kite, sand, tree. Numbers ascending: 13, 29, 45, 64, 71. Step I: bowl 13 tree 64 29 sand 71 kite drum 45. Step II: bowl 13 drum 29 tree 64 sand 71 kite 45. Step III: bowl 13 drum 29 kite 45 tree 64 sand 71. Step IV: bowl 13 drum 29 kite 45 sand 64 tree 71. Four steps.

examples.question: A calculation machine adds 3 to every number in each step. If the input has 12, 25 and 40, what are they in step II?
examples.solution: Each step adds 3, so after two steps every number grows by 6: 18, 31 and 46.

practice: Using the dictionary-and-ascending machine, how many steps are needed for the input tree 64 bowl 29 sand 71 kite 13 drum 45?
The steps are bowl 13…, then drum 29…, then kite 45…, and finally sand 64 tree 71. The line is fully arranged at step IV, so four steps are needed.
For the input tree 64 bowl 29 sand 71 kite 13 drum 45, Step II is: bowl 13 drum 29 tree 64 sand 71 kite 45. Which element is 6th from the left in Step II?
Counting in Step II: bowl, 13, drum, 29, tree and then 64. The sixth element from the left is 64.
In Step III: bowl 13 drum 29 kite 45 tree 64 sand 71, which element is 3rd from the right?
Reading Step III from the right gives 71, then sand, then 64. So the third element from the right is the number 64.
For the input fish 52 rope 17 cart 88 lamp 35, which is the last step of the machine?
After Step III the line reads cart 17 fish 35 lamp 52 rope 88. All words and numbers are in final order, so Step III is the last step.
A machine adds 3 to every number in each step. A number reads 31 in Step II. What was it in the input?
Two steps add 3 each, a total of 6. Subtracting 6 from 31 gives the original input value of 25.
faqs: Should I write every step in the exam?

Write the steps only as far as the questions need. If a question asks about Step III, writing Steps I to III is safer than jumping ahead. For the 'how many steps' question you may need the full sequence, but by then most steps are already written.
What if the rule seems different between steps?

Check whether the machine alternates: it may arrange words in odd steps and numbers in even steps, or move one element to the left end and one to the right. Compare three consecutive lines rather than two. If two rules fit, test both on the given final step.

items.title: Data Sufficiency in Reasoning: Method and Answer Options
items.description: Data sufficiency for bank PO and RBI exams: what 'sufficient' really means, the five standard options, and worked cases from ranking, coding and directions.
items.intro: Data sufficiency (DS) questions in reasoning do not ask you to find the answer — they ask whether the given statements are enough to find it. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B mains include DS sets, and the same idea appears in CAT and CMAT. Questions are drawn from every other reasoning topic: blood relations, directions, ranking, coding and seating. The skill is discipline: test each statement alone first, and only then together, without carrying information from one into the other.

concepts.heading: What 'sufficient' means
concepts.text: A statement is sufficient if it leads to exactly one answer. For a yes/no question, a definite 'no' is also sufficient. If it allows two or more answers, it is not sufficient, no matter how likely one answer looks.

concepts.heading: The standard options
concepts.text: Usually five: I alone is sufficient; II alone is sufficient; either I alone or II alone is sufficient; both together are needed; even both together are not sufficient. Some papers add a sixth option for 'both are needed and either is sufficient'. Read the option list once at the start of the set.

concepts.heading: Test alone, then together
concepts.text: Cover statement II with your hand and test I. Then cover I and test II. Only if both fail alone, combine them. The classic mistake is using a fact from I while judging II alone.

concepts.heading: Do not over-solve
concepts.text: You only need to know whether a unique answer exists. In a ranking question you do not have to find the full order; just check whether one person is fixed at the top.

shortcuts: If both statements alone give the same unique answer, choose 'either alone is sufficient', not 'both together'.
Gender gaps are a common trap in blood-relation DS: 'child of' does not tell you son or daughter.
In coding DS, a word's code is fixed only when it is the single unmatched word after eliminating common words.
For direction DS, one statement that links both points through a known reference is usually enough.
Before marking 'both together not sufficient', try one concrete counter-example; if you cannot build one, re-check.

examples.question: How is M related to K? I. M is the brother of N, and N is the daughter of K. II. K is the husband of P, and P is the mother of M.
examples.solution: From I, M is a male child of K, so M is K's son — sufficient. From II, M is K's child, but M's gender is unknown, so 'son' or 'daughter' cannot be fixed — not sufficient. Answer: I alone is sufficient.

examples.question: In which direction is P from Q? I. R is to the north of Q, and P is to the east of R. II. Q is to the west of S, and P is to the north of S.
examples.solution: From I, P is north and east of Q, so P is north-east of Q — sufficient. From II, S is east of Q and P is north of S, so again P is north-east of Q — sufficient. Answer: either statement alone is sufficient.

examples.question: Who is the tallest among A, B, C, D and E? I. A is taller than B and C but shorter than D. II. E is shorter than B.
examples.solution: I alone leaves E unplaced, so E or D could be tallest. II alone says nothing about A, C or D. Together: D > A > B > E and A > C, so D is the tallest. Both statements are needed.

examples.question: What is the code for 'gold'? I. 'gold silver rate' is 'la mi to' and 'silver price' is 'mi sa'. II. 'gold coin' is 'to re' and 'coin buy' is 're ka'.
examples.solution: I gives silver = mi, but gold and rate share la and to — not sufficient. II gives coin = re, so gold = to — sufficient. Answer: II alone is sufficient.

practice: On which day of the week did Rina visit the bank? I. She visited after Tuesday but before Thursday. II. She visited on a weekday.
Statement I leaves only Wednesday, a unique answer. Statement II allows five different weekdays, so only statement I is sufficient.
What is the code for 'pen'? I. 'pen cap' is written as '4 7'. II. 'pen book' is '4 9' and 'book bag' is '9 2'.
Statement I leaves pen as either 4 or 7. Statement II fixes book as 9 because it is common to both phrases, so pen must be 4.
Is T sitting at an end of a row of five people facing north? I. R sits in the middle and T sits second to the right of R. II. Exactly four people sit to the left of T.
From I, R is third and T is fifth, the right end. From II, four people to T's left also puts T fifth. Each statement alone answers the question.
Among P, Q, R and S, who is the heaviest? I. P is heavier than Q and R. II. R is heavier than S.
I alone leaves S unplaced and II alone says nothing about P or Q. Together P is heavier than Q and R, and R is heavier than S, so P is the heaviest.
Is X the father of Y? I. Y is the son of Z, and Z is the wife of X. II. X is the brother of W, and W is the aunt of Y.
From I, Z is Y's mother and X is her husband, so X is Y's father. From II, X could be Y's father or an uncle, so only I is sufficient.
faqs: Is a definite 'No' answer considered sufficient?

Yes. Data sufficiency only checks whether the question can be answered with certainty. If a statement proves that X is definitely not the father of Y, the question 'Is X the father of Y?' is answered, so that statement is sufficient. Many candidates lose marks by treating 'no' as insufficient.
How is reasoning DS different from quant DS?

The logic of the options is identical. Reasoning DS draws on puzzles, coding, directions and relations, so the traps are gender, ambiguous order and multiple arrangements. Quant DS relies on equations and number properties. Practising both sharpens the same habit of testing statements independently.

items.title: Statement and Assumption: Spotting Implicit Assumptions
items.description: Statement and assumption questions for bank PO and RBI exams: what makes an assumption implicit, the negation test, extreme words and Indian-context examples.
items.intro: Statement and assumption questions are part of the critical reasoning family tested in IBPS PO and SBI PO mains, RBI Grade B, and MBA entrances such as CMAT and MAT.
