practice: Argument: 'Sales of umbrellas in a town rose sharply in July. Therefore, the new advertising campaign launched in July increased umbrella sales.' Which option weakens it most?
July is the peak monsoon month in that town and rainfall was heavy
The shops stayed open late in July
Heavy monsoon rain is an alternative explanation for the rise in sales. It directly challenges the claim that the campaign caused the increase.
Argument: 'Branches that introduced token systems have shorter customer waiting times, so token systems reduce waiting time.' Which option strengthens it?
Waiting times at these branches fell right after tokens were introduced, with no change in staff numbers
Token systems are common in hospitals
The option links the fall in waiting time to the token system and rules out an increase in staff as another cause, strengthening the argument.
Argument: 'A survey of 50 people at a gym found that 90% prefer protein bars to biscuits. So most Indians prefer protein bars.' Which option weakens it most?
Gym members are not representative of the general population
The survey was done in the morning
The conclusion generalises from a gym sample to all Indians. Showing the sample is unrepresentative attacks that gap directly.
Argument: 'Schools should start later in the morning because teenagers who sleep more perform better in class.' Which option strengthens it?
School buses run on fixed routes
In schools that shifted to later starts, students slept more on average
The plan assumes later starts lead to more sleep. Evidence that students actually slept more after later starts closes that gap.
Argument: 'The new metro line will reduce road traffic because many car users will switch to the metro.' Which option weakens it?
Most car users in the city travel on routes the metro does not cover
Metro tickets can be bought with UPI
The metro line was completed on time
If the metro does not serve the routes car users take, few will switch. That undermines the assumption the plan depends on.
faqs: Does a weakener need to prove the conclusion false?

No. A weakener only needs to make the conclusion less likely. Showing another possible cause or a biased sample is enough. Options that try to completely disprove the conclusion are often too extreme or go beyond what the argument discusses.
How are these questions different in CAT and bank exams?

CAT arguments are longer and the options are closer to each other, so you must read the conclusion precisely. Bank and RBI papers use shorter, everyday arguments, often with Indian contexts like banking, transport or schemes. The method — find the gap, then target it — is the same.

items.title: Cause and Effect Reasoning: Independent and Common Causes
items.description: Cause and effect questions for RBI Grade B and bank PO mains: decide which event caused the other, spot independent causes and common-cause pairs.
items.intro: Cause and effect questions give two statements describing events and ask how they are related: is one the cause and the other its effect, are both effects of a common cause, or are they independent? RBI Grade B Phase I and IBPS and SBI PO mains include such questions, and they also appear in MBA entrance logical sections. Most errors come from looking at the order in which the statements are printed rather than the order in which the events must have happened.

concepts.heading: The usual answer choices
concepts.text: Typically: statement I is the cause and II its effect; II is the cause and I its effect; both are independent causes; both are effects of independent causes; both are effects of some common cause. Read the option list once before starting a set.

concepts.heading: Time order and mechanism
concepts.text: A cause must come before its effect and must plausibly produce it. 'Heavy rain lashed the city' and 'Several low-lying areas were waterlogged' — the rain clearly leads to waterlogging, so I is the cause.

concepts.heading: Common cause
concepts.text: Two events may both result from a third, unstated event. 'Vegetable prices rose sharply' and 'Transport of goods was disrupted' could both follow from a nationwide transport strike or floods. Look for a single event that would explain both.

concepts.heading: Independent events
concepts.text: If neither event can reasonably cause the other and no single event explains both, they are effects of independent causes. 'The bank raised its home-loan rate' and 'A cricket match was postponed due to rain' have nothing in common.

concepts.heading: Immediate versus principal cause
concepts.text: Some questions ask for the immediate cause of an event, meaning the trigger right before it, rather than a deeper background reason. If a building collapsed during heavy rain and the building was known to be old and weak, the heavy rain is the immediate cause while the poor condition is the underlying cause. Read the question stem to see which one is being asked.

shortcuts: Ask 'Could A alone make B happen?' then 'Could B alone make A happen?' If neither, look for a common cause.
Do not assume the first statement is the cause; examiners often reverse the order.
Policy actions (raising rates, imposing a ban) are usually responses to a problem, so the problem is often the cause.
Weather events, strikes and policy changes are common hidden common causes.
If both statements describe actions by different authorities on unrelated matters, mark them independent.
When a statement begins with words like 'following', 'after' or 'in response to', it is usually the effect; find the event it refers to.

examples.question: I. Several low-lying areas of the city were waterlogged. II. The city received very heavy rainfall over the past two days.
examples.solution: Rainfall causes waterlogging, not the other way round. II is the cause and I its effect, even though I is printed first.

examples.question: I. The prices of vegetables rose sharply in the city's markets. II. Supply of goods from neighbouring states was disrupted.
examples.solution: A supply disruption reduces arrivals and pushes up prices. II is the cause and I the effect. (If the statements were 'prices rose' and 'many shops shut early', both might be effects of a common cause such as a strike.)

examples.question: I. The state government declared a holiday for all schools on Monday. II. Many offices in the state reported low attendance on Monday.
examples.solution: A school holiday does not by itself empty offices, and low office attendance does not cause a school holiday. Both could follow from a common cause, such as a severe weather warning or a major festival. Both are effects of a common cause.

examples.question: I. A bank increased the interest rate on its fixed deposits. II. A city traffic police department launched a helmet-awareness drive.
examples.solution: There is no plausible link between the two, and no single event explains both. They are effects of independent causes.

practice: I. Many flights were cancelled at the city airport. II. Dense fog reduced visibility to near zero in the morning.
I is the cause and II is its effect
II is the cause and I is its effect
Both are effects of independent causes
Low visibility from fog makes it unsafe to fly, which leads to cancellations. Fog is clearly the cause and the cancellations are its effect.
I. The government reduced the import duty on edible oils. II. Domestic prices of edible oils had risen sharply in the preceding months.
I is the cause and II is its effect
Both are effects of independent causes
II is the cause and I is its effect
A duty cut is a policy response to high domestic prices. The earlier price rise is the cause, and the duty cut is the effect.
I. Attendance at the local market was very low on Sunday. II. Several roads in the town were closed on Sunday.
I is the cause and II is its effect
Both are effects of independent causes
Both are effects of a common cause
Low attendance does not close roads, and road closures alone may not fully explain it. Both could result from one event, such as a festival procession or a curfew.
I. A cricket stadium hosted a sold-out final. II. A bank launched a new credit card for students.
Both are effects of independent causes
I is the cause and II is its effect
II is the cause and I is its effect
Both are effects of a common cause
There is no plausible link between a cricket final and a student credit card launch. Each has its own unrelated reason, so they are effects of independent causes.
I. Many students in the district could not reach their exam centres on time. II. Bus services in the district were suspended due to a strike.
I is the cause and II is its effect
II is the cause and I is its effect
Both are effects of a common cause
Suspended bus services leave students without transport and delay them. The strike-related suspension is the cause and the delays are the effect.
faqs: How do I tell 'common cause' from 'independent causes'?

Try to name one single, realistic event that would produce both statements. If you can — a strike, a storm, a festival, a policy decision — choose common cause. If every explanation needs two separate events, choose independent causes. Do not invent far-fetched links to force a common cause.
Is cause and effect still asked in bank exams?

It appears more in RBI Grade B and in PO mains reasoning than in prelims, and its frequency varies from year to year. Because the questions are short, a few practice sets are usually enough to become comfortable, so it is worth covering if you are preparing for mains.

items.title: Reading Comprehension Strategy for Bank, SSC and CAT
items.description: A practical reading comprehension strategy: reading for structure, inference and tone questions, and avoiding extreme options in bank, SSC and CAT RCs.
items.intro: Reading comprehension (RC) is the single biggest block in most English sections. IBPS PO, SBI PO and IBPS Clerk prelims usually carry one or two passages with about eight to ten questions in total, RBI Grade B includes RCs in its English section, SSC CGL and CHSL ask a short passage with a few questions, and in CAT the RC questions form most of the verbal section. A consistent method — how to read, what to mark, how to judge options — matters more than reading speed alone.

concepts.heading: Read for structure, not detail
concepts.text: On the first read, note what each paragraph does: introduces a problem, gives an example, presents a counter-view, concludes. A two-word margin note per paragraph ('problem', 'RBI view') lets you locate details later in seconds.

concepts.heading: Question types
concepts.text: Direct-fact questions ask what the passage says. Inference questions ask what must be true based on it. Main-idea and title questions test the whole passage. Tone questions ask about the author's attitude. Vocabulary-in-context questions ask what a word means in that sentence, which may differ from its dictionary meaning.

concepts.heading: Judging options
concepts.text: The correct option is supported by the passage, usually in different words. Wrong options are often too extreme ('always', 'never', 'completely'), partly true, true in general but not stated, or a distortion of a detail. Paraphrase is a good sign; copied phrases with one changed word are a warning.

concepts.heading: Order of attack
concepts.text: In bank prelims, many toppers glance at the questions first to know what to look for, then read the passage once. In CAT, reading the passage fully first works better because questions are inference-heavy. Try both methods in mocks and keep the one that gives better accuracy.

shortcuts: For 'title' questions, choose the option that covers the whole passage, not just one paragraph.
For tone, look at adjectives and adverbs the author uses ('worryingly', 'commendable').
If two options look right, pick the one that needs fewer assumptions.
Vocabulary-in-context: substitute each option into the sentence and keep the one that preserves meaning.
Do not use outside knowledge; an option can be factually true and still wrong if the passage does not support it.
Attempt RC passages on familiar topics (economy, banking, technology) first if there is a choice.

examples.question: Passage: 'Small savings schemes have long been popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns. Yet younger savers increasingly prefer digital options that let them invest small amounts through a phone. Post offices have responded by offering online access to several schemes.' Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (a) Rural savers have stopped using small savings schemes. (b) Post offices are adapting to changing saver preferences. (c) Digital investments are safer than small savings schemes.
examples.solution: The passage says post offices responded to younger savers' digital preference by offering online access, so (b) is a fair inference. (a) is extreme — the passage says the schemes 'have long been popular'. (c) compares safety, which the passage never does. Answer: (b).

examples.question: Passage: 'Small savings schemes have long been popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns. Yet younger savers increasingly prefer digital options that let them invest small amounts through a phone. Post offices have responded by offering online access to several schemes.' What is the author's tone?
examples.solution: The author reports facts about trends and responses without praising or criticising anyone. The tone is neutral or informative, not critical, alarmed or celebratory.

examples.question: In the sentence 'The committee tabled the proposal until the next meeting', what does 'tabled' most nearly mean?
examples.solution: In Indian and British usage, 'table' often means to present for discussion, but here 'until the next meeting' shows the proposal was set aside for later. In context, 'postponed' fits best. This is why context, not the dictionary's first meaning, decides vocabulary questions.

examples.question: A passage discusses how UPI has made small payments easier and also mentions concerns about cyber fraud. Which title is best: (a) The Rise of Cyber Fraud (b) UPI: Convenience and Its Risks (c) How to File a Fraud Complaint?
examples.solution: (a) covers only the concern and (c) is not discussed. (b) captures both the benefit and the risk, so it reflects the whole passage. Answer: (b).

practice: Passage: 'Small savings schemes have long been popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns. Yet younger savers increasingly prefer digital options that let them invest small amounts through a phone. Post offices have responded by offering online access to several schemes.' According to the passage, why are small savings schemes popular in rural India?
They can only be bought online
They combine safety with modest returns
They are preferred by younger savers
The first sentence states that the schemes are popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns.

Passage: 'Small savings schemes have long been popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns. Yet younger savers increasingly prefer digital options that let them invest small amounts through a phone. Post offices have responded by offering online access to several schemes.' Which statement is NOT supported by the passage?
Younger savers like investing through phones
Post offices offer online access to several schemes
Small savings schemes give modest returns
Post offices have stopped offering small savings schemes
The passage says post offices responded by offering online access, which means they continue the schemes. The claim that they stopped is unsupported.

Passage: 'Small savings schemes have long been popular in rural India because they combine safety with modest returns. Yet younger savers increasingly prefer digital options that let them invest small amounts through a phone. Post offices have responded by offering online access to several schemes.' The word 'modest' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
In the context of returns, 'modest' describes an amount that is reasonable but not large, so 'moderate' fits. 'Shy' and 'humble' describe people.
Which option is usually a warning sign in reading comprehension answer choices?
A paraphrase of a sentence in the passage
A statement covering the main idea
Extreme words make an option claim more than most passages support. Correct options are typically cautious paraphrases of what the passage actually says.
A passage describes rising farm incomes in one state after an irrigation project. Which conclusion is best supported?
All Indian states have rising farm incomes
The irrigation project may have contributed to higher farm incomes there
Farm incomes will keep rising forever
The passage links one project to one state's incomes, so a cautious statement about contribution is supported. The other options generalise or predict beyond the passage.
faqs: Should I read the questions before the passage?

For fact-heavy bank prelims passages, skimming the questions first helps you read with a purpose. For inference-heavy CAT passages, reading the whole passage first usually works better. Test both approaches in at least five mock tests and keep the one that gives you higher accuracy, not just speed.
How can I improve reading speed for RC?

Read one editorial or long-form article daily on economy, banking, science or society, and summarise each paragraph in a few words. Over a few weeks this builds both speed and the habit of spotting structure. Avoid sub-vocalising every word; read in phrases instead.

items.title: Cloze Test Tricks: Grammar Clues, Context and Collocations
items.description: Solve cloze tests in IBPS, SBI and SSC exams: use grammar clues, the passage's theme and common word pairings to fill every blank with confidence.
items.intro: A cloze test is a short passage with blanks, each followed by options. IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO and SBI Clerk prelims frequently include a cloze test of five to seven blanks, and SSC CGL and CHSL papers have their own cloze passages. It tests grammar, vocabulary and comprehension together. Unlike fillers, the blanks share a context, so reading the whole passage first gives you clues that single sentences cannot.

concepts.heading: Read the passage once before filling
concepts.text: Skim the full passage to understand its topic and tone. A passage about rising non-performing assets will favour words like 'stress', 'default' and 'recovery'; a positive passage about financial inclusion will favour 'expanded', 'enabled' and 'access'.

concepts.heading: Grammar decides first
concepts.text: Check the part of speech needed. After an article you need a noun or adjective; after 'to' you often need a base verb; after 'has' you need a past participle. Eliminating grammatically wrong options usually leaves two choices.

concepts.heading: Collocations
concepts.text: Some words naturally pair: 'take a decision', 'pose a threat', 'bridge the gap', 'meet the target', 'heavy rainfall', 'strong demand'. If an option breaks a standard pairing, it is probably wrong even if its meaning is close.

concepts.heading: Logical connectors
concepts.text: Blanks before a clause often need a connector. 'However' shows contrast, 'therefore' shows result, 'moreover' adds a point, 'despite' is followed by a noun. Read the sentences on both sides of the blank to decide the relationship.

concepts.heading: Tone and direction of the passage
concepts.text: Every cloze passage has a direction — it may argue that a reform is working, warn about a risk, or describe a problem and a fix. Words that oppose this direction are usually wrong even if they are grammatically fine. In a passage praising improved rural banking access, 'hampered' or 'curtailed' would clash with the message, while 'expanded' or 'strengthened' fit naturally.

shortcuts: Fill the easiest blanks first; they reveal the passage's direction for the harder ones.
Watch tense consistency: if the passage is in past tense, a present-tense option is usually wrong.
Prepositions often decide the answer: 'comply with', 'depend on', 'aim at', 'insist on'.
Re-read the completed sentence; if it sounds awkward aloud, check the collocation.
When two options mean the same, neither is likely to be correct unless one fits the grammar better.
After 'one of the', use a plural noun ('one of the biggest challenges'); this simple check removes many wrong options.

examples.question: 'The new policy is expected to ______ the gap between rural and urban access to credit.' Options: bridge, fill, cross, close up.
examples.solution: 'Bridge the gap' is the standard collocation for reducing a difference. 'Fill' and 'close up' are less idiomatic here, and 'cross' changes the meaning. Answer: bridge.

examples.question: 'Exports grew strongly last year. ______, imports grew even faster, widening the trade deficit.' Options: Therefore, However, Moreover, Because.
examples.solution: The second sentence contrasts with the positive first one (deficit widened despite export growth). 'However' signals contrast. 'Therefore' would imply exports caused import growth. Answer: However.

examples.question: 'The committee has ______ its report to the ministry.' Options: submit, submitted, submitting, submits.
examples.solution: 'Has' requires a past participle to form the present perfect tense. Answer: submitted.

examples.question: 'Rising cyber fraud ______ a serious threat to digital payments.' Options: poses, makes, gives, does.
examples.solution: 'Pose a threat' is the standard collocation. The subject 'Rising cyber fraud' is singular, so 'poses'. Answer: poses.

examples.question: 'Thanks to wider broadband coverage, many villages have ______ access to online banking for the first time.' Options: lost, gained, denied, refused.
examples.solution: The opening 'Thanks to wider broadband coverage' signals a positive change, and 'for the first time' shows something new was obtained. 'Gained access' fits both the meaning and the standard collocation. Answer: gained.

practice: 'The bank aims to ______ its lending target before the end of the financial year.' Choose the best word.
'Meet a target' is the natural collocation for achieving a set goal. The other options are either unidiomatic or change the meaning.
'______ the heavy rain, the match started on time.' Choose the best option.
A noun phrase ('the heavy rain') follows the blank, and the sentence shows contrast. 'Despite' takes a noun; 'although' needs a full clause.
'The minister ______ the new scheme in Delhi last week.' Choose the correct form.
'Last week' marks a completed action in the past, so the simple past 'launched' is correct. The present perfect does not combine with a specific past time.
'Many small firms depend ______ timely payments from large buyers.' Choose the correct preposition.
The verb 'depend' takes the preposition 'on'. 'Depend from' and 'depend with' are incorrect in standard English.
'Prices remained stable for months. ______, the sudden spike surprised economists.' Choose the best connector.
Months of stable prices make the spike unexpected, so the surprise follows as a result. 'Therefore' shows that cause-and-result link.
faqs: How many cloze test blanks usually appear in bank prelims?

In recent IBPS and SBI prelims papers a cloze test, when asked, has generally had five to seven blanks, but the number and even the presence of a cloze test vary by year. Prepare for it along with fillers and word-swap questions, since they test the same skills.
What if two options fit both grammar and meaning?

Look for the collocation or the tone of the passage. One word usually pairs more naturally ('pose a threat' rather than 'make a threat') or matches the passage's positive or negative direction better. Reading the next sentence often settles the choice.

items.title: Error Spotting in English: Rules That Catch Most Errors
items.description: Error spotting for SSC and bank exams: subject-verb agreement, tense, pronouns, prepositions, comparatives and redundancy errors, with worked sentences.
items.intro: Error spotting (also called error detection or spotting the error) asks you to find the part of a sentence that contains a grammatical or usage mistake. It appears in nearly every SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS English section and in IBPS and SBI prelims, typically three to five questions. Although English grammar is vast, a small set of rules explains most exam errors. Learning to check those rules in a fixed order turns this into a fast-scoring area.

concepts.heading: Check the verb first
concepts.text: Most errors involve the verb: agreement with the subject ('The list of items are' → 'is'), tense consistency ('He said that he will come' → 'would come'), or wrong form after modals ('can goes' → 'can go'). Find the subject and main verb of each clause and test them together.

concepts.heading: Pronouns
concepts.text: Check agreement in number and gender, and case: 'between you and I' should be 'between you and me', since a preposition takes the object form. 'Each of the students must bring their' is accepted in modern usage, but many exam keys still prefer 'his or her', so read the options carefully.

concepts.heading: Prepositions and articles
concepts.text: Common errors: 'discuss about' (discuss takes no preposition), 'married with' (married to), 'senior than' (senior to), 'an university' (a university, because of the 'yu' sound), 'the both' (both the).

concepts.heading: Comparatives and degree
concepts.text: Avoid double comparatives ('more better'). Use 'than' after comparatives, 'to' after senior, junior, superior, inferior, prefer. 'One of the best student' should be 'students', since 'one of' takes a plural noun.

concepts.heading: Redundancy
concepts.text: Words that repeat meaning are errors: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'cousin brother', 'free gift', 'each and every one of them' in formal writing. Indian English has several such expressions that exam setters target.

shortcuts: Ignore the part marked 'No error' until you have checked the others; it is correct only when every other part passes.
With 'neither…nor' and 'either…or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
'Scarcely' and 'hardly' pair with 'when', while 'no sooner' pairs with 'than'.
'Lest' is followed by 'should' or the base verb, never by 'not'.
After 'It is time', use the past tense: 'It is time we left.'
Uncountable nouns (advice, information, furniture, luggage) take no plural form and a singular verb.

examples.question: Find the error: (a) The list of documents / (b) required for the loan / (c) are available / (d) on the website.
examples.solution: The subject is 'The list', which is singular; 'of documents' is only a modifier. So 'are' should be 'is'. Error in (c).

examples.question: Find the error: (a) No sooner did the train arrive / (b) when the passengers / (c) rushed towards / (d) the doors.
examples.solution: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', not 'when'. Part (b) should read 'than the passengers'. Error in (b).

examples.question: Find the error: (a) She is senior / (b) than me / (c) in the bank / (d) by three years.
examples.solution: 'Senior' takes 'to', not 'than'. Part (b) should read 'to me'. Error in (b).

examples.question: Find the error: (a) The manager asked us / (b) to discuss about / (c) the new targets / (d) before Friday.
examples.solution: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and does not take 'about'. Part (b) should read 'to discuss'. Error in (b).

examples.question: Find the error: (a) He gave me / (b) many useful advices / (c) before my interview / (d) No error.
examples.solution: 'Advice' is uncountable and has no plural. It should be 'much useful advice' or 'many useful pieces of advice'. Error in (b).

practice: Find the part with an error: 'Neither the manager nor the clerks / was present / at the meeting / yesterday.'
Neither the manager nor the clerks
With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Clerks' is plural, so 'was' should be 'were'.
Find the part with an error: 'He returned back / from Mumbai / after attending / the conference.'
'Return' already means to come back, so 'returned back' is redundant. The correct phrase is simply 'He returned'.
Find the part with an error: 'This is one of the / best book / I have read / this year.'
'One of the' is followed by a plural noun. The phrase should be 'best books', not 'best book'.
Find the part with an error: 'The furniture / in our new office / are very / comfortable.'
'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb. 'Are very' should be 'is very'.
Find the part with an error: 'Hardly had I reached / the station / than the train / left.'
'Hardly' pairs with 'when', not 'than'. The part should read 'when the train'.
faqs: How many grammar rules do I need for error spotting?

Around 40 to 50 core rules — agreement, tense, pronouns, articles, prepositions, comparatives, conjunction pairs and redundancy — explain most exam errors. Learn them with two example sentences each and revise weekly. Pair this with timed practice so you start checking the verb and subject automatically.
Is 'No error' often the correct answer?

It is correct in some questions, but setters usually place a real error in most sentences. Choose 'No error' only after checking each part against your rule list. If one part sounds slightly odd but you cannot name the rule, re-check the verb and preposition before deciding.

items.title: Sentence Improvement Questions: Method and Common Fixes
items.description: Sentence improvement for SSC and bank exams: test the underlined part, compare replacements for grammar and idiom, and know when 'no improvement' is right.
items.intro: Sentence improvement questions underline or bold a part of a sentence and offer replacements, usually with an option for 'No improvement'. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS use them regularly, and bank exams use a related format called phrase replacement. The skill combines error spotting with choosing the best fix: you must notice what is wrong and also recognise which option corrects it without creating a new error.

concepts.heading: Find the problem before reading options
concepts.text: Read the sentence and decide what is wrong with the underlined part — tense, agreement, preposition, idiom or word order. Then look for an option that fixes exactly that. Reading options first makes several of them sound acceptable.

concepts.heading: Keep the meaning
concepts.text: The right replacement corrects the grammar without changing what the sentence means. An option that is grammatical but alters the meaning (for example, changing 'must' to 'may') is wrong.

concepts.heading: Idioms and fixed phrases
concepts.text: Many questions test fixed expressions: 'by and large', 'in lieu of', 'with regard to' (not 'with regards to'), 'as soon as', 'in spite of' (not 'in spite'). Knowing the standard form often answers the question instantly.

concepts.heading: When 'No improvement' is right
concepts.text: Choose it only when the original is grammatically correct and natural. Test it with the same checklist you use for errors. Setters include it as the answer in some questions, so do not avoid it out of habit.

concepts.heading: Conditional and tense patterns
concepts.text: 'If I were you, I would…', 'If he had studied, he would have passed', 'If it rains, we will stay home'. Mixing these patterns ('If he would have studied') is a frequent error in Indian English that examiners test.

concepts.heading: Parallel structure
concepts.text: Items joined by 'and', 'or', 'not only… but also' or 'both… and' should share the same grammatical form. 'She likes reading, writing and to paint' should become 'reading, writing and painting'. 'He is not only intelligent but also works hard' is better as 'He is not only intelligent but also hard-working'. Options that restore this balance are frequently the answer.

shortcuts: Compare options side by side; they usually differ in just one or two words, which tells you the rule being tested.
Prefer the concise option when two are grammatical; wordy alternatives are often distractors.
'Unless' already carries 'not', so 'unless you do not' is wrong.
'Since' with time points (since 2020), 'for' with durations (for five years).
'Prefer X to Y', not 'prefer X than Y'.
'Lest' takes 'should' or a plain verb: 'Work hard lest you should fail', never 'lest you do not fail'.

examples.question: 'If I was the manager, I would approve the leave.' Improve the underlined part 'If I was'.
examples.solution: For an imaginary or unreal condition, standard grammar uses 'were' for all subjects: 'If I were the manager'. Answer: If I were.

examples.question: 'He has been working here since five years.' Improve 'since five years'.
examples.solution: 'Five years' is a duration, so it takes 'for'. Answer: for five years.

examples.question: 'Unless you do not submit the form, you cannot apply.' Improve 'Unless you do not submit'.
examples.solution: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'do not' creates a double negative. Answer: Unless you submit.

examples.question: 'If she would have left earlier, she would have caught the bus.' Improve 'If she would have left'.
examples.solution: In the third conditional, the 'if' clause uses past perfect: 'If she had left earlier'. Answer: If she had left.

examples.question: 'I prefer tea than coffee.' Improve 'than coffee'.
examples.solution: 'Prefer' is followed by 'to'. Answer: to coffee.

examples.question: 'The new app is fast, secure and it is easy to use.' Improve 'and it is easy to use'.
examples.solution: The list should keep the same form: three adjectives. Replace with 'and easy to use', giving 'fast, secure and easy to use'.

practice: Improve the bold part: 'She **is knowing** the answer to that question.'
'Know' is a stative verb and is not normally used in the continuous form. The simple present 'knows' is correct.
Improve the bold part: 'Each of the players **have received** a medal.'
'Each' is singular, so the verb must also be singular. 'Has received' agrees with the subject and keeps the meaning.
Improve the bold part: 'The meeting was cancelled **due to the reason that** the chairman was ill.'
'Due to the reason that' is wordy and awkward. 'Because' expresses the same cause concisely and correctly.
Improve the bold part: 'Hardly had she sat down **than the phone rang**.'
'Hardly' is paired with 'when' in standard English. The correct form is 'Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang'.
Improve the bold part: 'He insisted **to pay** the bill himself.'
'Insist' takes the preposition 'on' followed by a gerund. The correct phrase is 'insisted on paying'.
faqs: How is sentence improvement different from error spotting?

Error spotting only asks where the mistake is. Sentence improvement also asks you to choose the correct fix, so you need to know the right form, not just recognise the wrong one. Practising both together helps, since the underlying rules are the same.
What if two options are grammatically correct?

Choose the one that keeps the original meaning and sounds most natural and concise. Setters often add a grammatical but wordy or meaning-changing option as a distractor. Re-read the full sentence with each option before deciding.

items.title: Para Jumbles: Finding the Opening Line and Linking Pairs
items.description: Solve para jumbles for bank exams and CAT: spot the opening sentence, use pronouns, connectors and time clues to link pairs, and check the closing line.
items.intro: Para jumbles (sentence rearrangement) give four to six sentences in random order and ask for the correct sequence. IBPS PO and SBI PO prelims and mains often include a set of five questions, SSC papers ask single rearrangement questions, and CAT uses the harder 'type in the answer' version without options. The solution rarely comes from reading every arrangement; it comes from finding the opening sentence and a few fixed pairs.

concepts.heading: The opening sentence
concepts.text: The first sentence introduces the topic and can stand alone. It usually has no pronoun pointing back ('this', 'they', 'such'), no contrast word ('however', 'but') and no connector ('therefore', 'also') at the start. A general statement or a named subject ('The Reserve Bank of India…') is a strong candidate.

concepts.heading: Mandatory pairs
concepts.text: Some sentences must follow others. A sentence starting with 'This policy…' needs a previous sentence that names the policy. 'However' needs a statement to contrast with. Identify two or three such pairs and the order largely fixes itself.

concepts.heading: Time and logical order
concepts.text: Look for dates, 'first', 'later', 'finally', or a problem–cause–solution flow. Events and arguments usually move forward in time or from general to specific.

concepts.heading: The closing sentence
concepts.text: Conclusions often start with 'Thus', 'Therefore', 'In short' or give an outcome or recommendation. If a sentence clearly concludes, place it last and work backwards.

concepts.heading: Use the options
concepts.text: When options are given, check which options start with your chosen opening sentence and contain your mandatory pairs. Usually only one survives.

shortcuts: Acronyms are written in full first: 'Unified Payments Interface (UPI)' comes before a sentence using just 'UPI'.
Articles help: 'a scheme' introduces something new; 'the scheme' refers back to it.
If two sentences both look like openers, the more general one usually comes first.
In CAT, find the pair links first and then decide the opener; there are no options to lean on.
Read the final order once from start to finish; it should flow like a paragraph.
Sentences giving an example ('For instance…') follow the general point they illustrate, never the other way round.

examples.question: Arrange: (A) This has made it easier for small shops to accept digital payments. (B) The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was launched in 2016. (C) As a result, cash use for small purchases has fallen in many cities. (D) It allows instant transfers between bank accounts using a mobile phone.
examples.solution: B introduces UPI by full name and date, so it opens. D uses 'It' to describe UPI, so B–D. A uses 'This' to refer to the instant-transfer feature, so D–A. C begins 'As a result', giving the outcome. Order: BDAC.

examples.question: Arrange: (P) However, many of them still lack access to formal credit. (Q) Small farmers form a large share of India's agricultural workforce. (R) Schemes like the Kisan Credit Card aim to close this gap. (S) They often borrow from informal lenders at high interest rates.
examples.solution: Q names the subject and stands alone, so it opens. P contrasts with Q ('However… them'). S explains the consequence ('They… borrow from informal lenders'). R presents the solution and refers to 'this gap'. Order: QPSR.

examples.question: Which is the best opening sentence? (a) Therefore, the deadline was extended. (b) The income tax department sets a deadline for filing returns each year. (c) This caused a rush on the portal. (d) However, many taxpayers missed it.
examples.solution: (a), (c) and (d) begin with words that need an earlier sentence: 'Therefore', 'This' and 'However'. (b) introduces the topic independently. Answer: (b).

practice: Which sentence is most likely to open a paragraph?
However, it also regulates payment systems.
This role was given to it by law.
The Reserve Bank of India is the country's central bank.
As a result, it influences interest rates.
The opening sentence introduces the subject without referring back. The others start with 'However', 'This' or 'As a result', which depend on an earlier sentence.
Arrange: (A) They help track spending easily. (B) Many people now use budgeting apps. (C) As a result, some users save more each month.
B introduces budgeting apps, A uses 'They' to describe them, and C gives the result. The logical order is B, A, C.
A sentence begins with 'This scheme'. What must the sentence before it contain?
'This scheme' refers back to something already introduced. The preceding sentence must name or describe the scheme for the reference to make sense.
Arrange: (P) Finally, the results are declared online. (Q) First, candidates register on the portal. (R) Then they appear for the online exam.
Time markers decide the order: 'First' (Q), 'Then' (R) and 'Finally' (P). The correct sequence is Q, R, P.
Which word at the start of a sentence most strongly suggests it is the concluding sentence?
'Thus' introduces a result or summary, which typically closes a paragraph. 'However' and 'Moreover' continue an argument, and 'Firstly' begins a sequence.
faqs: How do I solve para jumbles without options, as in CAT?

Find two or three mandatory pairs using pronouns, connectors and acronyms, then decide the opener and closer. Build the chain around these fixed blocks. Always read the final sequence aloud mentally to check flow, because there is no option list to catch mistakes.
What if two sentences both seem like good openers?

Pick the more general one, or the one that introduces a name or term the other uses. A sentence that defines or introduces a concept almost always comes before a sentence that discusses its effects or examples.

items.title: Single and Double Fillers: Grammar Clues and Elimination
items.description: Fillers for IBPS, SBI and SSC exams: solve single and double blanks using grammar clues, contrast signals and collocations, with worked examples.
items.intro: Filler questions give a sentence with one or two blanks and ask for the word or pair that best completes it. IBPS PO, SBI PO and the clerk exams use single and double fillers often, sometimes as a set of five, and SSC papers include single-blank fill-in-the-blanks. Fillers reward vocabulary, but most can be solved with grammar and logic alone: the sentence usually tells you the part of speech and whether the missing word is positive or negative.

concepts.heading: Predict before you look
concepts.text: Read the sentence, cover the options and guess a simple word for the blank. Then pick the option closest to your guess. This prevents attractive but unrelated words from pulling you away.

concepts.heading: Signal words
concepts.text: Contrast words ('although', 'but', 'despite', 'yet') mean the blank opposes the other half of the sentence. Support words ('and', 'because', 'moreover', a semicolon) mean the blank continues the same direction.

concepts.heading: Double fillers: solve the easier blank first
concepts.text: In double-blank questions, decide one blank with certainty and eliminate every option whose word for that blank fails. Then test the remaining pairs for the second blank. Never choose a pair because one word fits perfectly while the other is doubtful.

concepts.heading: Grammar fit
concepts.text: Check part of speech, singular or plural, and the preposition that follows the blank. 'He was accused ___ fraud' needs 'of', so the verb must be one that takes 'of', such as 'accused' or 'convicted'.

concepts.heading: Collocations
concepts.text: Some word pairs are fixed: 'stringent norms', 'heavy losses', 'robust growth', 'curb inflation', 'avert a crisis'. If an option breaks such a pairing, it is likely wrong.

shortcuts: Positive or negative? Mark the blank + or − from context and drop options of the wrong charge.
After 'a', the next word starts with a consonant sound; after 'an', a vowel sound — useful when the article sits before the blank.
If two options are synonyms, both are usually wrong unless one fits the grammar better.
In double fillers, the second blank often depends on a word in the first half; read the whole sentence before choosing.
Formal sentences about policy and economy favour formal words ('mitigate', 'bolster') over casual ones.
Re-read the completed sentence; a correct filler sounds natural in context.

examples.question: 'Although the company reported higher sales, its profits ______ because of rising costs.' Options: soared, declined, doubled, stabilised.
examples.solution: 'Although' sets up a contrast with higher sales, so profits must have gone the other way. 'Declined' fits. Answer: declined.

examples.question: 'The RBI took steps to ______ inflation, which had ______ the comfort zone.' Options: (a) curb, exceeded (b) boost, crossed (c) curb, entered (d) fuel, exceeded.
examples.solution: Steps by a central bank against inflation aim to reduce it, so blank one is 'curb', removing (b) and (d). Inflation that prompts action has gone beyond the comfort zone, so 'exceeded' fits better than 'entered'. Answer: (a).

examples.question: 'The new norms are quite ______; even minor violations attract penalties.' Options: lenient, stringent, vague, optional.
examples.solution: The semicolon introduces support: minor violations being penalised shows strictness. 'Stringent' fits. Answer: stringent.

examples.question: 'She was ______ of the charges after a detailed inquiry.' Options: acquitted, convicted, accused, blamed.
examples.solution: 'After a detailed inquiry' and 'of the charges' suggest a final decision. Both 'acquitted' and 'convicted' take 'of', but 'accused' is usually before an inquiry. With no negative signal, 'acquitted' (freed) is the natural reading. Answer: acquitted.

examples.question: 'Timely rains helped ______ a drought that experts had feared.' Options: avert, invite, cause, prolong.
examples.solution: Rains that help against a feared drought prevent it. 'Avert a drought' is the standard collocation. Answer: avert.

practice: 'Despite repeated warnings, the residents ______ to leave the flood-prone area.' Choose the best word.
'Despite repeated warnings' signals a contrast, so the residents did not do what they were told. 'Refused' fits that meaning.
'The economy showed ______ growth, ______ expectations of a slowdown.' Choose the best pair.
Robust growth goes against expectations of a slowdown, so 'defying' fits the second blank. 'Robust, confirming' is contradictory.
'The bank ______ the loan application because the documents were incomplete.' Choose the best word.
Incomplete documents are a reason not to proceed with the application. 'Rejected' fits the cause given in the sentence.
'Her explanation was so ______ that nobody could understand it.' Choose the best word.
If nobody could understand the explanation, it must have been complicated. 'Convoluted' means complex and hard to follow, while 'lucid' means clear.
'Strict monitoring helped ______ losses that could have run into crores.' Choose the best word.
The phrase 'could have run into crores' shows the losses did not happen. Monitoring therefore helped prevent them.
faqs: How do I improve vocabulary for filler questions?

Read one quality editorial or business article daily and note five unfamiliar words with the sentence they appeared in. Revise the list weekly. Learning words in context, along with their usual pairings ('mitigate risk', 'stringent norms'), helps far more than memorising long word lists.
What should I do if no option fits perfectly?

Choose the option that fits both grammar and the direction of the sentence best. Exam fillers sometimes use a slightly formal or unusual word. Eliminate options that are clearly wrong in charge (positive versus negative) or grammar, and pick from what remains.

items.title: Synonyms and Antonyms Strategy: Roots, Context and Traps
items.description: Synonyms and antonyms for SSC and bank exams: use word roots, prefixes and context sentences, avoid look-alike traps and build vocabulary steadily.
items.intro: Synonym and antonym questions are a fixed part of SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS English, usually two to four questions per paper, and they appear in bank exams inside reading comprehension as vocabulary-in-context questions. Since no one can memorise the whole dictionary, the aim is to learn high-frequency exam words and to use roots, prefixes and context to handle unfamiliar ones. The biggest trap is a look-alike word that sounds similar but means something different.

concepts.heading: Roots and prefixes
concepts.text: Many difficult words break down. 'Bene' means good (benevolent: kind), 'mal' means bad (malicious: intending harm), 'chron' means time (chronic: lasting a long time), 'loqu' means speak (loquacious: talkative). Prefixes like 'in-', 'un-', 'dis-' and 'mis-' often signal opposites.

concepts.heading: Charge of the word
concepts.text: Even if you do not know the exact meaning, you often know whether a word feels positive or negative. 'Pernicious' sounds negative; its synonym must also be negative ('harmful'), and its antonym positive ('beneficial').

concepts.heading: Context sentences
concepts.text: When the word is given in a sentence, the sentence often defines it. 'The manager was frugal, spending only on essentials' shows frugal means economical. Antonym: extravagant.

concepts.heading: Look-alike traps
concepts.text: Exam options often include a word that looks or sounds like the question word: 'eminent' (distinguished) versus 'imminent' (about to happen), 'affect' versus 'effect', 'complement' versus 'compliment'. Read the options slowly.

concepts.heading: Best fit, not any fit
concepts.text: More than one option may be loosely related. Choose the one closest in meaning and in strength: the synonym of 'furious' is 'enraged', not 'annoyed', which is milder.

concepts.heading: Building a word bank that sticks
concepts.text: Keep a notebook or spreadsheet with four columns: word, meaning, synonym, antonym, plus one sentence you wrote yourself. Add words from editorials, mock tests and wrong answers. Review the list in short daily sessions and mark words you still miss. Words you write in your own sentence are remembered far longer than words you only read in a list, and the antonym column trains both question types together.

shortcuts: For antonyms, first find a synonym in your head, then look for its opposite among the options.
Words ending in '-ous' and '-ive' are adjectives; the answer will usually be an adjective too.
If an option is a synonym in an antonym question, eliminate it immediately; setters add one to catch hurried readers.
Keep a list of high-frequency exam words: abate, alleviate, candid, cordial, diligent, frugal, lucid, obsolete, prudent, tranquil.
Learn words in pairs of opposites: lucid–obscure, prudent–reckless, cordial–hostile, abundant–scarce.
When stuck between two options, pick the one used in the same context as the question word.

examples.question: Choose the synonym of 'BENEVOLENT': cruel, kind, angry, careful.
examples.solution: 'Bene' means good; benevolent means well-meaning and kind. Answer: kind.

examples.question: Choose the antonym of 'FRUGAL': thrifty, economical, extravagant, careful.
examples.solution: Frugal means spending little. 'Thrifty' and 'economical' are synonyms, a deliberate trap. The opposite is 'extravagant'. Answer: extravagant.

examples.question: Choose the synonym of 'IMMINENT': famous, about to happen, ancient, unclear.
examples.solution: 'Imminent' means about to happen, as in 'imminent rain'. 'Famous' is the meaning of the look-alike 'eminent'. Answer: about to happen.

examples.question: Choose the antonym of 'ALLEVIATE': ease, relieve, aggravate, reduce.
examples.solution: Alleviate means to make less severe. 'Ease', 'relieve' and 'reduce' are synonyms. The opposite, to make worse, is 'aggravate'. Answer: aggravate.

examples.question: In 'Her candid reply surprised the interview panel', what does 'candid' mean?
examples.solution: 'Candid' means frank and honest. The surprise suggests she spoke openly rather than giving a rehearsed answer. Synonym: frank.

examples.question: Choose the antonym of 'LUCID': clear, obscure, bright, simple.
examples.solution: Lucid means clear and easy to understand. 'Clear' and 'simple' are close in meaning, and 'bright' relates to light. The opposite, meaning unclear or hard to understand, is 'obscure'. Answer: obscure.

practice: Diligent describes someone who works with steady care and effort, so 'hard-working' is the closest synonym. 'Lazy' and 'careless' are opposites.
Abundant means existing in large quantities. 'Plentiful' and 'ample' are synonyms, while 'scarce', meaning in short supply, is the opposite.
Obsolete means no longer in use or out of date, as with old technology. 'Outdated' expresses the same idea.
Cordial means warm and friendly. The opposite, describing unfriendly and aggressive behaviour, is 'hostile'.
Prudent means acting with care and thought for the future. 'Sensible' is closest; 'proud' is a look-alike trap with a different meaning.
faqs: How many words should I learn for SSC synonyms and antonyms?

There is no fixed list, but learning around 800 to 1,000 high-frequency exam words, with their opposites and an example sentence, covers a large share of questions. Revise them in small daily sets and test yourself weekly; spaced revision works better than a single long session.
Are roots and prefixes reliable for unfamiliar words?

They give a strong clue, but not a guarantee, because some words have drifted from their roots. Use roots together with the word's charge and any context sentence. When all three point the same way, you can answer with reasonable confidence.

items.title: Idioms and Phrases for Exams: Meanings and Smart Guessing
items.description: Common idioms and phrases for SSC and bank exams with meanings, usage in sentences, phrasal verbs, and how to guess an unfamiliar idiom from context.
items.intro: Idioms and phrases are expressions whose meaning is different from the literal meaning of their words. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS ask two or more idiom questions in most papers, and bank exams use them inside fillers, phrase replacement and reading comprehension. A few hundred idioms come up again and again, so steady learning pays off. For unfamiliar idioms, the sentence context and the image behind the phrase usually lead to the right meaning.

concepts.heading: Literal versus figurative
concepts.text: 'Spill the beans' is not about beans; it means revealing a secret. Options often include a literal reading as a trap. If an option describes the literal action, it is almost never the answer.

concepts.heading: Common exam idioms
concepts.text: 'A blessing in disguise' (a hidden advantage), 'bite the bullet' (face something unpleasant bravely), 'burn the midnight oil' (work late into the night), 'at the eleventh hour' (at the last moment), 'hit the nail on the head' (describe exactly), 'once in a blue moon' (rarely), 'a piece of cake' (very easy).

concepts.heading: Phrasal verbs
concepts.text: Verb-plus-particle combinations are also tested: 'call off' (cancel), 'put off' (postpone), 'look into' (investigate), 'carry out' (perform), 'turn down' (reject), 'bring up' (raise a topic or a child), 'give in' (surrender).

concepts.heading: Guessing from imagery
concepts.text: Picture the idiom. 'To be in the same boat' suggests sharing the same situation. 'To add fuel to the fire' suggests making things worse. The image usually points to the meaning even if you have not seen the idiom before.

concepts.heading: Use the sentence
concepts.text: When the idiom is in a sentence, the rest of the sentence tests the meaning. 'The match was called off because of rain' tells you 'called off' means cancelled.

shortcuts: Eliminate literal-meaning options first.
Group idioms by theme: effort (burn the midnight oil, go the extra mile), time (at the eleventh hour, in the nick of time), honesty (above board, cut corners).
'Put off' and 'call off' are often confused: put off is postpone, call off is cancel.
Learn 10 idioms a day with one sentence each; revise every weekend.
Indian contexts help memory: 'burning the midnight oil before exams', 'at the eleventh hour before the ITR deadline'.
For phrasal verbs, the particle often hints at direction: 'turn down' (refuse, lower), 'take up' (start).

examples.question: Meaning of 'at the eleventh hour': (a) at 11 o'clock (b) at the last moment (c) very early (d) after a long delay.
examples.solution: The idiom means doing something at the latest possible time. (a) is the literal trap. Answer: (b).

examples.question: 'Many candidates burn the midnight oil before the exam.' What does the idiom mean?
examples.solution: It means studying or working late into the night. The image of an oil lamp burning at midnight suggests late-night work. Answer: work late into the night.

examples.question: 'Losing that job turned out to be a blessing in disguise.' What does it mean?
examples.solution: Something that seemed bad but turned out to be good. The sentence shows the job loss led to something better later. Answer: a hidden advantage.

examples.question: Choose the correct phrasal verb: 'The board decided to ______ the meeting until next week.' Options: call off, put off, turn down, give in.
examples.solution: 'Until next week' shows the meeting is postponed, not cancelled. 'Put off' means postpone. Answer: put off.

examples.question: Meaning of 'to add fuel to the fire': (a) to cook food (b) to make a bad situation worse (c) to solve a problem (d) to save energy.
examples.solution: Adding fuel makes a fire bigger, so the idiom means making a bad situation worse. Answer: (b).

practice: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
A blue moon is an uncommon event, so the idiom describes something that happens very rarely, not regularly or often.
What does 'to spill the beans' mean?
The idiom means to reveal secret information, often by accident. Options about food are literal traps.
Choose the meaning of the phrasal verb 'turn down' in 'She turned down the job offer.'
To turn down an offer is to refuse or reject it. The sentence makes clear she did not take the job.
What does 'to hit the nail on the head' mean?
The idiom means to describe a situation or problem precisely. The carpentry image of striking the nail squarely suggests accuracy.
What does 'a piece of cake' mean?
The idiom describes a task that is very easy to do. Food-related options are literal readings and are incorrect.
faqs: How many idioms should I learn for SSC?

Aim for around 300 to 400 commonly tested idioms and phrasal verbs, learned with example sentences. Many recur across papers. Revise them in themed groups and test yourself with mixed lists so that you can recognise them quickly in any question format.
Can I guess an idiom I have never seen?

Often, yes. Picture the literal image, decide whether it suggests something positive or negative, and check how it fits the sentence. Then eliminate literal-meaning options. This approach works for many unfamiliar idioms, though learning the common ones remains the most reliable strategy.

items.title: One-Word Substitution: High-Frequency Words and Roots
items.description: One-word substitution for SSC exams: high-frequency words for people, places, fear, government and study, plus root clues to crack unfamiliar options.
items.intro: One-word substitution asks you to replace a phrase or sentence with a single word — for example, 'a person who cannot be corrected' becomes 'incorrigible'. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS ask two or three such questions per English section, and the same vocabulary helps in bank-exam fillers and reading comprehension. Many words share roots with other exam words, so learning them in themed groups is far more effective than memorising a random list.

concepts.heading: People by habit or role
concepts.text: Philanthropist (one who loves and helps mankind), misanthrope (one who hates mankind), optimist and pessimist, introvert and extrovert, polyglot (one who speaks many languages), novice (a beginner), veteran (an experienced person), connoisseur (an expert judge of art or taste).

concepts.heading: Fears and '-cide' words
concepts.text: Fears end in '-phobia': hydrophobia (water), claustrophobia (closed spaces), acrophobia (heights). Killing words end in '-cide': homicide (a person), suicide (oneself), fratricide (a brother), genocide (a whole group).

concepts.heading: Government and society
concepts.text: Democracy (rule by the people), autocracy (rule by one person with absolute power), bureaucracy (rule by officials), plutocracy (rule by the wealthy), anarchy (absence of government), theocracy (rule by religious leaders).

concepts.heading: Places and collections
concepts.text: Apiary (bees), aviary (birds), aquarium (fish), granary (grain), arsenal (weapons), archives (records), mint (where coins are made), dispensary (where medicines are given).

concepts.heading: Study of things
concepts.text: '-logy' means study: ornithology (birds), anthropology (humans), seismology (earthquakes), etymology (word origins), entomology (insects). Etymology and entomology are a favourite look-alike pair.

concepts.heading: Words about speech and writing
concepts.text: Several frequent words describe speaking or writing: soliloquy (speaking to oneself, especially in a play), monologue (a long speech by one person), eulogy (praise for someone, often after death), epitaph (words written on a tomb), autobiography (a life story written by the person), biography (a life story written by someone else), anonymous (of unknown name), and pseudonym (a false name used by a writer).

shortcuts: 'Omni-' means all: omniscient (all-knowing), omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent (present everywhere).
'-cracy' means rule by; '-archy' also means rule (monarchy, anarchy).
'In-' or 'im-' often means not: incorrigible (cannot be corrected), invincible (cannot be defeated), illegible (cannot be read).
Pair opposites: optimist–pessimist, introvert–extrovert, theist–atheist.
Watch look-alikes: etymology (words) versus entomology (insects); aviary (birds) versus apiary (bees).
When unsure, break the option into root + suffix and check which combination matches the phrase.
'-ist' and '-er' usually mark a person (philatelist: stamp collector; numismatist: coin collector), while '-ary' and '-ium' often mark a place (granary, aquarium).

examples.question: A person who speaks many languages: polyglot, linguist, translator, orator.
examples.solution: 'Poly' means many and 'glot' relates to tongue or language. A linguist studies language and need not speak many. Answer: polyglot.

examples.question: A place where bees are kept: aviary, apiary, aquarium, granary.
examples.solution: An apiary houses bees ('apis' is Latin for bee). An aviary is for birds — the usual trap. Answer: apiary.

examples.question: Government by the wealthy: aristocracy, plutocracy, autocracy, democracy.
examples.solution: 'Pluto' relates to wealth, and '-cracy' means rule. Aristocracy is rule by nobles. Answer: plutocracy.

examples.question: Handwriting that cannot be read: illegible, ineligible, illiterate, indelible.
examples.solution: 'Legible' means readable, so 'illegible' means not readable. 'Ineligible' means not qualified and 'indelible' means cannot be erased. Answer: illegible.

examples.question: The study of insects: etymology, entomology, ornithology, zoology.
examples.solution: Entomology is the study of insects. Etymology is the study of word origins — a close look-alike. Answer: entomology.

examples.question: A life history of a person written by himself or herself: biography, autobiography, memoir, chronicle.
examples.solution: 'Auto' means self, so autobiography is a life story written by the person. A biography is written by someone else. A memoir is close but usually covers selected experiences rather than a full life. Answer: autobiography.

practice: Incorrigible describes a person whose bad habits cannot be corrected. Invincible means unbeatable and infallible means never wrong.
Acrophobia is the fear of heights. Claustrophobia is fear of closed spaces, hydrophobia fear of water and xenophobia fear of foreigners.
'Omni' means all and 'scient' relates to knowing, so omniscient means all-knowing. Omnipotent means all-powerful.
A place where coins are made:
A mint is where coins are produced. An arsenal stores weapons, an archive stores records, and a treasury manages public money.
A misanthrope dislikes humankind in general. A philanthropist helps people, and a misogynist specifically dislikes women.
faqs: What is the best way to learn one-word substitutions?

Learn them in themed groups — people, fears, killing, government, places, study — along with their roots. Grouping makes look-alikes easier to separate. Revise the same set several times over two weeks, then mix groups in self-tests to check recall under pressure.
Are one-word substitutions asked in bank exams?

Not usually as a separate question type, but the vocabulary appears in fillers, cloze tests and reading comprehension. SSC exams test them directly. If you are preparing for both, the time spent on one-word substitutions supports your bank-exam English as well.

items.title: Active and Passive Voice Rules for Every Tense
items.description: Active and passive voice for SSC exams: conversion rules for each tense, modals, imperatives and questions, plus common errors with by-agent and pronouns.
items.intro: Voice conversion is a regular SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS question: you are given a sentence in active voice and asked for the correct passive form, or the reverse. Bank exams do not usually ask it directly, but knowing passive structures helps with error spotting and sentence improvement. The rules are mechanical — the object becomes the subject, the verb takes 'be' plus the past participle, and the tense of 'be' matches the original tense — so careful practice gives near-certain marks.

concepts.heading: The basic change
concepts.text: Active: Subject + verb + object ('The clerk checked the form'). Passive: Object + form of 'be' + past participle + by + subject ('The form was checked by the clerk'). The tense is carried by 'be'; the main verb always becomes the past participle.

concepts.heading: Tense table
concepts.text: Simple present: is/am/are + V3 (is written). Present continuous: is/am/are being + V3 (is being written). Present perfect: has/have been + V3 (has been written). Simple past: was/were + V3. Past continuous: was/were being + V3. Past perfect: had been + V3. Simple future: will be + V3. Future perfect: will have been + V3.

concepts.heading: Tenses with no passive in exam usage
concepts.text: Perfect continuous tenses (has been writing, had been writing, will have been writing) and future continuous are generally not converted into passive in exam questions. If an option tries ('has been being written'), it is usually wrong.

concepts.heading: Modals
concepts.text: Modal + be + V3: 'You must submit the form' → 'The form must be submitted by you'. 'They can solve it' → 'It can be solved by them'.

concepts.heading: Imperatives and questions
concepts.text: Commands use 'Let': 'Close the door' → 'Let the door be closed'. Requests often use 'You are requested to…'. Questions keep question form: 'Did she write the letter?' → 'Was the letter written by her?'; 'Who wrote this?' → 'By whom was this written?'

concepts.heading: Getting the past participle right
concepts.text: Many errors come from the wrong verb form rather than the wrong tense. Irregular verbs must use their third form: written (not wrote), chosen, taken, given, broken, begun, sung, spoken, stolen, forgotten. 'The letter was wrote by him' and 'The song was sang beautifully' are classic wrong options. Revise a list of the 60 to 70 most common irregular verbs with all three forms; it helps in voice, tense and error-spotting questions alike.

shortcuts: Pronouns change case: I → me, he → him, they → them, we → us, after 'by'.
When the doer is unknown or obvious ('Someone stole my bag'), drop the 'by' phrase: 'My bag was stolen.'
Check that 'be' agrees with the new subject: 'The letters were written', not 'was written'.
Verbs without objects (sleep, arrive, die) cannot be made passive.
With two objects, either can become the subject: 'He gave me a book' → 'I was given a book by him' or 'A book was given to me by him'.
Some verbs take 'with', 'to' or 'at' instead of 'by': 'known to', 'pleased with', 'surprised at'.

examples.question: Change to passive: 'The manager approves all loans.'
examples.solution: Simple present, plural object: 'All loans are approved by the manager.'

examples.question: Change to passive: 'They are repairing the road.'
examples.solution: Present continuous → are being + V3: 'The road is being repaired by them.' 'Road' is singular, so 'is'.

examples.question: Change to passive: 'She has completed the project.'
examples.solution: Present perfect → has been + V3: 'The project has been completed by her.'

examples.question: Change to passive: 'Open the window.'
examples.solution: Imperative → Let + object + be + V3: 'Let the window be opened.'

examples.question: Change to passive: 'Who taught you English?'
examples.solution: Question with 'who' → 'By whom were you taught English?' The past tense and question form are kept.

practice: Choose the passive form: 'The committee will announce the results tomorrow.'
The results would be announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results are announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results will announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow.
Simple future becomes 'will be' plus the past participle. 'The results will be announced' keeps the tense and agrees with the plural subject.
Choose the passive form: 'He was writing a letter.'
A letter was being written by him.
A letter is being written by him.
A letter has been written by him.
A letter was written by him.
Past continuous changes to 'was/were being' plus the past participle. 'A letter was being written by him' is correct.
Choose the passive form: 'You must follow the rules.'
The rules must follow by you.
The rules must be followed by you.
The rules must have followed by you.
The rules are followed by you.
With a modal, the passive uses modal plus 'be' plus the past participle: 'must be followed'.
Choose the passive form: 'Did the bank send the statement?'
Has the statement been sent by the bank?
Is the statement sent by the bank?
Was the statement sent by the bank?
Did the statement sent by the bank?
A simple past question becomes 'Was/Were' plus subject plus past participle. 'Was the statement sent by the bank?' is correct.
Choose the active form: 'The match was won by India.'
The passive is in the simple past ('was won'), so the active must also be simple past: 'India won the match'.
faqs: Can every sentence be changed into passive voice?

No. Only sentences with transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be made passive. 'She sleeps early' or 'The train arrived' have no object to become the subject. In exams, perfect continuous tenses are also generally treated as having no standard passive form.
Is 'by + agent' always needed in the passive?

No. If the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, it is usually dropped: 'The bridge was built in 1990.' Exam options sometimes keep 'by someone' or 'by people', which is acceptable but less natural; check the other options before choosing it.

items.title: Direct and Indirect Speech: Tense, Pronoun and Time Rules
items.description: Direct and indirect speech for SSC exams: reporting-verb changes, backshift of tenses, pronoun and time-word changes, questions, commands and exceptions.
items.intro: Narration (direct and indirect speech) questions ask you to convert a sentence from quoted words to reported form, or back. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS include them in many English sections, and the same rules help in error spotting. Each conversion involves up to four changes — reporting verb, tense, pronouns and words of time and place — and errors usually come from forgetting one of them. Checking all four in order makes this topic very reliable.

concepts.heading: Reporting verb
concepts.text: 'Said' stays 'said' for statements, or 'said to' becomes 'told'. Questions use 'asked' or 'enquired'; commands use 'ordered', 'told' or 'requested'; exclamations use 'exclaimed with joy/sorrow'. The conjunction changes too: 'that' for statements, 'if/whether' for yes-no questions, the question word itself for wh-questions, and 'to' + verb for commands.

concepts.heading: Tense backshift
concepts.text: If the reporting verb is in the past, move the reported tense one step back: present → past, present continuous → past continuous, present perfect → past perfect, simple past → past perfect, will → would, can → could, may → might.

concepts.heading: No backshift cases
concepts.text: If the reporting verb is in the present or future ('He says'), the tense does not change. Universal truths and habitual facts usually keep their tense: 'The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.'

concepts.heading: Pronoun changes
concepts.text: First-person pronouns change to match the speaker, second-person to match the listener, and third-person usually stays the same. 'He said to me, "I like your idea"' → 'He told me that he liked my idea.'

concepts.heading: Time and place words
concepts.text: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, ago → before, this → that, here → there, next week → the following week.

concepts.heading: Exclamations, wishes and suggestions
concepts.text: Exclamations change to statements with an expressive reporting verb: 'He said, "What a beautiful view!"' becomes 'He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view.' Wishes use 'wished' or 'prayed': 'She said, "May you succeed!"' becomes 'She wished that I might succeed.' Suggestions with 'Let us' become 'suggested that we should…'. Interjections such as 'Alas' or 'Hurrah' disappear and are replaced by 'exclaimed with sorrow' or 'exclaimed with joy'.

shortcuts: Change in this order: reporting verb, conjunction, pronouns, tense, time words.
In reported questions, use statement word order: 'She asked where I lived', not 'where did I live'.
For negative commands, use 'not to': 'Don't shout' → 'He told me not to shout.'
'Must' usually becomes 'had to' when it shows obligation.
Remove quotation marks and question marks in indirect speech; reported questions end with a full stop.
'Let's' in suggestions becomes 'suggested that we should…' or 'proposed that…'.

examples.question: Convert: He said, "I am busy today."
examples.solution: Statement, past reporting verb: He said that he was busy that day. (I → he, am → was, today → that day)

examples.question: Convert: She said to me, "Have you finished your work?"
examples.solution: Yes-no question: She asked me if I had finished my work. (said to → asked, if, you → I, your → my, have finished → had finished)

examples.question: Convert: The officer said to the clerk, "Submit the report by evening."
examples.solution: Command: The officer ordered the clerk to submit the report by evening.

examples.question: Convert: He said, "Where do you live?"
examples.solution: Wh-question with statement word order: He asked me where I lived. ('where did I live' is the common wrong option.)

examples.question: Convert: The teacher said, "Water boils at 100 °C at sea level."
examples.solution: A scientific fact keeps its tense: The teacher said that water boils at 100 °C at sea level.

practice: Choose the indirect form: Ravi said, "I will call you tomorrow."
Ravi said that he would call me the next day.
Ravi said that I will call you tomorrow.
Ravi said that he will call me tomorrow.
Ravi told that he would call me tomorrow.
Will becomes would, I becomes he, you becomes me and tomorrow becomes the next day. Only the option with all four changes is correct.
Choose the indirect form: She said to him, "Please help me."
She told him please help her.
She requested him to help her.
She said him to help me.
She asked that he helps her.
A polite request uses 'requested' with 'to' plus the verb. The pronoun me changes to her to match the speaker.
Choose the indirect form: He said, "Why are you late?"
He asked me why was I late.
He said why I am late.
He asked me why I was late.
He asked me that why I was late.
A wh-question keeps the question word, uses statement order and backshifts the tense, giving 'why I was late' without 'that'.
Choose the indirect form: The doctor said, "Don't eat oily food."
The doctor said don't eat oily food.
The doctor advised me to not eating oily food.
The doctor told that I should not eat oily food.
The doctor advised me not to eat oily food.
Negative advice uses 'not to' plus the base verb after an advising verb. 'Advised me not to eat' is correct.
Choose the indirect form: She says, "I am learning French."
She says that she is learning French.
She says that she was learning French.
She said that she is learning French.
She says that I am learning French.
The reporting verb 'says' is present tense, so there is no backshift. Only the pronoun changes from I to she.
faqs: When does the tense not change in indirect speech?

When the reporting verb is in the present or future tense, and when the reported words state a universal truth, a scientific fact or a habitual action that is still true. In such cases only pronouns and, where needed, time words change.
Why is 'He asked me where did I live' wrong?

Reported questions are no longer real questions, so they take normal statement word order: subject before verb. The correct form is 'He asked me where I lived'. The auxiliary 'did' disappears, and the sentence ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

items.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Rules with Exam-Style Sentences
items.description: Subject-verb agreement rules for SSC and bank exams: collective nouns, either-or, each and every, 'one of', amounts, and phrases between subject and verb.
items.intro: Subject-verb agreement is behind a large share of error spotting and sentence improvement questions in SSC CGL, CHSL, IBPS and SBI exams. The basic idea is simple — a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb — but exam sentences hide the true subject behind phrases, collective nouns and connectors like 'as well as'. Knowing about a dozen special rules lets you catch most of these errors in seconds.

concepts.heading: Find the real subject
concepts.text: Ignore phrases between the subject and the verb. In 'The quality of the mangoes is good', the subject is 'quality', not 'mangoes'. Prepositional phrases ('of the…', 'with the…') and clauses ('who…') never change the number of the subject.

concepts.heading: Connectors that do not add
concepts.text: 'As well as', 'along with', 'together with', 'with' and 'in addition to' do not make the subject plural. 'The manager, along with his team, was present' — the verb follows 'manager'.

concepts.heading: Either/neither and or/nor
concepts.text: With 'either…or' and 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the clerk nor the officers were present'; 'Neither the officers nor the clerk was present'. 'Either' and 'neither' alone take singular verbs.

concepts.heading: Each, every and one of
concepts.text: 'Each', 'every', 'everyone', 'somebody' and 'one of the…' take singular verbs: 'Each of the students has a laptop'; 'One of my friends is a banker'. But 'one of those who' usually takes a plural verb, since 'who' refers to the plural group.

concepts.heading: Collective nouns and amounts
concepts.text: Collective nouns take a singular verb when acting as one unit ('The jury has reached a verdict') and plural when members act individually ('The jury were divided'). Amounts of money, time and distance as one quantity are singular: 'Five lakh rupees is a large sum.'

concepts.heading: Repeating the article
