concepts.text: When two nouns refer to different people or things, repeat the article; when they refer to one person, use it once. 'The secretary and the treasurer were present' means two people. 'The secretary and treasurer was present' means one person holding both posts, so the verb is singular. Exams test this together with subject-verb agreement, so check both the article and the verb in such sentences.

shortcuts: 'The number of' + plural noun → singular verb; 'A number of' + plural noun → plural verb.
Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, unless they describe one thing ('Bread and butter is my breakfast').
Nouns like news, mathematics, economics and politics (as a subject) take singular verbs.
Scissors, trousers and spectacles take plural verbs, but 'a pair of scissors' takes singular.
'Many a' + singular noun takes a singular verb: 'Many a candidate has tried.'
In 'There is / There are', the verb agrees with the noun that follows.

examples.question: Correct the error: 'The quality of these products are excellent.'
examples.solution: The subject is 'quality' (singular); 'of these products' is a modifier. Correct: 'The quality of these products is excellent.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'The chairman, along with the directors, have arrived.'
examples.solution: 'Along with' does not add to the subject. Correct: 'The chairman, along with the directors, has arrived.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'A number of customers has complained.'
examples.solution: 'A number of' means many and takes a plural verb. Correct: 'A number of customers have complained.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'Economics are my favourite subject.'
examples.solution: Subjects like economics take singular verbs. Correct: 'Economics is my favourite subject.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'There is many reasons for the delay.'
examples.solution: The verb agrees with 'reasons', which is plural. Correct: 'There are many reasons for the delay.'

practice: Choose the correct verb: 'The number of applicants ______ increased this year.'
'The number of' refers to a single figure, so it takes a singular verb. 'The number of applicants has increased' is correct.
Choose the correct verb: 'Either the manager or his assistants ______ responsible.'
With either…or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Assistants' is plural, so 'are' is correct.
Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the branches ______ a security guard.'
'Each' is singular and takes a singular verb. 'Each of the branches has a security guard' is the correct form.
Choose the correct verb: 'Ten kilometres ______ a long distance to walk daily.'
A distance considered as one quantity takes a singular verb. 'Ten kilometres is a long distance' is correct.
Choose the correct verb: 'The news of the merger ______ surprised everyone.'
'News' is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb, so 'has surprised' is correct despite the final 's'.
faqs: Is 'Everyone have finished' ever correct?

No. 'Everyone', 'everybody', 'someone' and 'nobody' are grammatically singular and take singular verbs: 'Everyone has finished.' The pronoun that refers back to them is often 'their' in modern English, but the verb itself stays singular.
How should I treat collective nouns like 'team' or 'committee'?

In exam questions, use a singular verb when the group acts as a single unit and a plural verb when members act separately or disagree. If the sentence shows division ('The committee were divided in their opinions'), plural is correct; otherwise singular is safer.

items.title: Articles A, An and The: Rules, Sounds and Exceptions
items.description: Article rules for SSC and bank exams: a versus an by sound, when to use 'the', when to omit articles, and common Indian-English errors with examples.
items.intro: Articles — a, an and the — look minor, but they appear in error spotting, fillers, cloze tests and sentence improvement across SSC CGL, CHSL, MTS and bank exams. Indian speakers often drop articles or add them where English does not, and examiners use these habits as traps. The rules are short: 'a' and 'an' depend on sound, 'the' marks something specific or unique, and some nouns take no article at all.

concepts.heading: A versus an: sound, not spelling
concepts.text: Use 'an' before a vowel sound and 'a' before a consonant sound: an hour, an honest officer, an MBA (em-bee-ay), an SBI branch (es-bee-eye); but a university (yu-), a European (yu-), a one-day match (wun-), a useful book.

concepts.heading: When to use 'the'
concepts.text: Use 'the' for something already mentioned or clear from context ('I bought a pen. The pen is blue'), unique things (the sun, the RBI), superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first), rivers, seas, mountain ranges and groups of islands (the Ganga, the Arabian Sea, the Himalayas, the Andamans), and newspapers and holy books (the Hindu, the Gita).

concepts.heading: No article
concepts.text: Do not use an article before most proper nouns of people, cities, countries and single mountains (Delhi, India, Mount Everest), before languages (She speaks Marathi), meals (We had lunch), games (He plays cricket), and uncountable or plural nouns used in a general sense ('Honesty is the best policy', 'Banks offer loans').

concepts.heading: Countries with 'the'
concepts.text: Countries with plural or descriptive names take 'the': the USA, the UK, the Netherlands, the Maldives.

concepts.heading: Institutions
concepts.text: 'Go to school / hospital / church' without an article when used for their main purpose; with 'the' when visiting for another reason: 'She went to the school to meet the principal.'

concepts.heading: Relative clauses and 'who'
concepts.text: In a relative clause the verb agrees with the noun that 'who', 'which' or 'that' refers to. 'He is one of the officers who have been promoted' uses 'have' because 'who' refers to 'officers'. But 'He is the only one of the officers who has been promoted' uses 'has', since 'who' now refers to 'the only one'. This pair of sentences is a favourite in SSC error spotting, so learn both versions together.

shortcuts: Say the next word aloud: if it starts with a vowel sound, use 'an'.
Abbreviations read letter by letter follow the letter's sound: an LIC agent (el-), a UPI app (yu-).
'The + adjective' means a group of people: the poor, the rich, the unemployed.
'The' before a comparative in parallel phrases: 'The more you practise, the better you score.'
No article before 'most' meaning 'majority': 'Most candidates', but 'the most important'.
'Both the' is correct; 'the both' is wrong.

examples.question: Fill in: 'He waited for ______ hour at ______ SBI branch.'
examples.solution: 'Hour' begins with a silent h, so 'an hour'. 'SBI' is read 'es-bee-eye', starting with a vowel sound, so 'an SBI branch'. Answer: an, an.

examples.question: Fill in: 'She is ______ university topper and ______ honest person.'
examples.solution: 'University' starts with a 'yu' consonant sound → 'a'. 'Honest' has a silent h → 'an'. Answer: a, an.

examples.question: Correct the error: 'The Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.'
examples.solution: Single mountains take no article. Correct: 'Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.' 'The highest' is correct because it is a superlative.

examples.question: Correct the error: 'He plays the cricket every evening.'
examples.solution: Names of games take no article. Correct: 'He plays cricket every evening.'

examples.question: Fill in: '______ Ganga is one of ______ longest rivers in India.'
examples.solution: Rivers take 'the', and 'longest' is a superlative, also with 'the'. Answer: The, the.

practice: Choose the correct article: 'She has applied for ______ MBA programme.'
MBA is read letter by letter as em-bee-ay, which starts with a vowel sound. So 'an MBA programme' is correct.
Choose the correct article: 'He is ______ European tourist.'
'European' begins with a 'yu' sound, which is a consonant sound. So it takes 'a', not 'an'.
The honesty is the best policy.
A honesty is the best policy.
Abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article, and superlatives like 'best' take 'the'.
The Himalayas protect India from cold winds.
He visited the Delhi last year.
We had the dinner at eight.
Mountain ranges take 'the', so 'The Himalayas' is correct. Languages, cities and meals in a general sense take no article.
Choose the correct option: 'The government launched schemes for ______.'
'The' plus an adjective refers to a whole group of people. 'The poor' means poor people in general and takes no plural ending.
faqs: Why is it 'a university' but 'an umbrella'?

Articles depend on the sound at the start of the next word, not the letter. 'University' starts with a 'yu' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a'. 'Umbrella' starts with an 'uh' vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.
Do we say 'the RBI' or 'RBI'?

Both appear in Indian newspapers, but formal English uses 'the' with the full name of an institution that includes a common noun like 'Bank' or 'Commission': the Reserve Bank of India, the Election Commission. With abbreviations, 'the RBI' is common and safe. In exams, the option with 'the' is usually preferred.

items.title: Prepositions in English: Time, Place and Fixed Pairings
items.description: Preposition rules for SSC and bank exams: in, on and at for time and place, since versus for, verb-preposition pairs and common Indian-English slips.
items.intro: Prepositions are small words with a big share of English errors. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS error-spotting and fill-in-the-blank questions test them often, and IBPS and SBI cloze tests and fillers frequently hinge on one preposition. Some uses follow clear rules, like 'in', 'on' and 'at' for time and place; many others are fixed pairings that simply have to be learned, such as 'comply with' or 'accused of'. Indian English habits like 'discuss about' are frequent traps.

concepts.heading: In, on, at for time
concepts.text: 'At' for exact times and short points (at 9 a.m., at noon, at night). 'On' for days and dates (on Monday, on 15 August, on Diwali day). 'In' for longer periods (in July, in 2026, in the morning, in summer).

concepts.heading: In, on, at for place
concepts.text: 'At' for a point or address (at the bank, at the station). 'On' for surfaces and lines (on the table, on the road, on page 10). 'In' for enclosed spaces and larger areas (in the room, in Mumbai, in India).

concepts.heading: Since and for
concepts.text: 'Since' marks the starting point (since 2020, since Monday); 'for' marks the length of time (for six years, for two days). Both are normally used with perfect tenses: 'She has worked here since 2020 / for six years.'

concepts.heading: Verbs that need no preposition
concepts.text: Some verbs take a direct object without a preposition: discuss, describe, reach, enter (a room), attack, resemble, approach, order. 'Discuss about', 'reach to' and 'enter into the room' are errors (though 'enter into an agreement' is correct).

concepts.heading: Fixed pairings
concepts.text: Learn common pairs: accused of, afraid of, comply with, consist of, depend on, insist on, interested in, married to, prefer to, senior to, superior to, congratulate on, abstain from, aim at, apply for (a job), apply to (a person or body).

concepts.heading: Between and among; beside and besides
concepts.text: 'Between' for two people or things, 'among' for more than two. 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to. 'Divide the money between the two brothers' but 'among the five sisters'. Adjectives also take fixed prepositions: aware of, capable of, good at, keen on, responsible for, satisfied with, similar to, jealous of, proud of, eligible for. 'She is eligible for the scholarship' and 'He is responsible for the branch' are typical exam sentences, and options often swap 'for' with 'to' or 'of' to test you.

shortcuts: 'Since' never goes with a duration: 'since five years' is always wrong.
'Married to', not 'married with'; 'senior to', not 'senior than'.
'Comprise' takes no 'of'; 'consist of' does: 'The board comprises five members' / 'consists of five members'.
'Different from' is the safest choice in exams; avoid 'different than'.
'In time' means early enough; 'on time' means punctually.
When unsure, recall a standard phrase from newspapers: 'comply with norms', 'insist on transparency'.

examples.question: Fill in: 'The exam starts ______ 10 a.m. ______ Sunday ______ March.'
examples.solution: Exact time → at; day → on; month → in. 'The exam starts at 10 a.m. on Sunday in March.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'We will discuss about the proposal tomorrow.'
examples.solution: 'Discuss' takes a direct object. Correct: 'We will discuss the proposal tomorrow.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'She has been living in Pune since three years.'
examples.solution: 'Three years' is a duration, so use 'for'. Correct: 'She has been living in Pune for three years.'

examples.question: Fill in: 'All branches must comply ______ the new KYC norms.'
examples.solution: 'Comply' takes 'with'. Answer: with.

examples.question: Fill in: 'The profit was divided ______ the three partners.'
examples.solution: More than two people → 'among'. Answer: among.

examples.question: Fill in: 'She applied ______ the post of probationary officer and sent her form ______ the recruitment board.'
examples.solution: You apply 'for' a job or post and 'to' the organisation or person who receives the application. Answer: for, to. Mixing these two is a frequent error in cover letters as well as in exams.

practice: Choose the correct preposition: 'He was accused ______ cheating in the exam.'
'Accuse' is followed by 'of' in standard English. 'Accused of cheating' is the correct fixed pairing.
Choose the correct preposition: 'The train reached ______ Chennai late at night.'
'Reach' takes a direct object, so no preposition is needed. 'The train reached Chennai' is correct.
Choose the correct preposition: 'She is married ______ a doctor.'
The correct fixed expression is 'married to'. 'Married with' is a common Indian-English error tested in exams.
Choose the correct preposition: 'Besides English, he speaks Kannada and Telugu. He sat ______ me during the meeting.'
'Beside' means next to, which fits sitting during a meeting. 'Besides' means in addition to, as used in the first sentence.
Choose the correct preposition: 'I prefer working in the morning ______ working late at night.'
'Prefer' is followed by 'to' when comparing two things. 'Prefer working in the morning to working late' is correct.
faqs: Is 'in the night' wrong?

Standard usage is 'at night' for night-time in general and 'in the night' for something happening during a particular night ('I woke up in the night'). In exam sentences about general habits, 'at night' is the expected answer, while 'in the morning', 'in the afternoon' and 'in the evening' use 'in'.
How do I learn fixed prepositions efficiently?

Make a list of about 100 common verb-preposition and adjective-preposition pairs with one example sentence each. Revise a section daily and test yourself with fill-in-the-blank drills. Noticing these pairs while reading newspapers reinforces them much faster than memorising alone.

items.title: Tenses in English: Usage Rules and Exam Error Patterns
items.description: Tense rules for SSC and bank exams: present perfect versus simple past, time markers, sequence of tenses, conditionals and stative verbs, with examples.
items.intro: Tenses decide whether a sentence sounds right in English, and tense errors are among the most tested in SSC CGL, CHSL, MTS, IBPS and SBI papers through error spotting, sentence improvement, fillers and cloze tests. You do not need to recite all twelve tense forms; you need to know which time markers fix which tense, how the tenses of two clauses relate, and a few habits like 'I am knowing' that examiners target repeatedly.

concepts.heading: Simple past versus present perfect
concepts.text: Use the simple past with a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago): 'I met him yesterday.' Use the present perfect for past actions connected to now, without a finished time: 'I have met him.' 'I have met him yesterday' is wrong.

concepts.heading: Time markers
concepts.text: 'Since' and 'for' with perfect tenses; 'just', 'already', 'yet', 'ever' and 'never' usually with present perfect; 'every day', 'usually' and 'always' with simple present; 'at the moment' and 'now' with present continuous; 'by the time' with perfect tenses.

concepts.heading: Sequence of tenses
concepts.text: When the main clause is in the past, the subordinate clause usually moves to a past form: 'He said that he was tired', 'I knew that she would come.' Universal truths are an exception: 'He knew that the sun rises in the east.'

concepts.heading: Past perfect for the earlier action
concepts.text: When two past actions are described, the earlier one takes the past perfect: 'The train had left before we reached the station.' Using simple past for both is acceptable when 'before' or 'after' makes the order clear, but exams usually expect the past perfect.

concepts.heading: Stative verbs
concepts.text: Verbs of state — know, believe, understand, love, hate, own, belong, seem, consist — are not normally used in continuous forms. 'I am understanding' should be 'I understand'.

concepts.heading: Future in time clauses
concepts.text: After 'when', 'if', 'as soon as', 'until' and 'before' referring to the future, use the simple present, not 'will': 'I will call you when I reach home', not 'when I will reach'. The present continuous can describe fixed future plans: 'We are meeting the branch manager tomorrow.' This is correct and should not be marked as an error. 'Will' is used for decisions made at the moment or predictions, while 'going to' shows intention or evidence: 'Look at those clouds — it is going to rain.'

shortcuts: A finished time marker (yesterday, last week, ago) rules out the present perfect.
'Since' + point in time and 'for' + duration both pair with perfect tenses.
'No sooner had… than', 'Hardly had… when' use the past perfect in the first clause.
'It is high time' + simple past: 'It is high time we started.'
'Would' in both clauses of a conditional is wrong: 'If I would know' → 'If I knew'.
Check the verb against the subject and the time marker together; most tense errors fail one of the two.

examples.question: Correct the error: 'I have submitted the form yesterday.'
examples.solution: 'Yesterday' is a finished time, so use the simple past: 'I submitted the form yesterday.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'I will inform you when the results will be declared.'
examples.solution: In a future time clause, use the simple present: 'I will inform you when the results are declared.'

examples.question: Correct the error: 'She is knowing the answer.'
examples.solution: 'Know' is a stative verb: 'She knows the answer.'

examples.question: Fill in: 'By the time the police arrived, the thieves ______ (escape).'
examples.solution: The escape happened before the police arrived (both past), so the earlier action takes past perfect: 'had escaped'.

examples.question: Fill in: 'He has been working at the bank ______ 2019.'
examples.solution: 2019 is a point in time, so 'since'. Answer: since.

examples.question: Correct the error: 'No sooner did he finish his speech when the audience started clapping.'
examples.solution: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', not 'when'. Correct: 'No sooner did he finish his speech than the audience started clapping.' The form 'No sooner had he finished… than' is also correct.

practice: Choose the correct form: 'I ______ him two days ago.'
'Two days ago' is a finished time in the past, so the simple past 'met' is correct, not the present perfect.
Choose the correct form: 'We will start the meeting as soon as the chairman ______.'
After 'as soon as' referring to the future, English uses the simple present. 'As soon as the chairman arrives' is correct.
Choose the correct form: 'The film ______ before we reached the theatre.'
The film started before another past action, our arrival. The earlier past action takes the past perfect 'had started'.
Choose the correct form: 'This laptop ______ to my brother.'
'Belong' is a stative verb and is not normally used in the continuous form. The simple present 'belongs' is correct.
Choose the correct form: 'If I ______ you, I would accept the offer.'
An unreal present condition uses 'were' for all subjects in the if-clause. 'If I were you, I would accept' is correct.
faqs: Is 'I have done it yesterday' acceptable in Indian English?

It is common in speech, but standard grammar and exam answer keys treat it as an error. A finished time like 'yesterday' requires the simple past: 'I did it yesterday.' Present perfect is used only when no finished past time is mentioned.
Why is 'when I will reach' wrong?

In English, clauses beginning with 'when', 'if', 'as soon as', 'before' and 'until' use the simple present to talk about the future. The main clause carries the future meaning: 'I will call you when I reach.' Using 'will' in both clauses is a common exam error.

items.title: Phrase Replacement and Word Usage Questions Explained
items.description: Phrase replacement and word usage for IBPS, SBI and RBI exams: fix the bold phrase, test a word in several sentences and avoid confusable-word traps.
items.intro: Phrase replacement questions bold a part of a sentence and ask which option should replace it, while word usage questions give a word and several sentences and ask in which sentence the word is used correctly or incorrectly. IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and clerk exams use both formats, often as sets of three to five questions. They combine grammar, idiom and vocabulary, and they reward slow, careful reading over quick guessing.

concepts.heading: Phrase replacement: identify the error type
concepts.text: Read the full sentence and decide what is wrong with the bold phrase: tense, agreement, preposition, idiom, parallelism or word choice. Then pick the option that fixes exactly that error without adding another. Many papers include 'No replacement required' as an option.

concepts.heading: Word usage: meaning and part of speech
concepts.text: A word like 'address' can be a noun ('my address') or a verb ('address the issue'). Word usage questions test whether the word fits each sentence in both meaning and grammar. Check each sentence independently rather than comparing them.

concepts.heading: Confusable words
concepts.text: Common pairs: affect (verb) and effect (noun), principal (main, or head of a school) and principle (rule), stationary (not moving) and stationery (paper and pens), complement (complete) and compliment (praise), loose and lose, council and counsel.

concepts.heading: Formal register
concepts.text: Bank-exam sentences usually come from editorials about economy and policy, so the correct option tends to be formal and precise. Casual words ('a lot of', 'got') in options are often weaker than formal equivalents ('considerable', 'received').

concepts.heading: Meaning must stay the same
concepts.text: The replacement must not change the sense of the sentence. If the original says a policy 'may' help, an option saying it 'will certainly' help changes the meaning and is wrong even if grammatical.

concepts.heading: Multiple correct sentences
concepts.text: Newer word-usage formats ask which sentences are correct, with options like 'Only A and C'. Judge every sentence carefully, because a single misjudgement changes the answer.

shortcuts: Read the option inside the sentence, not on its own.
If the bold part is idiomatic and correct, do not replace it just because an option looks more formal.
'Affect' is usually a verb and 'effect' usually a noun; 'to effect change' (bring about) is a formal exception.
Watch singular/plural carefully: 'one of the reasons' + 'is'.
For word usage, try replacing the word with a synonym; if the synonym fits, the usage is probably correct.
Eliminate options that are wordy or repeat meaning ('return back', 'combine together').
If two options differ only by an article or preposition, the question is testing that small word; check the fixed pairing first.

examples.question: Replace the bold part if needed: 'The new rules will **effect** small traders the most.'
examples.solution: The sentence needs a verb meaning 'influence', which is 'affect'. Replacement: 'affect'.

examples.question: Replace the bold part if needed: 'The company bought new **stationary** for its offices.'
examples.solution: Paper and pens are 'stationery'; 'stationary' means not moving. Replacement: 'stationery'.

examples.question: Replace the bold part if needed: 'She **is working here since** 2021.'
examples.solution: 'Since 2021' needs a perfect tense: 'has been working here since'.

examples.question: In which sentence is 'address' used incorrectly? (A) Please address the letter to the manager. (B) The minister will address the gathering. (C) We must address to the problem quickly.
examples.solution: As a verb meaning 'deal with', 'address' takes a direct object; 'address to the problem' is wrong. Answer: (C).

examples.question: Replace the bold part if needed: 'Inflation, along with rising interest rates, **are hurting** household budgets.'
examples.solution: 'Along with' does not change the subject 'Inflation', which is singular. Replacement: 'is hurting'.

practice: Replace the bold part if needed: 'The principal **complemented** the students on their results.'
Praising someone is 'complimenting' them. 'Complement' means to complete or go well with something, so it is wrong here.
Replace the bold part if needed: 'He was careful not to **loose** his ID card.'
The verb meaning to misplace is 'lose'. 'Loose' is an adjective meaning not tight, so the sentence needs 'lose'.
Replace the bold part if needed: 'The panel **gave a decision** after hearing both sides.'
The standard collocations are 'reach a decision' or 'take a decision'. 'Gave a decision' is not natural for a panel's conclusion.
In which sentence is 'book' used incorrectly?
The police booked him for speeding.
He read a book on banking.
'Book' as a verb means to reserve or to register a charge. 'They booked about the delay' has no clear meaning and is incorrect.
Replace the bold part if needed: 'Honesty is one of his strongest **principals**.'
A rule or belief is a 'principle'. 'Principal' means main or the head of a school, so 'principles' is required.
faqs: How is phrase replacement different from sentence improvement?

They are essentially the same task with different names. SSC tends to say 'sentence improvement' and bank exams 'phrase replacement'. Both require you to find the error in the bold or underlined part and choose a fix that keeps the meaning.
How do I prepare for word usage questions?

Learn common words that work as both nouns and verbs (address, book, check, plant, conduct) and the main confusable pairs. When reading, notice how such words are used in different contexts. Practising mixed sets of sentences builds the judgement these questions need.

items.title: Spelling Error Questions: Rules and Commonly Misspelt Words
items.description: Spot misspelt words in SSC and bank exams: doubling rules, ie versus ei, silent letters, -ance and -ence endings, and a list of frequently tested words.
items.intro: Spelling questions ask you to find the misspelt word among four options, or the correctly spelt one. SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS include them in most English sections, and bank exams occasionally hide a misspelt word inside error-detection or word-usage questions. Spelling looks like pure memory, but a handful of rules explain many of the tested words, and the rest come from a fairly stable list of frequently misspelt words that you can learn in a few weeks.

concepts.heading: Doubling the final consonant
concepts.text: In words where the stress falls on the last syllable and the word ends in one vowel plus one consonant, double the consonant before adding -ed or -ing: occur → occurred, begin → beginning, commit → committed. If the stress is not on the last syllable, do not double: benefit → benefited, offer → offered.

concepts.heading: ie and ei
concepts.text: The rhyme 'i before e except after c' works for many words: believe, achieve, receive, ceiling. Exceptions are tested often: seize, weird, foreign, height, neighbour, their.

concepts.heading: Silent letters
concepts.text: Many errors involve dropped silent letters: government (n), February (r), Wednesday (d), environment (n), knowledge (k), psychology (p), receipt (p), debt (b).

concepts.heading: -ance/-ence and -able/-ible
concepts.text: No simple rule covers all words, so learn the frequent ones: maintenance, guidance, existence, independence, occurrence, perseverance; responsible, accessible, eligible, available, reliable, noticeable.

concepts.heading: Double letters in the middle
concepts.text: Commonly tested: accommodation (double c, double m), committee (double m, double t, double e), embarrass (double r, double s), occasion (double c, single s), necessary (one c, double s), millennium (double l, double n), questionnaire (double n).

concepts.heading: British versus American spelling
concepts.text: Indian exams follow British spelling: colour, favour, programme (for a plan or show), centre, licence (noun) and license (verb), cheque, organise or organize (both accepted). Do not mark British forms as errors. Similarly, 'practice' is the noun and 'practise' the verb in British usage, while 'advice' (noun) and 'advise' (verb) differ in both spelling and pronunciation; exam sentences sometimes test these pairs inside error-spotting questions.

shortcuts: 'Necessary': one collar (c), two sleeves (s).
'Separate' has 'a rat' in it: sep-a-rate.
'Accommodate' has room for two c's and two m's.
'Definitely' comes from 'finite': defin-ite-ly, not 'definately'.
'Privilege' has no 'd': privi-lege.
Read each option letter by letter; spelling questions punish skimming.
Words ending in silent e usually drop it before -ing (write → writing) but keep it before -ment (manage → management, except argument and judgment).
'Leisure', 'seize', 'weird', 'foreign' and 'height' break the 'i before e except after c' rule; memorise them as a set.

examples.question: Find the misspelt word: (a) accommodation (b) committee (c) occassion (d) necessary.
examples.solution: 'Occasion' has double c and a single s. 'Occassion' is wrong. Answer: (c).

examples.question: Find the correctly spelt word: (a) recieve (b) receive (c) receeve (d) riceive.
examples.solution: After 'c', the order is 'ei': receive. Answer: (b).

examples.question: Find the misspelt word: (a) beginning (b) occurred (c) comitted (d) referred.
examples.solution: 'Commit' has a double m, and because the stress falls on the last syllable, the t doubles before -ed: 'committed'. 'Comitted' drops one m. Answer: (c).

examples.question: Find the misspelt word: (a) government (b) enviroment (c) February (d) knowledge.
examples.solution: 'Environment' contains a silent n before -ment. 'Enviroment' is wrong. Answer: (b).

examples.question: Find the correctly spelt word: (a) maintainance (b) maintenence (c) maintenance (d) maintanance.
examples.solution: The noun drops the 'ai' of 'maintain': maint-e-nance. Answer: (c).

examples.question: Find the misspelt word: (a) independence (b) perseverence (c) existence (d) occurrence.
examples.solution: The noun from 'persevere' is 'perseverance', with -ance. 'Perseverence' is wrong. The other three correctly end in -ence. Answer: (b).

practice: 'Embarrass' has a double r and a double s. 'Embarass' with a single r is the misspelt option.
The word comes from 'definite', so it is spelt d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e-l-y. The other forms are common misspellings.
'Weird' is an exception to the 'i before e' rule and is spelt w-e-i-r-d. 'Wierd' is incorrect.
The correct spelling is s-e-p-a-r-a-t-e, with 'a' in the middle. 'Seperate' is the most common misspelling.
'Privilege' has no letter d. 'Priviledge' is the misspelt option; the other three words are spelt correctly.
faqs: Are American spellings marked wrong in Indian exams?

Indian exams generally follow British spelling, so 'colour' and 'programme' are standard. American forms are rarely the only options. If a question offers both 'colour' and 'color' as separate choices, look for the clearly misspelt word instead, because setters avoid testing regional variants.
How can I improve spelling quickly?

Collect the 150 to 200 most frequently misspelt words from SSC papers and practice books, write each correctly three times, and test yourself weekly. Pay attention to double letters and silent letters, which cause most errors. Reading carefully also helps, since you start noticing correct forms.

items.title: Sentence Connectors and Linkers: Choosing the Right Joiner
items.description: Sentence connector questions for IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI: contrast, cause, addition and condition linkers, sentence-combining rules and grammar fit.
items.intro: Connector questions give two sentences and ask which word or phrase can join them into one meaningful sentence, or which connector fits a blank. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B have used several variants — 'starters', 'connectors' and 'column-matching' — usually as sets of three to five questions. Success depends on two checks: the logical relationship between the sentences (contrast, cause, addition, condition) and the grammar the connector needs (a clause, a noun phrase or an -ing form).

concepts.heading: Contrast
concepts.text: Although, though, even though, whereas, while + clause; despite, in spite of + noun or -ing; however, nevertheless + new sentence. 'Despite the rain, the match continued' but 'Although it rained, the match continued'.

concepts.heading: Cause and result
concepts.text: Because, since, as + clause give the reason; because of, due to, owing to + noun. So, therefore, hence and consequently introduce the result. 'Owing to heavy traffic, he was late.'

concepts.heading: Addition
concepts.text: Moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides, not only… but also. These add a point in the same direction and should not join sentences that contrast.

concepts.heading: Condition and purpose
concepts.text: If, unless, provided that, as long as, in case + clause for conditions; so that, in order to + purpose. 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it should not be followed by a negative.

concepts.heading: Sentence starters
concepts.text: Some questions ask which word could begin the combined sentence. 'Despite' at the start needs a noun phrase next ('Despite his efforts…'), 'Having' needs a participle structure ('Having completed the form, she…'), and 'Not only' needs inversion ('Not only did he…').

concepts.heading: Meaning must not change
concepts.text: The combined sentence must keep the meaning of both originals. If the second sentence explains the first, a contrast connector distorts the meaning, even if the grammar works.

shortcuts: First label the relationship: contrast, cause, result, addition or condition. Then pick from that group only.
'Despite of' is always wrong; use 'despite' or 'in spite of'.
'Although… but' is wrong in standard English; use one connector only.
'Due to' is safest after a form of 'be': 'The delay was due to rain.'
When the starter is an -ing word, the subject of both clauses must be the same person or thing.
'Not only' at the start forces question order: 'Not only did the bank cut rates, but it also…'

examples.question: Join: 'The company made record sales. It reported a loss.' Choose: Because, Although, Moreover, So.
examples.solution: Record sales and a loss contrast with each other. 'Although the company made record sales, it reported a loss.' Answer: Although.

examples.question: Join: 'Heavy rain lashed the city. Schools were closed.' Choose: Despite, Owing to, However, Unless.
examples.solution: Rain is the cause and closure the result. 'Owing to heavy rain, schools in the city were closed.' Answer: Owing to.

examples.question: Starting with 'Despite', combine: 'He prepared well. He could not clear the cut-off.'
examples.solution: 'Despite' needs a noun phrase: 'Despite preparing well, he could not clear the cut-off' or 'Despite his good preparation, he…'.

examples.question: Starting with 'Not only', combine: 'The bank reduced loan rates. It waived processing fees.'
examples.solution: 'Not only did the bank reduce loan rates, but it also waived processing fees.' Inversion ('did the bank reduce') is required after 'Not only'.

examples.question: Join: 'You submit the documents. Your application will not be processed.' Choose: Unless, If, Although, Since.
examples.solution: The second sentence describes what happens when documents are not submitted: 'Unless you submit the documents, your application will not be processed.' Answer: Unless.

practice: Join: 'She was tired. She finished the report.' Choose the best connector.
Being tired and still finishing the report show contrast. 'Though she was tired, she finished the report' keeps the meaning.
Which starter correctly combines: 'The train was delayed. Many passengers missed their connecting flights.'
Because of the delay of the train
The delay caused the missed flights, so a cause connector with a noun phrase fits. 'Because of the delay of the train, many passengers missed…' works.
Despite of the rain, the event continued.
In spite of the rain, the event continued.
Although it rained, but the event continued.
Despite it rained, the event continued.
'In spite of' is followed by a noun phrase. 'Despite of' and 'although… but' are errors, and 'despite' cannot take a full clause.
Join: 'The scheme is simple. It is free.' Choose the best connector.
Both sentences give positive points in the same direction, so an addition connector fits. 'The scheme is simple; moreover, it is free.'
Having completed the training, the branch welcomed her.
Having completing the training, she joined.
Having complete the training, she joined the branch.
Having completed the training, she joined the branch.
The -ing participle clause must share its subject with the main clause and use 'having' plus past participle. Only 'Having completed the training, she joined the branch' meets both conditions.
faqs: Why is 'Although… but' wrong?

Each connector already links the two clauses. Using both 'although' and 'but' joins the same pair twice. Standard English uses only one: 'Although it rained, the event continued' or 'It rained, but the event continued.' Indian speakers often use both, so exams test it.
What is a dangling participle in starter questions?

It is an -ing or 'having' clause whose subject does not match the main clause. 'Having completed the training, the branch welcomed her' suggests the branch completed the training. Make sure the person doing the action in the opening clause is the subject right after the comma.

items.title: Para Summary Questions for CAT and MBA Entrances
items.description: Solve para summary questions in CAT, CMAT and MAT: find the core idea, avoid detail-only and extreme options, and judge scope with worked examples.
items.intro: Para summary questions give a short paragraph and four options, and ask which option best captures its essence. CAT includes a few of them in the verbal section every year, and CMAT, MAT and some bank mains papers use similar 'main idea' or 'best summary' questions. Unlike reading comprehension, there is no long passage — but the options are deliberately close, so the skill is judging scope precisely: not too narrow, not too broad, and not adding anything new.

concepts.heading: Find the core claim
concepts.text: Most paragraphs have one central claim and supporting material — examples, data, background. Before reading the options, write the core claim in under 15 words. If you cannot, read the paragraph again focusing on its first and last sentences.

concepts.heading: Scope: not too narrow, not too broad
concepts.text: An option that covers only an example is too narrow. An option that generalises beyond the paragraph ('all economies', 'always') is too broad. The correct summary matches the paragraph's own scope.

concepts.heading: No new information
concepts.text: A summary must not add ideas, causes or recommendations absent from the paragraph. Options that sound sensible but bring in outside reasoning are traps.

concepts.heading: Keep the author's stance
concepts.text: If the author is cautious ('may', 'some evidence suggests'), the summary must be cautious too. If the author criticises a view, the summary must reflect that criticism, not simply state the view.

concepts.heading: Contrast paragraphs
concepts.text: Many paragraphs present a common belief and then challenge it. The summary should capture the challenge, since that is the author's point. Options that repeat only the common belief are wrong.

concepts.heading: Elimination works best
concepts.text: Rather than looking for a perfect option, eliminate those that are too narrow, too broad, distorted or add new ideas. The last one standing is usually right, even if its wording is not how you would have put it.

shortcuts: Read the first and last sentences twice; the core claim usually sits in one of them.
Cross out examples and statistics mentally; they are support, not the summary.
Watch for changed modals: 'can' versus 'will', 'some' versus 'most'.
If two options look similar, compare them word by word and find the one that distorts.
Do not choose an option just because it uses the paragraph's exact words; correct summaries often paraphrase.
If an option would fit a different paragraph on the same topic equally well, it is probably too broad.

examples.question: Paragraph: 'Digital payments in India have grown rapidly, driven by cheap smartphones and interoperable systems like UPI. Yet a sizeable share of small transactions in rural markets still happens in cash, as many sellers worry about connectivity and unfamiliar dispute processes.' Best summary?
examples.solution: Core claim: digital payments have grown fast, but cash persists in rural small transactions due to practical concerns. An option saying only 'UPI made payments interoperable' is too narrow; 'Cash will soon disappear' contradicts the paragraph. The best option balances growth with continuing rural cash use and its reasons.

examples.question: Paragraph: 'It is often assumed that higher interest rates always cool inflation quickly. However, when inflation is driven by supply shocks such as poor harvests, rate hikes act slowly and may hurt growth before prices respond.' Best summary?
examples.solution: The author challenges the belief that rate hikes always work quickly, especially for supply-driven inflation. A summary stating 'Rate hikes control inflation' repeats the belief being challenged. The best summary: rate hikes are less effective and slower against supply-driven inflation.

examples.question: Paragraph: 'Some studies suggest that short daily revision sessions improve long-term recall more than occasional long sessions.' Which summary is best? (a) Long study sessions are useless. (b) Frequent short revision may aid long-term memory better than infrequent long sessions. (c) Students should revise for exactly 20 minutes daily.
examples.solution: (a) is extreme and (c) adds a specific number not in the paragraph. (b) keeps the cautious 'may' and the comparison. Answer: (b).

practice: Paragraph: 'Many first-time investors chase recent top performers, but past returns often fail to predict future performance, especially over short periods.' Best summary?
Recent strong returns are an unreliable guide to future returns, particularly in the short term.
Investors should never invest in top-performing funds.
Past returns always predict future returns.
First-time investors earn the highest returns.
The paragraph cautions that past returns are unreliable predictors, especially short term. The other options are extreme, reversed or unsupported by the text.
Paragraph: 'Libraries in several cities are reinventing themselves as community spaces, hosting workshops and digital-skills classes alongside lending books.' Best summary?
Some urban libraries are expanding their role beyond book lending into community activities.
Digital-skills classes are the only reason people visit libraries.
All libraries in India now host workshops.
The paragraph describes libraries adding activities alongside lending. The correct option keeps 'some' and 'beyond lending' without exaggerating scope.
Which option is usually WRONG as a para summary?
One that paraphrases the main claim
One that keeps the author's cautious tone
One that summarises only an example used in the paragraph
One that matches the paragraph's scope
A summary built only on an example is too narrow because it misses the central claim. The other three describe features of a good summary.
Paragraph: 'While remote work saves commuting time, managers report that informal learning among junior staff has declined.' Best summary?
Commuting time has increased for everyone.
Junior staff prefer working from office.
Remote work offers time savings but may reduce informal learning for junior employees.
The paragraph balances a benefit with a reported drawback. Only the option mentioning both time savings and reduced informal learning captures both sides without adding a new claim.
In para summary questions, what should you do with statistics and examples in the paragraph?
Treat them as support for the core claim, not the summary itself
Include all of them in your answer
Choose the option with the most numbers
Examples and data support the main idea. A good summary states the central claim they support rather than repeating the supporting details.
faqs: How long should a good summary option be?

Length does not decide correctness. Some correct summaries are short; others are long because the paragraph has two balanced ideas. Judge scope, tone and accuracy instead. A long option is wrong if it adds ideas, and a short one is wrong if it leaves out the core claim.
Is para summary the same as finding the title of a passage?

They are related but not identical. A title can be catchy and brief, while a summary must capture the central claim accurately and completely. In para summary questions, prefer the option that states the idea clearly, even if it would make a dull title.

items.title: Odd Sentence Out: Spotting the Sentence That Does Not Fit
items.description: Odd sentence out questions for CAT and bank mains: find the coherent group, test pronoun and topic links, and spot same-topic but off-focus sentences.
items.intro: Odd sentence out (odd one out in para jumbles) gives four or five sentences, all but one of which form a coherent paragraph. You must find the sentence that does not belong. CAT asks a few every year in its verbal section, and IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B mains have used similar 'find the incoherent sentence' formats. The trap is that the odd sentence is usually on the same broad topic; it differs in focus, time frame or tone rather than subject.

concepts.heading: Build the paragraph first
concepts.text: Try to arrange the sentences into a logical order, as in a para jumble. The sentence that refuses to attach to any other, or breaks the chain wherever you place it, is the odd one.

concepts.heading: Same topic, different focus
concepts.text: If four sentences discuss the causes of urban flooding and one discusses the history of a city's drainage department, all mention drainage, but the fifth shifts focus. Topic overlap alone does not make a sentence fit.

concepts.heading: Linking words and pronouns
concepts.text: Sentences in a coherent paragraph are linked by pronouns ('this', 'they'), repeated nouns and connectors. A sentence with no link to the others, or whose pronoun has nothing to refer to, is a strong candidate.

concepts.heading: Tone and perspective
concepts.text: A shift from neutral analysis to personal opinion, or from general discussion to a narrow anecdote, often marks the odd sentence.

concepts.heading: Time frame
concepts.text: If four sentences describe current trends and one describes a historical event without a bridge to the present, the historical one may be the odd sentence.

concepts.heading: Watch for the decoy
concepts.text: Setters sometimes include a sentence that seems odd because it introduces a contrast ('However…'), but it actually fits as the turn in the argument. Check whether a contrast sentence links back to an earlier point before marking it odd.

shortcuts: Find a pair of sentences that clearly link; build outward from that pair.
Identify the paragraph's specific focus in one phrase, then test each sentence against it.
A sentence stating a general fact that the others do not develop is often the odd one.
Do not mark a sentence odd just because it starts with 'However' or 'But'.
In CAT, write the sentence numbers in your arranged order on the rough sheet; the leftover number is your answer.
If two sentences seem odd, the one that cannot be placed anywhere is the answer; the other usually fits at the start or end.

examples.question: 1. Small finance banks were set up to serve underbanked customers. 2. They focus on small loans to micro-enterprises and farmers. 3. Many of them grew out of microfinance institutions. 4. The Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935. 5. Their deposit base has been growing steadily. Which sentence is odd?
examples.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 discuss small finance banks, linked by 'They', 'them' and 'Their'. Sentence 4 mentions banking but gives an unrelated historical fact about the RBI. Answer: 4.

examples.question: 1. Regular exercise improves heart health. 2. It also helps manage stress. 3. However, many urban professionals find little time for it. 4. Short workouts at home can solve this problem. 5. Gyms charge high membership fees in metro cities. Which is odd?
examples.solution: 1–4 form a chain: benefit, more benefit, problem (time), solution. Sentence 5 shifts to gym costs, which none of the others discuss. Note that 3, starting with 'However', fits as the turn. Answer: 5.

examples.question: 1. Monsoon rainfall is vital for Indian agriculture. 2. A weak monsoon can reduce kharif output. 3. This often pushes up food prices. 4. Higher food prices affect household budgets. 5. The word 'monsoon' comes from an Arabic word for season. Which is odd?
examples.solution: 1–4 form a cause–effect chain from rainfall to budgets. Sentence 5 is a word-origin fact with no link to the chain. Answer: 5.

practice: 1. Online learning platforms have grown rapidly. 2. They allow students to learn at their own pace. 3. The printing press was invented in the fifteenth century. 4. Many offer free courses from leading institutions. Which sentence is odd?
Sentences 1, 2 and 4 discuss online learning platforms and are linked by 'They' and 'Many'. Sentence 3 is an unrelated historical fact.
Which feature most often marks the odd sentence?
It shares the broad topic but shifts focus
The odd sentence usually stays on the broad subject but moves to a different focus or time frame. A 'However' sentence often fits as the turn in the argument.

1. Electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions. 2. Their batteries, however, need critical minerals. 3. Mining these minerals raises environmental concerns. 4. Cricket is the most popular sport in India. Which is odd?
Sentences 1 to 3 form a chain about electric vehicles, batteries and mining. Sentence 4 has no link to that chain, so it does not belong.
1. Savings rates among young earners have fallen. 2. Rising rents take a large share of income. 3. Easy credit encourages spending. 4. The rupee was decimalised in 1957. Which is odd?
Sentences 1 to 3 discuss why young earners save less. Sentence 4 is a historical fact about currency that does not explain falling savings.
When two sentences both seem odd, how should you decide?
Choose the one that cannot be placed anywhere in the paragraph
Choose the one with a pronoun
One of the two usually fits at the start or end as an introduction or conclusion. The sentence that cannot be linked anywhere is the real odd one out.
faqs: Is odd sentence out asked with options in CAT?

In recent CAT patterns it has usually been a type-in-the-answer question without options, so you must enter the number of the odd sentence. Check the official pattern for the current year. Without options, careful paragraph-building matters even more than in MCQ versions.
How is it different from a normal para jumble?

In a para jumble every sentence belongs and you find the order. In odd sentence out, one sentence does not belong, so you build the paragraph and identify the leftover. The skills overlap heavily, so practising both together is efficient.

items.title: RBI and Monetary Policy Basics: Repo, CRR, SLR and MPC
items.description: Static RBI notes for bank exams: history, functions, the Monetary Policy Committee, and how repo, SDF, MSF, CRR, SLR and OMOs work, explained simply.
items.intro: Questions on the Reserve Bank of India and monetary policy are certain in RBI Grade B Phase I, IBPS PO and SBI PO mains, JAIIB and CAIIB, and they come up in almost every bank interview. Rates change through the year, so this page focuses on the stable framework: what the RBI is, who sets policy, and how each tool works. For the latest rate figures, always check the RBI's most recent monetary policy statement on rbi.org.in.

concepts.heading: Origin and status
concepts.text: The RBI was set up on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. It was nationalised in 1949 and is wholly owned by the Government of India. Its central office is in Mumbai. It issues currency notes (except the one-rupee note, which the Government issues), regulates banks, manages foreign exchange under FEMA, acts as banker to the government and banks, and oversees payment systems.

concepts.heading: Monetary Policy Committee
concepts.text: Since 2016, under amendments to the RBI Act, a six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets the policy repo rate. Three members are from the RBI, including the Governor, who has a casting vote, and three are external members appointed by the central government. The framework is flexible inflation targeting based on CPI inflation; the target band has been 4% with a tolerance of ±2%. Check the RBI for the current target period.

concepts.heading: Policy rates
concepts.text: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against government securities overnight. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), introduced in 2022, lets banks park surplus funds with the RBI without collateral and forms the floor of the policy corridor. The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) lets banks borrow overnight at a rate above repo in emergencies and forms the ceiling. The bank rate is aligned with the MSF rate.

concepts.heading: Reserve requirements
concepts.text: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is the share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that must be kept as cash balance with the RBI; it earns no interest. The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is the share that banks must hold in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities.

concepts.heading: Open market operations
concepts.text: Through open market operations (OMOs), the RBI buys government securities to inject liquidity or sells them to absorb it. Variable-rate repo and reverse repo auctions fine-tune short-term liquidity.

concepts.heading: Direction of policy
concepts.text: To fight inflation, the RBI may raise the repo rate or tighten liquidity, making loans costlier. To support growth, it may cut rates or add liquidity. Policy works with a lag, often several quarters, before it fully affects prices and output.

shortcuts: Corridor: SDF at the bottom, repo in the middle, MSF at the top.
CRR is held with the RBI as cash; SLR is held by the bank itself in liquid assets.
MPC: six members, Governor's casting vote, decision by majority.
Higher CRR or repo → less money with banks → tighter policy (hawkish).
The RBI is the lender of last resort to banks.
Learn the concept now; update the actual rate numbers from the latest policy before your exam.

examples.question: The RBI raises the repo rate. What is the likely effect on home-loan EMIs linked to an external benchmark?
examples.solution: Many floating home loans are linked to the repo rate through the external benchmark lending rate. A repo hike raises the benchmark, so the loan rate and either the EMI or the tenure increases after the reset date.

examples.question: A bank has net demand and time liabilities of ₹10,000 crore. If CRR were 4%, how much must it keep with the RBI?
examples.solution: 4% of ₹10,000 crore = ₹400 crore, held as cash balance with the RBI. (The 4% figure is only for illustration; check the current CRR.)

examples.question: Which tool would the RBI use to absorb surplus liquidity overnight without giving collateral to banks?
examples.solution: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) absorbs liquidity without the RBI having to provide government securities as collateral. That is why it replaced the fixed-rate reverse repo as the floor of the corridor.

examples.question: Who has the casting vote in the MPC if votes are tied?
examples.solution: The RBI Governor. With six members, a 3–3 tie is possible, and the Governor's second or casting vote decides.

practice: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?
The RBI began operations on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act of 1934. It was nationalised later, in 1949.
How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
The MPC has six members: three from the RBI, including the Governor, and three external members appointed by the central government.
Which facility forms the floor of the RBI's liquidity adjustment corridor?
Since 2022 the Standing Deposit Facility, which absorbs surplus funds without collateral, has formed the floor of the corridor. MSF forms the ceiling.
Banks must keep a portion of their liabilities as cash balance with the RBI. What is this called?
The Cash Reserve Ratio is the share of net demand and time liabilities held as cash with the RBI. SLR is held by banks in liquid assets.
When the RBI buys government securities in the open market, what is the effect on liquidity?
Buying securities pays money to banks, which adds rupee liquidity to the system. Selling securities has the opposite effect.
faqs: Should I memorise the current repo rate for bank exams?

Yes, but only from the latest RBI policy statement shortly before your exam, because rates can change at any of the policy meetings held during the year. Learn the concepts and relationships now, and keep a small updated note of the current repo, SDF, MSF, CRR and SLR figures.
What is the difference between repo and reverse repo today?

Repo is the RBI lending to banks against securities. The fixed-rate reverse repo still exists but is no longer the floor of the corridor; the Standing Deposit Facility took that role in 2022. For current rates and their roles, refer to the RBI's latest monetary policy statement.

items.title: Indian Banking Structure: Scheduled, Commercial, Co-op
items.description: Indian banking structure for exams: scheduled and non-scheduled banks, public, private and foreign banks, RRBs, small finance, payments and co-op banks.
items.intro: Understanding how Indian banks are classified is basic banking awareness for RBI Grade B, IBPS and SBI mains, JAIIB, and bank interviews. Questions ask which schedule makes a bank 'scheduled', who owns regional rural banks, what payments banks cannot do, and which year banks were nationalised. These facts are stable and appear year after year, so learning the structure once pays off across exams.

concepts.heading: Scheduled and non-scheduled banks
concepts.text: Scheduled banks are those listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934. They must meet RBI criteria and can access RBI facilities such as refinance. Non-scheduled banks are not in the schedule. Most commercial banks in India are scheduled.

concepts.heading: Commercial banks
concepts.text: Public sector banks are majority-owned by the government, such as SBI and Bank of Baroda. Private sector banks are majority-owned by private shareholders. Foreign banks operate in India through branches or wholly owned subsidiaries. Regional rural banks, small finance banks and payments banks are also commercial banks with special licences.

concepts.heading: Regional rural banks
concepts.text: RRBs were set up under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 to serve rural areas, with the first RRBs established in 1975 under an ordinance. Their share capital is held by the central government (50%), the sponsor bank (35%) and the state government (15%). Several rounds of amalgamation have reduced their number.

concepts.heading: Small finance and payments banks
concepts.text: Small finance banks provide basic banking and lending mainly to small businesses, farmers and the unorganised sector, with priority sector lending requirements higher than those for universal banks. Payments banks accept deposits up to a limit set by the RBI, offer remittances and issue debit cards, but cannot lend or issue credit cards. Check the RBI for the current deposit limit.

concepts.heading: Cooperative banks
concepts.text: Cooperative banks are owned by their members. Urban cooperative banks serve towns and cities. The rural short-term structure has three tiers: State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies. Since the 2020 amendment to the Banking Regulation Act, the RBI's supervisory powers over cooperative banks have been strengthened.

concepts.heading: Nationalisation milestones
concepts.text: The Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India in 1955. Fourteen major banks were nationalised in July 1969 and six more in April 1980. Later decades saw mergers that reduced the number of public sector banks.

shortcuts: Second Schedule of the RBI Act = scheduled bank.
RRB ownership: 50 : 35 : 15 (Centre : sponsor bank : state).
Payments banks: deposits yes, lending no, credit cards no.
Nationalisation: 14 banks in 1969, 6 banks in 1980.
SBI was formed in 1955 from the Imperial Bank of India.
Rural cooperative short-term structure: StCB → DCCB → PACS.

examples.question: A new payments bank wants to offer personal loans to its customers. Is this allowed?
examples.solution: No. Payments banks may accept deposits up to the RBI's limit, provide remittance services and issue debit cards, but they are not permitted to lend. They could distribute loans of other institutions as an agent, but not lend from their own books.

examples.question: An RRB has total share capital of ₹100 crore. How much would the sponsor bank hold?
examples.solution: Under the standard pattern, the sponsor bank holds 35%, so ₹35 crore. The central government holds ₹50 crore and the state government ₹15 crore.

examples.question: What makes a bank a 'scheduled bank'?
examples.solution: Inclusion in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934. The RBI includes banks that meet criteria such as minimum paid-up capital and reserves, and conduct their affairs in a way not detrimental to depositors.

examples.question: Interview question: 'Why were banks nationalised in 1969?'
examples.solution: A balanced answer: to extend banking to rural areas and neglected sectors such as agriculture and small industry, to direct credit according to national priorities, and to reduce the concentration of banking in the hands of a few business groups.

practice: Banks listed in which schedule of the RBI Act are called scheduled banks?
Scheduled banks are those included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, which gives them access to RBI facilities.
What share of an RRB's capital is held by the sponsor bank?
Under the RRB Act, the share capital is split as 50% central government, 35% sponsor bank and 15% state government.
Which of these can a payments bank NOT do?
Payments banks are licensed for deposits within the RBI limit, remittances and debit cards, but they are not permitted to lend money.
How many banks were nationalised in 1969?
Fourteen major commercial banks were nationalised in July 1969. A further six banks were nationalised in April 1980.
The State Bank of India was formed in 1955 from which bank?
The Imperial Bank of India was converted into the State Bank of India in 1955. The Imperial Bank itself had been formed by merging three presidency banks.
faqs: Are small finance banks the same as payments banks?

No. Both are niche licences introduced around 2015, but small finance banks can lend and accept deposits like regular banks with a focus on underserved customers, while payments banks cannot lend at all. Some small finance banks have applied to convert into universal banks.
How many public sector banks are there now?

The number has fallen through mergers, especially the major consolidation that took effect in April 2020. Since further changes are possible, verify the current count and list from the Department of Financial Services or RBI before your exam rather than relying on older study material.

items.title: Financial Inclusion Schemes: PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY, APY
items.description: Static notes on India's financial inclusion schemes for bank exams: PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana, Mudra and Stand-Up India, with key features.
items.intro: Government financial inclusion schemes are a favourite in RBI Grade B, IBPS and SBI mains, JAIIB, and bank interviews, where candidates are often asked to explain a scheme to a rural customer. The launch years, target groups and basic structure of these schemes are stable, but premiums, cover amounts and limits are revised from time to time. Learn the structure from this page and confirm the current figures on the official scheme or Department of Financial Services websites before your exam.

concepts.heading: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)
concepts.text: Launched in August 2014 to give every household access to a basic bank account. Accounts can be opened with zero balance, come with a RuPay debit card with accident insurance cover, and are eligible for an overdraft facility subject to conditions. PMJDY accounts are widely used for direct benefit transfers.

concepts.heading: PMJJBY and PMSBY
concepts.text: Both launched in 2015 and run through banks with auto-debit. Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana is a one-year renewable life insurance cover of ₹2 lakh for death from any cause, for account holders in a specified age band. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana is a one-year accident cover of ₹2 lakh for accidental death or total disability (₹1 lakh for partial disability). Premiums were revised in 2022; check the current figures.

concepts.heading: Atal Pension Yojana (APY)
concepts.text: Launched in 2015 for workers mainly in the unorganised sector, administered by PFRDA. Subscribers join between 18 and 40 years of age and choose a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 from age 60, with contributions depending on age at entry and the pension chosen. Income-tax payers have been excluded from joining since October 2022.

concepts.heading: Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY)
concepts.text: Launched in 2015 for non-farm micro and small enterprises, offering collateral-free loans through banks, NBFCs and MFIs in categories: Shishu (smallest loans), Kishore and Tarun. The upper limits of the categories have been revised over time, including a new Tarun Plus category; verify current limits from the Mudra website.

concepts.heading: Stand-Up India
concepts.text: Launched in 2016 to support at least one SC or ST borrower and at least one woman borrower per bank branch in setting up a greenfield enterprise, with loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore.

shortcuts: 2014: PMJDY. 2015: PMJJBY, PMSBY, APY, Mudra. 2016: Stand-Up India.
PMJJBY = life cover (any cause); PMSBY = accident cover only.
APY is administered by PFRDA; pension starts at 60.
Mudra loan categories in increasing size: Shishu → Kishore → Tarun.
Stand-Up India targets SC/ST and women entrepreneurs for greenfield projects.
For premiums, limits and age bands, always confirm the latest official figures.

examples.question: A 30-year-old customer asks which scheme covers death due to illness. What would you suggest?
examples.solution: PMSBY covers only accidents. For death from any cause, including illness, PMJJBY is the relevant scheme, as it provides ₹2 lakh life cover. The customer can enrol through their bank with auto-debit of the annual premium.

examples.question: A street vendor needs a small collateral-free loan to buy a cart. Which scheme fits?
examples.solution: The Shishu category of the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana is meant for the smallest loans to micro-enterprises and does not require collateral. (Vendors may also qualify for PM SVANidhi, a separate scheme for street vendors.)

examples.question: A 45-year-old wants to join Atal Pension Yojana. Can she?
examples.solution: No. APY entry is allowed only between 18 and 40 years of age. She could consider other options such as the National Pension System.

examples.question: Interview question: 'How has PMJDY helped direct benefit transfer?'
examples.solution: PMJDY gave crores of people a bank account, and linking these accounts with Aadhaar and mobile numbers allowed subsidies and benefits to be credited directly. This reduced leakages and middlemen, though challenges such as dormant accounts and last-mile access remain.

practice: In which year was Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana launched?
PMJDY was launched in August 2014 as a national mission to provide universal access to basic bank accounts.
Which scheme provides accident insurance cover through banks?
Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana is an accident insurance scheme. PMJJBY provides life cover for death from any cause.
Which body administers Atal Pension Yojana?
Atal Pension Yojana is administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, which also regulates the National Pension System.
What is the order of Mudra loan categories from smallest to largest?
Mudra categories grow with the stage of business: Shishu for the smallest loans, then Kishore, then Tarun for larger loans.
Stand-Up India supports which groups of entrepreneurs?
Stand-Up India aims to finance at least one SC or ST borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch for greenfield enterprises.
faqs: Why do premiums of PMJJBY and PMSBY differ in older books?

Premiums were revised in 2022 after years at the original level, so older material shows outdated amounts. Cover amounts and age limits may also be revised. Always confirm the figures on the official Jan Suraksha or Department of Financial Services website before an exam or interview.
Are financial inclusion schemes asked in prelims?

Bank prelims usually do not have a General Awareness section, so these questions appear mainly in mains papers, RBI Grade B Phase I, JAIIB and CAIIB, and interviews. SSC General Awareness also asks scheme launch years and objectives occasionally.

items.title: Union Budget Terms: Fiscal, Revenue and Primary Deficit
items.description: Union Budget terms for exams: Article 112, revenue versus capital, fiscal, revenue, effective revenue and primary deficit, with worked number examples.
items.intro: Budget terminology is tested in RBI Grade B (economic and social issues and GA), IBPS and SBI mains, SSC CGL and CHSL General Awareness, and CMAT. Every year's budget numbers change, but the definitions do not: what counts as revenue or capital, and how the different deficits are calculated. Once these definitions are clear, you can read any budget headline and answer conceptual or numerical questions with confidence.

concepts.heading: Constitutional basis
concepts.text: The Union Budget is called the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 of the Constitution. Money bills are defined in Article 110. Government money flows through the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266), the Contingency Fund of India (Article 267) and the Public Account.

concepts.heading: Revenue and capital
concepts.text: Revenue receipts (taxes, dividends, interest received) neither create liabilities nor reduce assets. Capital receipts do one of those, for example borrowings, loan recoveries and disinvestment. Revenue expenditure (salaries, interest, subsidies) creates no assets; capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities, for example building roads or repaying loans.

concepts.heading: Fiscal deficit
concepts.text: Fiscal deficit is the government's total borrowing requirement for the year.
concepts.formula: Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)

concepts.heading: Revenue and primary deficit
concepts.text: Revenue deficit shows whether day-to-day spending is covered by revenue income. Primary deficit removes interest payments from the fiscal deficit to show current borrowing needs excluding past debt.
concepts.formula: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts; Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments

concepts.heading: Effective revenue deficit
concepts.text: Effective revenue deficit is the revenue deficit minus grants given for the creation of capital assets, recognising that some revenue spending (grants to states for asset creation) actually builds assets.

concepts.heading: Vote on account and interim budget
concepts.text: A vote on account allows the government to draw money from the Consolidated Fund for a short period until the full budget is passed, usually in an election year. An interim budget presents a short-term statement of accounts in such years.

shortcuts: Non-debt capital receipts = loan recoveries + disinvestment and similar receipts.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
Zero primary deficit means the government is borrowing only to pay interest on past debt.
Article 112 = Annual Financial Statement; Article 110 = Money Bill.
Deficits are usually quoted as a percentage of GDP.
Use only the latest Budget documents (indiabudget.gov.in) for current deficit targets.
Gross fiscal deficit includes borrowing to pay interest; that is why primary deficit is always smaller than fiscal deficit when interest payments are positive.

examples.question: Illustrative figures (₹ lakh crore): total expenditure 50, revenue receipts 33, non-debt capital receipts 1, interest payments 11, revenue expenditure 38. Find the fiscal, primary and revenue deficits.
examples.solution: Fiscal deficit = 50 − (33 + 1) = 16. Primary deficit = 16 − 11 = 5. Revenue deficit = 38 − 33 = 5. These are teaching numbers, not actual budget data.

examples.question: Total expenditure is 20, revenue receipts 12, non-debt capital receipts 2 and interest payments 4. Find the fiscal and primary deficits.
examples.solution: Fiscal deficit = 20 − (12 + 2) = 6. Primary deficit = 6 − 4 = 2.

examples.question: Is money raised by selling a part of the government's stake in a public sector company a revenue or a capital receipt?
examples.solution: Disinvestment reduces the government's assets, so it is a capital receipt (a non-debt capital receipt). It reduces the fiscal deficit without adding debt.

examples.question: Revenue expenditure is 15 and revenue receipts are 12. What is the revenue deficit, and what does it signal?
examples.solution: Revenue deficit = 15 − 12 = 3. It shows that part of day-to-day spending is being financed by borrowing or capital receipts, which is generally seen as weaker fiscal quality.

practice: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Union Budget presented as the Annual Financial Statement?
Article 112 requires the President to cause the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before Parliament each year.
If fiscal deficit is ₹6 lakh crore and interest payments are ₹4 lakh crore, what is the primary deficit?
Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments, so 6 − 4 = ₹2 lakh crore.
Which of these is a capital receipt?
Borrowings create a liability for the government, so they are capital receipts. Taxes and dividends are revenue receipts.
Which of these is revenue expenditure?
Salaries do not create assets or reduce liabilities, so they are revenue expenditure. The other items create assets or reduce liabilities.
Revenue expenditure is 15 and revenue receipts are 12 (same units). What is the revenue deficit?
Revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, which gives 15 − 12 = 3.
faqs: Why is fiscal deficit considered the most important deficit?

Fiscal deficit shows the total amount the government needs to borrow in a year, which affects public debt, interest burden and pressure on interest rates in the economy. That is why governments announce fiscal deficit targets as a percentage of GDP and why rating agencies watch it closely.
Do I need current budget numbers for exams?

For RBI Grade B and bank mains, questions on the latest budget's deficit targets and major announcements are common, but they count as current affairs. Learn definitions from this page and update numbers from the official budget documents for the year of your exam.

items.title: Important Financial Regulators and Bodies of India
items.description: Static GA on India's financial regulators and institutions: SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank, NHB, NPCI and DICGC, with roles and headquarters.
items.intro: Questions on regulators and development financial institutions are a staple of RBI Grade B, IBPS and SBI mains, JAIIB, CAIIB, SSC General Awareness and bank interviews. Typical questions ask which body regulates what, where it is headquartered and when it was set up. These facts change rarely, so a well-organised note covers many marks. Leadership names do change, so treat those as current affairs and check them separately.

concepts.heading: Financial sector regulators
concepts.text: RBI (Mumbai) regulates banks, NBFCs and payment systems. SEBI (Mumbai), set up in 1988 and made statutory by the SEBI Act, 1992, regulates securities markets. IRDAI (Hyderabad), under the IRDA Act, 1999, regulates insurance. PFRDA (New Delhi) regulates pension funds and the National Pension System and became statutory under the PFRDA Act, 2013.

concepts.heading: Development financial institutions
concepts.text: NABARD (Mumbai, 1982) supports agriculture and rural development and refinances rural lending. SIDBI (Lucknow, 1990) supports micro, small and medium enterprises. EXIM Bank (Mumbai, 1982) finances and promotes exports and imports. NHB (New Delhi, 1988) supports housing finance; its regulation of housing finance companies was transferred to the RBI in 2019.

concepts.heading: Payments and deposit protection
concepts.text: NPCI (Mumbai, 2008) is an umbrella organisation for retail payments, operating UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH and others; it was promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association. DICGC (Mumbai, 1978) is an RBI subsidiary that insures bank deposits up to a limit per depositor per bank — ₹5 lakh since 2020; confirm the current limit with DICGC.

concepts.heading: Other key bodies
concepts.text: The Competition Commission of India (New Delhi) enforces the Competition Act, 2002. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (New Delhi) regulates insolvency professionals under the IBC, 2016. The Indian Banks' Association (Mumbai) represents banks. IIBF (Mumbai) conducts JAIIB and CAIIB.

concepts.heading: Ministry and departments
