concepts.text: The Department of Financial Services in the Ministry of Finance handles banks, insurance and pension policy, and the Department of Economic Affairs handles the budget and capital-market policy. Knowing which department owns which policy helps in interview questions.

concepts.heading: How to remember who regulates what
concepts.text: Follow the product. A bank deposit, loan or UPI payment points to the RBI; a share, mutual fund or bond issue points to SEBI; a life, health or motor policy points to IRDAI; an NPS or APY account points to PFRDA. Interviewers often give a customer situation and ask which regulator a complaint should finally go to, so practise mapping everyday products to their regulator rather than memorising the list alone.

shortcuts: Mumbai: RBI, SEBI, NABARD, EXIM Bank, NPCI, DICGC, IBA, IIBF.
Hyderabad: IRDAI. Lucknow: SIDBI. New Delhi: PFRDA, NHB, CCI, IBBI.
1982 twins: NABARD and EXIM Bank.
SEBI: set up 1988, statutory 1992.
DICGC is a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI.
Heads of these bodies change; check names separately as current affairs.

examples.question: A complaint about an insurance company's claim rejection — which regulator oversees insurers?
examples.solution: IRDAI, headquartered in Hyderabad. The customer can also approach the Insurance Ombudsman after first complaining to the insurer.

examples.question: Which institution would refinance a cooperative bank's crop loans?
examples.solution: NABARD, which provides refinance to rural financial institutions for agricultural and rural lending.

examples.question: A customer has ₹7 lakh in a savings account and ₹3 lakh in a fixed deposit at the same bank. How much is insured by DICGC, assuming a ₹5 lakh limit?
examples.solution: The limit applies per depositor per bank, combining principal and interest across accounts in the same capacity. Total ₹10 lakh, so ₹5 lakh is insured (under the ₹5 lakh limit in force since 2020).

examples.question: Which body operates UPI?
examples.solution: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), headquartered in Mumbai.

examples.question: A customer's mutual fund distributor mis-sold a scheme. Which regulator oversees mutual funds?
examples.solution: SEBI regulates mutual funds and their distribution rules, while AMFI, the industry body, registers distributors. The customer should first complain to the fund house and can then use SEBI's SCORES complaint system.

practice: Where is the headquarters of IRDAI?
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India is headquartered in Hyderabad. Most other financial regulators are in Mumbai or New Delhi.
Which institution primarily supports micro, small and medium enterprises?
The Small Industries Development Bank of India, headquartered in Lucknow, is the principal financial institution for the MSME sector.
Which organisation operates UPI, IMPS and RuPay?
The National Payments Corporation of India runs retail payment systems including UPI, IMPS, RuPay and NACH.
When did SEBI get statutory powers?
SEBI was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body and gained statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992.
DICGC, which insures bank deposits, is a subsidiary of which body?
The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India.
faqs: Do I need to know the heads of these bodies?

Yes for RBI Grade B, bank mains and interviews, but names change, so treat them as current affairs. Note the current RBI Governor, SEBI Chairperson, IRDAI Chairperson and similar from official websites shortly before your exam, separately from these static facts.
Is NHB still the regulator of housing finance companies?

No. Since 2019, housing finance companies are regulated by the RBI, while NHB continues to supervise them and provide refinance. Older study material may still describe NHB as the regulator, which is outdated.

items.title: Banking Awareness for Interviews: Key Terms Explained
items.description: Banking terms every bank-exam interview expects: CASA, NIM, NPA, provision coverage, CRAR, priority sector lending, KYC, SARFAESI and IBC, explained simply.
items.intro: Bank interviews for IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and specialist posts almost always test basic banking awareness: what a bank earns from, how bad loans are classified, why capital matters. The same terms appear in mains General Awareness, JAIIB and CAIIB. Interviewers care less about memorised definitions than about whether you can explain a term in plain words with an example. This page covers the static concepts; ratios and limits change, so confirm current figures from RBI circulars.

concepts.heading: CASA and cost of funds
concepts.text: CASA is the share of current and savings account deposits in total deposits. These deposits pay low or no interest, so a higher CASA ratio lowers a bank's cost of funds. Example: if a bank has ₹300 crore of CASA out of ₹1,000 crore deposits, its CASA ratio is 30%.

concepts.heading: Net interest margin
concepts.text: NIM measures how much a bank earns from lending and investing over what it pays on deposits and borrowings, relative to its earning assets. It is a core indicator of profitability for a lending business.

concepts.heading: Non-performing assets
concepts.text: A loan generally becomes an NPA when interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days. NPAs are classified as substandard, doubtful and loss assets depending on how long they remain non-performing. Gross NPA is before provisions; net NPA subtracts provisions held.

concepts.heading: Provisioning and capital
concepts.text: Provision coverage ratio shows how much of gross NPAs is covered by provisions. Capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) measures a bank's capital against its risk exposure, following the Basel III framework as implemented by the RBI. Higher capital means a bank can absorb more losses.

concepts.heading: Priority sector lending
concepts.text: The RBI requires banks to lend a portion of their adjusted net bank credit to priority sectors such as agriculture, MSMEs, education, housing and weaker sections, with sub-targets. Domestic scheduled commercial banks have an overall target of 40%; check the RBI master direction for current targets.

concepts.heading: Recovery laws and KYC
concepts.text: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 lets secured lenders take possession of and sell secured assets without court intervention. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 provides a time-bound resolution process through the NCLT. KYC norms under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act require banks to verify customer identity and address and to update records periodically.

shortcuts: NPA trigger: overdue for more than 90 days.
High CASA = cheaper funds = better margins.
Gross NPA − provisions = net NPA (in simple terms).
SARFAESI = enforce security without court; IBC = resolve insolvency through NCLT.
Priority sector overall target for domestic SCBs: 40% of ANBC (verify current norms).
In interviews, define the term, give a one-line example, and add why it matters to a bank.

examples.question: Interview: 'What is CASA and why do banks want a high CASA ratio?'
examples.solution: CASA is the share of current and savings deposits in total deposits. These deposits cost less than fixed deposits, so a bank with a higher CASA ratio has lower funding costs and can lend competitively while protecting its margin. Example: ₹300 crore CASA out of ₹1,000 crore deposits is a 30% ratio.

examples.question: A borrower's EMI due on 1 June remains unpaid. Roughly when would the loan be classified as an NPA if nothing is paid?
examples.solution: Once the amount stays overdue for more than 90 days, the account becomes an NPA, so around the end of August or beginning of September, based on the RBI's day-end classification rules.

examples.question: A bank has gross NPAs of ₹120 crore and provisions of ₹45 crore. What is its approximate net NPA and provision coverage?
examples.solution: Net NPA ≈ 120 − 45 = ₹75 crore. Provision coverage ratio ≈ 45 ÷ 120 = 37.5% (ignoring technical write-offs for simplicity).

examples.question: Interview: 'How is SARFAESI different from IBC?'
examples.solution: SARFAESI is a tool for secured creditors to recover dues by taking over and selling collateral without going to court. IBC is a broader insolvency process, run through the NCLT, that tries to resolve the whole company, often by finding a new owner, within a time limit.

practice: After how many days of non-payment does a loan generally become an NPA?
Under RBI norms, a loan is generally classified as non-performing when interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days.
A bank has ₹300 crore in current and savings deposits out of total deposits of ₹1,000 crore. What is its CASA ratio?
CASA ratio equals CASA deposits divided by total deposits, so 300 ÷ 1,000 = 30%.
Which law allows secured lenders to take possession of collateral without court intervention?
The SARFAESI Act, 2002 empowers secured creditors to enforce their security interest and recover dues without approaching a court.
Which international framework guides capital adequacy norms for Indian banks?
The RBI implements the Basel III framework for capital adequacy, which sets minimum capital and buffer requirements for banks.
Under the IBC, which body hears corporate insolvency cases?
Corporate insolvency resolution under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is handled by the National Company Law Tribunal.
faqs: How should I prepare banking awareness for an interview?

Pick about 40 core terms — CASA, NIM, NPA, PCR, CRAR, repo, CRR, SLR, priority sector, KYC, SARFAESI, IBC and similar — and practise explaining each in two or three sentences with an example. Add recent developments from RBI press releases. Interviewers value clarity and accuracy over long memorised answers.
Will interviewers ask for exact current ratios?

Sometimes, especially in RBI and PO interviews. Keep a short note of current figures such as the repo rate, CRR, SLR and the system's gross NPA level from the latest RBI Financial Stability Report, and be ready to say 'as per the latest RBI data' when quoting them.

items.title: Payment Systems in India: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI and More
items.description: Static notes on Indian payment systems for bank exams: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI, NACH, CTS, AePS and BBPS — who runs them, timings and how they differ.
items.intro: Payment systems are a frequent topic in RBI Grade B, IBPS and SBI mains, JAIIB and CAIIB, and bank interviews, where candidates may be asked to compare NEFT with RTGS or explain how UPI works. The core facts — which system is run by whom, whether settlement is in batches or real time, and what each is used for — are stable. Transaction limits and charges change more often, so confirm them from the RBI or NPCI before quoting numbers.

concepts.heading: Legal and institutional framework
concepts.text: The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 gives the RBI powers to regulate and supervise payment systems. The RBI itself runs NEFT and RTGS. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) runs retail systems such as IMPS, UPI, NACH, RuPay, AePS, BBPS and the cheque truncation system.

concepts.heading: NEFT and RTGS
concepts.text: NEFT settles transactions in half-hourly batches and has no minimum amount. RTGS settles each transaction individually and in real time, and is meant for large-value payments with a minimum of ₹2 lakh. Both have been available 24×7 since NEFT went round-the-clock in December 2019 and RTGS in December 2020.

concepts.heading: IMPS and UPI
concepts.text: IMPS, launched in 2010, allows instant 24×7 interbank transfers using account number and IFSC or mobile number. UPI, launched in 2016, builds on IMPS rails and lets users pay using a virtual payment address or QR code from a single app linked to multiple bank accounts.

concepts.heading: Bulk and cheque systems
concepts.text: NACH handles bulk and repetitive payments such as salary credits, dividends, EMIs and subsidy transfers. The Cheque Truncation System (CTS) clears cheques using images instead of moving physical cheques.

concepts.heading: Inclusion-focused systems
concepts.text: AePS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System) lets customers withdraw cash or check balances at a business correspondent using Aadhaar authentication. BBPS (Bharat Bill Payment System) offers a single interoperable platform for paying utility and other recurring bills.

concepts.heading: Cards
concepts.text: RuPay is India's domestic card network, run by NPCI, used for debit cards including PMJDY accounts, and also for some credit cards. RuPay credit cards can be linked to UPI.

shortcuts: RBI runs NEFT and RTGS; NPCI runs IMPS, UPI, NACH, CTS, AePS, BBPS and RuPay.
NEFT = batches; RTGS = real time, gross, minimum ₹2 lakh.
NEFT 24×7 from December 2019; RTGS 24×7 from December 2020.
IMPS 2010; UPI 2016; NPCI 2008.
Payment and Settlement Systems Act: 2007.
Check limits and charges on the RBI and NPCI websites before quoting them.

examples.question: A company must pay a supplier ₹50 lakh with immediate final settlement. Which system is best?
examples.solution: RTGS, because it settles each transaction individually and in real time, and the amount is well above the ₹2 lakh minimum.

examples.question: A student wants to send ₹500 to a friend instantly using only the friend's mobile-linked UPI ID. Which system works?
examples.solution: UPI. It allows instant transfers using a virtual payment address without sharing account numbers, around the clock.

examples.question: A company pays monthly salaries to 5,000 employees. Which system is designed for this?
examples.solution: NACH (National Automated Clearing House), which processes bulk, repetitive credits and debits such as salaries and EMIs.

examples.question: A rural customer without a smartphone wants to withdraw cash from her bank account at a village business correspondent. Which system helps?
examples.solution: AePS, which authenticates the customer through Aadhaar biometrics at the business correspondent's micro-ATM.

examples.question: A customer sends ₹10,000 through NEFT at 11:50 p.m. on a Sunday. Will it be processed?
examples.solution: Yes. NEFT has run 24×7, including holidays, since December 2019, and settles in half-hourly batches, so the payment goes out in the next batch. Before 2019, NEFT worked only during banking hours on working days.

practice: Which payment system settles each transaction individually and in real time for large values?
RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement. Each transaction is settled individually as it occurs, with a minimum amount of ₹2 lakh.
UPI is operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, which also runs IMPS, NACH and RuPay.
Which Act governs payment and settlement systems in India?
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 empowers the RBI to regulate and supervise payment systems in India.
Which system is designed for bulk, repetitive payments such as salaries and EMIs?
NACH (National Automated Clearing House) processes high-volume, repetitive credits and debits like salaries, dividends and loan EMIs.
In which year was UPI launched?
UPI was launched by NPCI in 2016. IMPS, on which UPI builds, had been launched earlier in 2010.
faqs: Is UPI regulated by the RBI or NPCI?

NPCI operates UPI, but the RBI regulates payment systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and NPCI itself is authorised by the RBI. So operational rules come from NPCI, while overall regulation and policy direction come from the RBI.
Why are UPI limits different in different sources?

NPCI and the RBI have revised limits for certain categories, such as tax payments, hospitals and education, and banks may set their own lower limits. Always check the latest NPCI circulars or your bank's page for current limits instead of relying on older notes.

items.title: Constitutional Bodies and Key Articles for GA Sections
items.description: Static GA on India's constitutional bodies and key Articles: Finance Commission, CAG, Election Commission, UPSC, GST Council, Attorney General and more.
items.intro: Constitutional bodies and important Articles appear in SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS General Awareness almost every year, and in RBI Grade B and bank mains through questions on financial bodies like the Finance Commission and GST Council. The Article numbers and functions of these bodies change only through constitutional amendments, so they are reliable static marks. Pair each body with its Article and one key function, and most questions become simple recall.

concepts.heading: Financial bodies
concepts.text: Finance Commission (Article 280): constituted every five years or earlier by the President to recommend how central taxes are shared with states and among states. Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148): audits the accounts of the Union and states. GST Council (Article 279A, added by the 101st Amendment, 2016): recommends GST rates and rules; chaired by the Union Finance Minister.

concepts.heading: Electoral and service bodies
concepts.text: Election Commission (Article 324): superintends elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. Union Public Service Commission (Article 315 onwards): conducts recruitment to all-India and central services. State Public Service Commissions are also covered from Article 315.

concepts.heading: Law officers
concepts.text: Attorney General of India (Article 76): the highest law officer of the Union government. Advocate General of a state (Article 165): the state's highest law officer.

concepts.heading: Commissions for specific groups
concepts.text: National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338), National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A) and National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B, given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment).

concepts.heading: Financial provisions
concepts.text: Article 110: definition of Money Bill. Article 112: Annual Financial Statement (budget). Article 266: Consolidated Fund. Article 267: Contingency Fund. Article 360: financial emergency. Article 263: Inter-State Council.

concepts.heading: Statutory versus constitutional
concepts.text: Constitutional bodies are created by the Constitution itself, such as the Election Commission and the CAG. Statutory bodies are created by Acts of Parliament, such as SEBI and the National Human Rights Commission. Some bodies are neither: NITI Aayog was created in 2015 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet. Exams often ask which category a body belongs to.

shortcuts: 280 = Finance Commission; 148 = CAG; 324 = Election Commission; 315 = UPSC.
279A = GST Council (101st Amendment); 76 = Attorney General.
338, 338A, 338B = SC, ST and Backward Classes commissions.
110 Money Bill, 112 Budget, 266 Consolidated Fund, 267 Contingency Fund, 360 Financial Emergency.
NITI Aayog: executive resolution (2015), replacing the Planning Commission.
Link each Article with one function; recall improves when facts are paired.

examples.question: Which constitutional body recommends the share of states in central taxes?
examples.solution: The Finance Commission under Article 280. Its recommendations cover vertical sharing (centre to states) and horizontal sharing (among states).

examples.question: Who chairs the GST Council, and under which Article is it constituted?
examples.solution: The Union Finance Minister chairs it. It is constituted under Article 279A, inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment, 2016.

examples.question: Is NITI Aayog a constitutional body?
examples.solution: No. It was set up in 2015 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet, replacing the Planning Commission. It is neither constitutional nor statutory.

examples.question: Which Article deals with financial emergency?
examples.solution: Article 360. It allows the President to proclaim a financial emergency if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has never been used so far.

examples.question: Classify as constitutional or statutory: Election Commission, SEBI, UPSC, National Green Tribunal.
examples.solution: The Election Commission (Article 324) and UPSC (Article 315) are constitutional. SEBI (SEBI Act, 1992) and the National Green Tribunal (NGT Act, 2010) are statutory, created by Acts of Parliament.

practice: Under which Article is the Finance Commission constituted?
Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, which recommends the distribution of tax revenues between the centre and the states.
Which Article provides for the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
Article 148 establishes the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General, who audits government accounts.
The GST Council was created by inserting which Article?
The 101st Constitutional Amendment, 2016 inserted Article 279A to create the GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
Which Article deals with the Election Commission?
Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India.
NITI Aayog was set up in 2015 through a resolution of the Union Cabinet. It is therefore neither a constitutional nor a statutory body.
faqs: How many Articles should I memorise for SSC GA?

Focus on 40 to 60 high-frequency Articles: fundamental rights (12–35), directive principles basics, key offices (President, Prime Minister, Parliament), financial provisions and constitutional bodies. Learning them in groups with one function each is more effective than memorising a long numbered list.
Are commission heads and members asked?

Names of current heads, such as the Chief Election Commissioner or the chair of the current Finance Commission, are asked as current affairs. Note them separately from official sources close to your exam date, since they change over time.

items.title: Money Market vs Capital Market Instruments in India
items.description: Money market and capital market basics for bank exams: T-bills, CPs, CDs, call money, TREPS, G-secs, bonds and shares, with tenors and regulators.
items.intro: Financial markets questions are common in RBI Grade B (Finance and GA), IBPS and SBI mains, JAIIB, CAIIB and NISM-adjacent interviews. The basic split is simple: the money market deals in short-term funds of up to one year, the capital market in long-term funds. Exams ask about tenors, issuers and regulators of instruments such as treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit, which are stable facts worth learning once.

concepts.heading: Money market versus capital market
concepts.text: The money market handles borrowing and lending for up to one year and is regulated mainly by the RBI. The capital market handles long-term funds through equity and debt securities and is regulated mainly by SEBI (with the RBI for government securities).

concepts.heading: Treasury bills
concepts.text: T-bills are short-term government debt issued by the RBI on behalf of the central government in three tenors: 91, 182 and 364 days. They are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value; the difference is the investor's return.

concepts.heading: Commercial paper and certificates of deposit
concepts.text: Commercial paper (CP) is an unsecured promissory note issued by companies and other eligible entities, with maturity from 7 days to one year. Certificates of deposit (CDs) are issued by banks (7 days to one year) and certain financial institutions (one to three years), in dematerialised form.

concepts.heading: Call, notice and term money
concepts.text: Call money is borrowing for one day (overnight); notice money for 2 to 14 days; term money for 15 days to one year. These markets mainly involve banks and primary dealers.

concepts.heading: Repo and TREPS
concepts.text: In a market repo, one party sells securities with an agreement to buy them back later, effectively borrowing against collateral. TREPS (Tri-party Repo Dealing and Settlement), run by the Clearing Corporation of India, is a widely used collateralised short-term borrowing platform.

concepts.heading: Capital market instruments
concepts.text: Equity shares give ownership and variable returns through dividends and price changes. Debentures and bonds are debt with fixed or floating interest. Government securities (G-secs) are long-term central government bonds; state development loans are state government bonds. Primary markets handle new issues; secondary markets handle trading.

shortcuts: Money market: up to 1 year; capital market: more than 1 year.
T-bills: 91, 182, 364 days, issued at a discount.
CP: companies, 7 days–1 year, unsecured.
CD: banks 7 days–1 year; FIs 1–3 years.
Call money = 1 day; notice money = 2–14 days; term money = 15 days–1 year.
SEBI regulates securities markets; the RBI regulates money markets and G-sec markets.
Primary market = new issues (IPO, new bond issue); secondary market = trading of existing securities on exchanges.

examples.question: A 91-day T-bill with face value ₹100 is issued at ₹98.50. What is the approximate annualised yield?
A large company needs funds for 90 days to manage working capital. Which money market instrument can it issue?
examples.solution: Commercial paper, an unsecured short-term promissory note that eligible companies can issue for 7 days to one year.

examples.question: A bank borrows from another bank for one day. Which market is this?
examples.solution: The call money market, which covers overnight borrowing and lending between banks and primary dealers.

examples.question: Is a 10-year government bond a money market or capital market instrument?
examples.solution: Capital market, because its maturity is more than one year. G-secs of long tenor form a major part of India's debt capital market.

examples.question: A bank wants to raise funds for six months from institutional investors through a negotiable instrument. What can it issue?
examples.solution: A certificate of deposit. Banks can issue CDs for 7 days to one year; they are negotiable and held in dematerialised form, unlike ordinary fixed deposits.

practice: Which tenor is NOT used for Indian treasury bills?
Treasury bills in India are issued in 91-day, 182-day and 364-day tenors. A 270-day T-bill is not issued.
Which instrument is an unsecured short-term note issued by companies?
Commercial paper is an unsecured promissory note issued by eligible companies for 7 days to one year.
Borrowing between banks for 2 to 14 days is called:
Notice money covers interbank borrowing for 2 to 14 days. Call money is overnight and term money runs from 15 days to one year.
Which regulator primarily oversees India's securities markets such as shares and corporate bonds?
SEBI regulates securities markets, including equity and corporate bond issuance and trading. The RBI handles money markets and government securities.
At face value with monthly interest
At a discount to face value
Treasury bills are zero-coupon instruments issued below face value and redeemed at face value, so the discount is the investor's return.
faqs: What is the difference between a CD and a fixed deposit?

Both are bank deposits, but a certificate of deposit is a negotiable, dematerialised instrument that can be traded in the secondary market and is usually issued in large denominations to institutional investors. A fixed deposit is non-negotiable and is typically held by retail customers until maturity or premature withdrawal.
Who can invest in T-bills now?

Banks, financial institutions, companies and individuals can invest. Retail investors can participate through the RBI Retail Direct platform and through their brokers via non-competitive bidding. Check the RBI Retail Direct website for current processes.

items.title: Indian Economy Basics: GDP, GVA, Inflation, CPI and WPI
items.description: Static Indian economy concepts for exams: GDP, GVA and GNP, nominal versus real growth, CPI versus WPI, types of inflation, fiscal and monetary policy.
items.intro: Basic economy concepts are tested across RBI Grade B, IBPS and SBI mains, SSC CGL and CHSL, CMAT and bank interviews. The questions are rarely about this year's figures alone; they ask what GDP measures, why the RBI tracks CPI rather than WPI, or how real growth differs from nominal growth. These concepts are stable, so they are worth learning properly. Base years and data series are revised from time to time, so check MoSPI and the Office of the Economic Adviser for the current base years.

concepts.heading: GDP, GNP and NNP
concepts.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a period. Gross National Product (GNP) adds net factor income from abroad (earnings of residents abroad minus earnings of foreigners in India). Net National Product (NNP) subtracts depreciation from GNP.

concepts.heading: GVA
concepts.text: Gross Value Added (GVA) measures output by sector — agriculture, industry, services — at basic prices. GDP equals GVA plus product taxes minus product subsidies. GVA is useful for seeing which sectors drive growth.

concepts.heading: Nominal and real
concepts.text: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant prices of a base year, removing inflation. If nominal GDP grows 10% and inflation (measured by the GDP deflator) is 4%, real growth is roughly 6%.

concepts.heading: CPI and WPI
concepts.text: The Consumer Price Index measures retail price changes for households and is compiled by the National Statistics Office under MoSPI. The Wholesale Price Index measures wholesale prices and is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. The RBI's inflation target is based on headline CPI.

concepts.heading: Types of inflation
concepts.text: Demand-pull inflation comes from demand exceeding supply; cost-push from rising input costs like fuel. Stagflation combines high inflation with low growth. Deflation is a sustained fall in prices; disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation while prices still rise.

concepts.heading: Fiscal and monetary policy
concepts.text: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxes and spending, presented through the budget. Monetary policy is the RBI's management of interest rates and liquidity. Both influence growth and inflation, and they work best when aligned.

shortcuts: GDP = inside the borders; GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad.
NNP = GNP − depreciation.
Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation (approximation).
CPI → NSO (MoSPI); WPI → Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT).
Disinflation: inflation slows but stays positive; deflation: prices actually fall.
Check current base years with MoSPI before your exam; they get revised.

examples.question: Nominal GDP grew from ₹220 lakh crore to ₹242 lakh crore. What was nominal growth? If inflation was 4%, what was approximate real growth?
examples.solution: Nominal growth = (242 − 220) ÷ 220 × 100 = 10%. Approximate real growth = 10 − 4 = 6%.

examples.question: Inflation falls from 7.5% to 5% in a year. Is this deflation?
examples.solution: No. Prices are still rising, only more slowly. This is disinflation of 2.5 percentage points. Deflation would mean inflation below zero.

examples.question: A software engineer from India works in the US and sends home earnings. Does this add to India's GDP or GNP?
examples.solution: It is earned abroad, so it is not part of India's GDP. It is factor income from abroad and counts towards India's GNP.

examples.question: Interview: 'Why does the RBI target CPI and not WPI?'
examples.solution: CPI reflects the prices households actually pay, including services and food, so it better represents the cost of living and inflation expectations. WPI covers wholesale goods and excludes most services, making it less relevant for consumers.

practice: Which index is used for the RBI's inflation target?
The flexible inflation targeting framework uses headline CPI inflation, which reflects retail prices paid by households.
GNP adds net factor income from abroad to GDP, capturing income earned by residents outside the country minus income paid to foreigners.
Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is this called?
Prices are still rising, but more slowly, which is disinflation. Deflation would require a negative inflation rate.
Which office compiles the Wholesale Price Index in India?
Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT
WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade.
Nominal GDP grew 10% and inflation was 4%. What is the approximate real growth?
Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation, so 10% − 4% gives about 6% real growth.
faqs: Why do GDP numbers change after release?

Initial GDP estimates are based on partial data and are revised as fuller data arrives, through advance, provisional and revised estimates. Base-year revisions also change the series. For exams, note which estimate a figure refers to and take the latest numbers from MoSPI releases.
Is GVA or GDP better for measuring growth?

Both are used. GVA is better for understanding which sectors are growing, since it measures output at basic prices by industry. GDP includes net product taxes and is the headline measure used internationally. India's official releases report both, and exam questions may ask about either.
